docs.title: Evidence-Driven AI Agent and MCP Security
docs.text:
AI Security · Research

Separate configuration, observed activity, authorization, and exploitability when assessing AI agents and their tools.

An agent security assessment should explain what an agent can reach, which authority it receives, and what evidence supports each conclusion. Counting discovered tools or drawing an impressive relationship graph does not answer those questions.

These findings synthesize source-level research into repository discovery, agent settings, CI workflows, remote MCP assessment, and runtime metadata. They are engineering findings and recommendations, not a claim of production compromise, complete prompt-injection coverage, or tests reproduced in this article. The diagrams are illustrative. See the authorization lab for the separate, bounded controls exercised by this repository.

docs.title: Decision: keep evidence states separate
docs.text:
Configuration, effective permission, observed activity, and inference should remain separate facts. A workflow granting write access is configured authority. A recorded tool call is observed activity. Neither proves that an attack succeeded.

flowchart TD
  C[Repository configuration] --> P[Parse supported formats]
  P --> A[Assets and configured relationships]
  T[Allowlisted runtime metadata] --> O[Observed activity]
  A --> E[Evidence-aware assessment]
  O --> E
  E --> F[Finding with source and limitations]
  E --> U[Unsupported or unknown coverage]

Attach source revision, file location, rule version, evidence state, and limitations to every finding. Preserve conflicting observations rather than silently overwriting a configured edge with an observed edge. A static reference to an external endpoint can establish a configured destination; it does not establish that traffic reached it.

For protocols, use the MCP specification as the primary reference and identify the exact revision during review. A tool server's advertised interface does not establish that its implementation, operator, or returned content is trustworthy.

docs.title: Findings from configuration and workflow analysis
docs.text:
The reviewed detection approach focuses on explicit, inspectable authority:

Evidence Security implication Qualification Package launched without an exact version or image digest Future launches may execute changed code A pin does not prove artifact integrity or benign behavior Literal credential in tool environment, headers, or arguments Secret may be exposed through repository access or diagnostics Detection and redaction can miss unknown formats Non-loopback HTTP tool endpoint Transport lacks TLS protection A loopback exception is not a remote security boundary Broad filesystem root or host mount Tool can potentially reach unrelated material Effective access still depends on identity and runtime policy Privileged container, host namespace, or daemon socket Tool execution may cross the intended isolation boundary Container presence alone is insufficient isolation evidence Unrestricted shell or disabled approval prompts Untrusted planning can acquire broad execution authority Restricting a prompt does not replace deterministic authorization Comment-triggered CI agent with write permissions Attacker-controlled text can reach a privileged automation path Actor checks must cover the actual event and identity model

Treat these as reviewable risk conditions. A configuration detector must not describe an unexecuted prompt injection as a reproduced exploit. The GitHub Actions security reference explains why workflow permissions, untrusted inputs, and dependency pinning require explicit review at the automation boundary.

docs.title: Bound active assessment independently
docs.text:
Passive discovery reads approved sources. Active probing sends requests to a system and needs its own authorization. An authenticated dashboard session is insufficient permission to probe every URL present in a repository.

flowchart TD
  R[Assessment request] --> M{Current membership and permission?}
  M -->|No| D[Deny]
  M -->|Yes| S{Approved target and bounded scope?}
  S -->|No| D
  S -->|Yes| B[Apply request, time, and response budgets]
  B --> P[Run authorized protocol probe]
  P --> E[Record response and uncertainty]
  B --> C[Propagate cancellation]
  C --> E

For a remote MCP authentication check, an unauthenticated protocol response is bounded evidence about that endpoint and request. An accepted initialization does not prove arbitrary tool execution, cross-tenant access, or authentication bypass on every method. Redirect targets, DNS changes, internal address ranges, response sizes, and cancellation need independent controls before enabling server-side requests. This article does not claim those protections are fully implemented in the reviewed code or verified against a live service.

docs.title: Minimize evidence before it becomes durable
docs.text:
Redact credentials before storage, not just in the browser. Keep restricted evidence behind its own read permission. A user who can see a finding title may not be entitled to see the underlying document or transcript.

flowchart TD
  I[Untrusted source or event] --> V[Validate schema and size]
  V --> R[Redact secret-like values]
  R --> S[Store tenant-scoped evidence]
  S --> A{Evidence-read permission?}
  A -->|Yes| T[Render escaped content]
  A -->|No| M[Return metadata without content]

Runtime telemetry should use an explicit allowlist, bounded field lengths, and clear retention policy. Model names, tool names, endpoints, and timestamps can still reveal sensitive operational information even when prompt and response bodies are absent. The OpenTelemetry GenAI conventions are a vocabulary reference, not permission to collect every available attribute.

A new-destination signal is an inference for investigation. Legitimate rollout can produce the same pattern, and missing telemetry can conceal actual activity. Keep severity, evidence confidence, and coverage distinct in both exports and charts.

docs.title: Validation and limitations
docs.text:
A useful validation matrix includes malformed configuration, unknown launchers, mutable action references, plaintext secrets, denied evidence access, cross-tenant identifiers, cancelled jobs, missing telemetry, and active probes without scope. Test successful and denied paths using synthetic inputs and authorized endpoints.

Source review establishes how a design is expressed; it does not reproduce a remote assessment, validate an identity-provider deployment, or establish production safety. Configuration formats evolve, secret redaction is incomplete, and absence of a finding is meaningful only within the declared parser and rule coverage. Full source review and protocol-version confirmation remain required before promoting this article's review status.

docs.title: Research question and hypothesis
docs.text:
Question: Can an assessment keep configured capability, attempted activity and executed authority distinct?

Falsifiable hypothesis (bounded experiment): A proposed call rejected by the broker has no executor side effect and is recorded as a denial; any report that calls it execution overstates the evidence.

docs.title: Method and evidence requirements
docs.text:
Follow the evidence standards. The related lab owns setup, prerequisites, expected output, safety, evidence collection and teardown. From repository root:

node --test labs/ai-agent-security/tests/broker.test.js

This command is a tested local check, with the scope below. Review test inputs and failure assertions before interpreting a pass. For a deployment study, capture exact versions/configuration, one allowed control, every intended denial, state before/after and independent audit evidence. A policy file or syntax check is T1, not enforcement proof. Do not deploy cloud resources from repository validation.

docs.text: Claim class Evidence tier and boundary Observed local result T2/T3 within the linked harness: The broker test provides a local decision/execution distinction. The SSRF study supplies a separate URL-tool boundary and does not establish real model exploitability. Architecture explanation in this article T0: sourced explanation or engineering judgment under its stated assumptions Configuration/schema examples At most T1 unless a linked runtime test explicitly covers that example Production effectiveness Not established by this repository's local result

docs.title: Practical guidance and failure containment
docs.text:
Preserve unknown states and source revisions rather than deriving exploitability from a graph edge. Apply minimization before durable storage, and scope active tests independently.

Count exercised allow/deny cases against the declared corpus, keeping structural, native-policy and runtime results separate. Preserve failure, unknown and missing telemetry states. Roll back the exact reviewed control change while retaining evidence; broad privilege or global bypass is not an automatic recovery path.

docs.title: Limitations and what was not tested
docs.text:
The local experiment does not validate the complete reference architecture, live cloud enforcement, hosted CI, production data, independent audit storage or representative adversarial coverage. Retained implementation and historical source-inspection descriptions are not newly reproduced results. Review status remains requires-review until a reviewer rechecks the retained product claims against validatedAgainst and the linked evidence.

Time to detect, time to contain, population false-positive/negative rates, pipeline impact and monthly operational cost are not measured in this article. Use the measurement contract to define clocks, denominators, repeated workloads and residual capabilities before claiming those outcomes. Report local fixture counts separately from live coverage.

docs.title: MCP Tool Authorization Lab: A Gateway That Holds When the Model Does Not
docs.text:
AI Security · Research

A policy gateway between an agent runtime and a mock MCP-style server, tested against a stand-in agent that obeys every injected instruction, covering allowlists, scoped identity, taint, approval gates, descriptor pinning, output validation and tamper-evident audit.

When an agent can call tools, the question that matters is not "will the model behave?" but "what happens when it does not?". A model that reads a hostile document may be instructed to call a tool it was never meant to use. This study builds a gateway that answers by construction: every proposed call passes a deterministic decision made from identity the model cannot supply, and the test agent is a stand-in that obeys every instruction it finds in tool output, so a passing test does not depend on the model resisting anything.

There is no language model in this lab. NaiveAgent is a deterministic worst-case stand-in for a compromised planner, not a model and not a claim about any model. It cannot show whether a real model is injectable, how often, or how well a prompt or classifier resists. No LLM API is contacted and no credential is used. The tool server is a local child process whose every effect is an in-memory array append; all data is synthetic.

Evidence labels: tested locally (executed here; output in the lab's evidence/), policy model (decision logic evaluated against a stand-in, not a real model or identity provider), source-reviewed (read in the named primary source), requires-review (no independent reviewer yet). They map to T2/T3, T1, T0 and review status in the evidence standards. This article extends, and does not repeat, the external tool-broker lab (action-bound approval, replay resistance) and the broader agent and MCP evidence article; URL-fetching tools are covered by the SSRF lab.

docs.title: Scope
docs.text: The authorization decision for an agent-proposed tool call: which tools exist, whose authority applies, when a human must decide, what a tool may return, and what is recorded. Out of scope: authenticating users or agents (the context is a trusted input), token issuance and exchange, the MCP authorization specification, transport security, sandboxing the tool server, and any real model behaviour.

docs.title: What I built
docs.text:
The code is in the mcp-tool-authorization lab: a mock stdio server (tools/list, tools/call; five tools; five failure modes), the gateway, a hash-chained audit log, a stand-in agent, 35 mechanism tests and a 16-scenario decision matrix.

flowchart LR
  U["User<br/>authenticated, holds scopes"] --> RT["Agent runtime<br/>context: user, agent, session"]
  RT --> M["Model or stand-in<br/>proposes a call"]
  M -->|"tool name + arguments only"| GW
  subgraph GW["Policy gateway: the only path to a tool"]
    direction TB
    A1["allowlist + descriptor pin"] --> A2["closed schema + strict path or recipient"]
    A2 --> A3["authority = user scopes AND agent scopes"]
    A3 --> A4{"risk class and session taint"}
    A4 -->|"deny"| DEN["deny with a reason code"]
    A4 -->|"needs a human"| APR["approval request<br/>bound to the exact action"]
    A4 -->|"allow"| LOGA["audit the decision first"]
  end
  APR --> H["Human approver<br/>separate surface, policy-listed ids"]
  H -->|"approve once or refuse"| GW
  LOGA --> S["Tool server<br/>local stdio child"]
  S --> OV["output validation<br/>text only, size, controls, links, schema"]
  OV -->|"tool output is untrusted: taints the session"| RT
  DEN --> LOG[("audit log<br/>hash chain")]
  LOGA --> LOG
  OV --> LOG
  H --> LOG

Status: tested locally. Every box is a function in gateway.js; the stand-in agent and the approval surface are separate objects, and the agent holds no reference to either the approval function or the log.

The trust boundaries the design relies on:

flowchart TD
  subgraph TRUSTED["Decided outside the model"]
    ID["identity: user, tenant, scopes, agent id, session"]
    POL["policy: allowlist, pinned descriptors, egress allowlist, risk classes"]
    APP["approvers: policy-listed human ids"]
  end
  subgraph UNTRUSTED["Never trusted to decide anything"]
    MODEL["model output: tool names and arguments"]
    TOOLOUT["tool output: text, links, annotations"]
    DESC["server-advertised descriptors until pinned"]
  end
  MODEL -->|"proposal"| CHECK["gateway checks"]
  TOOLOUT -.->|"taints session, can change what is gated"| CHECK
  DESC -.->|"must hash to a reviewed pin"| CHECK
  ID --> CHECK
  POL --> CHECK
  APP --> CHECK

docs.title: Control decisions
docs.text: Control What it stops What it does not Evidence Tool allowlist plus descriptor pin Calling an unreviewed tool; a description or schema silently changed after review A malicious tool whose reviewed behaviour is malicious tested locally: shell_exec, __proto__, constructor denied; rug-pull quarantined Closed schema, strict paths and recipients Smuggled arguments (cc, an identity field, __proto__), traversal, multi-recipient strings Semantically harmful values that are well-formed tested locally: 9 schema and 8 path cases, none repaired into a match Authority = user AND agent scopes A confused deputy in either direction A user and an agent who both hold too much tested locally: private note denied when only the user (or only the agent) holds the scope Destination allowlist behind scopes Exfiltration when scopes are over-broad (email:send:*) An allowed destination that is itself attacker-controlled tested locally: both layers exercised independently Taint plus risk gating A write or deletion proposed after untrusted content entered the context Harm that needs no tool call tested locally; the taint input is a modeling assumption (below) Approval bound to the exact action Replay, argument swap after approval, approval by the agent, expired approval, reviewer flooding A reviewer who approves what they should not tested locally Output validation Oversize or control-character output, non-text content, undeclared structured fields, off-allowlist links Persuasive false text tested locally Audit before execute, hash chain An unrecorded effect; editing or deleting a record in the middle Tail truncation (documented gap) tested locally

docs.title: Research question and hypothesis
docs.text:
Question: Does a deterministic gateway keep tool authority independent of a compromised model's behaviour, and does every decision leave a verifiable record?

Falsifiable hypothesis (bounded experiment): With a stand-in that obeys every injected instruction, no denied or unapproved call produces a side effect on the independent observation channel, every decision (allow, deny, approval required) has an audit record whose chain verifies, and every reason code the gateway can emit is exercised by a test. One observed side effect without an allow, an unrecorded decision, or an unexercised reason code refutes it.

docs.title: Research threat model
docs.text: Element Declared scope Actor Text the model reads (a note, an email, a web page) that carries instructions; a tool server that changes after review; a model that follows both Assets Data the user can read, the ability to send data out, the ability to delete, and the integrity of the record of what happened Entry points Tool names and arguments proposed by the model; tool descriptors; tool results Trust boundaries Model → gateway → tool server; user and agent identity (trusted input here); the human approver Impact under investigation Exfiltration to an unlisted recipient, a destructive call, privilege borrowed across user and agent, an unrecorded effect Trusted assumptions The runtime supplies correct user, agent and session identity; the approver surface is not reachable by the model; the gateway process is not compromised; a real model's behaviour is not modeled

docs.title: Method and evidence requirements
docs.text:
Follow the evidence standards (AI agent row: principal and delegation map, untrusted-input entry, tool schema and authorization, denied tool invocation, egress decisions, bounded evidence retention; simulated tool calls distinguished from a real model run). The lab owns setup, prerequisites, expected output, safety, evidence collection and teardown. From repository root:

node --test labs/mcp-tool-authorization/tests/gateway.test.js

This command is a tested local check with the scope below. Review the test inputs and the failure assertions before interpreting a pass. The decision matrix is produced by node labs/mcp-tool-authorization/scripts/run-scenarios.js, where each step's expected decision, reason and side-effect count are declared before the step runs. A policy file or a passing test is T1/T2 evidence about this gateway, not about a deployment. Do not deploy cloud resources from repository validation.

docs.title: How the lab maps to the specification's security statements
docs.text:
Read in the MCP specification source, revision 2025-11-25 (source-reviewed). The gateway is a client-side control layer; it does not rely on the server doing its part.

Specification statement (paraphrased) Where it lands here Servers MUST validate inputs, implement access controls, rate limit and sanitize outputs The gateway enforces all four independently, so a server that fails any of them is still bounded Clients SHOULD prompt for confirmation on sensitive operations and show inputs before calling Approval gating; the summary shown to the human is built from the actual arguments, never from model text Clients SHOULD validate tool results before passing them to the model Output validation; rejected output is withheld Clients SHOULD implement timeouts and log tool usage Per-request timeout; every decision is audited before the call runs Clients MUST treat tool annotations as untrusted unless the server is trusted Annotations are never an input to a decision; the whole descriptor is pinned instead Servers MUST return structured results that conform to a declared outputSchema; clients SHOULD validate them structuredContent is validated against the pinned outputSchema; extra fields and missing content are rejected stdio messages are newline-delimited and MUST NOT contain embedded newlines The mock and the gateway use exactly that framing

docs.title: Validation
docs.text:
Recorded run (evidence/versions.txt): Node.js v22.23.4, Linux 6.18.44, policy version 2026-11-05.1. All tested locally.

Command Observed node scripts/pin.js all pins match for five tools node --test labs/mcp-tool-authorization/tests/gateway.test.js tests 35, pass 35, fail 0 node labs/mcp-tool-authorization/scripts/run-scenarios.js 16 scenarios, 31 proposed calls: 11 allow, 5 approval required, 15 deny; all expectations met; audit chains valid

Selected rows of the decision matrix (full table in evidence/decision-matrix-table.txt; "effects" are observed on the server's stderr channel, separate from the protocol):

Scenario Proposed call Decision Reason Effects Audit seq A1 read_note /workspace/notes/meeting.md allow ALLOWED 0 5 A1 create_ticket after that read (session now holds untrusted content) approval required APPROVAL_REQUIRED 0 6 A1 the same create_ticket, human approved allow ALLOWED_WITH_APPROVAL 1 9 D2 read_note /workspace/notes/../private/salary.md deny PATH_INVALID 0 2 D3 read_note /workspace/private/salary.md (user may, agent not delegated) deny AGENT_SCOPE_DENIED 0 2 D5 send_email to attacker@evil.test with over-broad scopes deny RECIPIENT_NOT_ALLOWED 0 2 I1 injected send_email to an outsider after reading a poisoned note deny RECIPIENT_NOT_ALLOWED 0 4 I2 injected send_email to an allowed recipient approval required, then the human refuses APPROVAL_DENIED 0 6 P1 send_email replayed with the same approval deny APPROVAL_CONSUMED 0 7 T1 delete_note after untrusted content entered the context deny TAINTED_SESSION_DESTRUCTIVE 0 4 R1 read_note after the server changed its description deny DESCRIPTOR_DRIFT 0 5 O1 read_note from a server returning oversize, control-character, non-text output allow, result withheld OUTPUT_INVALID 0 3 U1 approved send_email, server never answers allow, not executed UPSTREAM_TIMEOUT 0 5 L1 any call while the audit log is unavailable deny AUDIT_UNAVAILABLE 0 none (the log is down; the response says it could not record)

docs.title: Findings and interpretation
docs.text: Claim class Evidence tier and boundary The gateway's decisions are independent of the stand-in's behaviour T3, tested locally: injected instructions were obeyed by construction and denied or gated by the gateway No denied or unapproved call had a side effect T2/T3, independent observation channel on all 16 scenarios Every decision has a verifiable audit record T2, hash chain verifies for every scenario A real model would or would not be injectable Not established; not modeled Operating cost of approvals on real reviewers Not tested MCP spec alignment T0, paraphrased from the 2025-11-25 source

docs.title: What the lab found that I did not plan for
docs.text:
1. Two egress layers, and the first one hides the second. My first injection test expected RECIPIENT_NOT_ALLOWED and got USER_SCOPE_DENIED: the user's email:send:example.test scope already excluded the domain, earlier in the pipeline. That is correct, but it meant the gateway's destination allowlist was never exercised. It exists for the realistic mistake of an over-broad scope (email:send:*), so both layers now have their own test, and a third case shows approval cannot widen the allowlist.
  2. Rate-limiting calls punished approvals. I first counted every call that reached the limiter. One email needs a request, possibly a premature retry, and the approved retry: three calls against a limit of two. A rate limit should bound executions; it now does, and a separate cap on pending approvals per agent (3) stops a compromised planner from burying its reviewers instead. Without that cap, moving the limit would have created a new denial-of-attention channel.
  3. A keyword filter is a signal, not a control. The output scan flags ignore previous instructions and CALL tool { patterns. A differently worded note (Ign0re pr1or directives ...) is not flagged, yet the session is tainted anyway, because taint is set by the source of the content, not by recognizing the attack. The control that works is the one that does not require recognizing anything.
  4. A withheld output does not taint the session. If output validation rejects a result, the model never saw it, so there is nothing to taint. The tests assert this; it also means a hostile server that fails validation costs a call, not the session.
  5. The audit chain does not catch tail truncation. Editing a record or deleting one in the middle breaks verification (both tested). Removing the last N records yields a valid shorter chain (also tested, and asserted so the limitation cannot be forgotten). Detecting that needs the head hash anchored somewhere the attacker cannot also rewrite; this lab does not provide one.
  6. Bare directory paths are outside a /** glob. notes:read:/workspace/notes/** does not match /workspace/notes (no trailing component), by design. A tool that lists a directory needs the directory form or a second scope. Easy to get wrong in policy, and a source of "why was this denied" tickets.
  7. The summary shown to the human is a security surface. It is built from the actual arguments (recipient, subject, body length), with control characters stripped, and never from model-written justification text. The test asserts the body text does not appear in it.
  8. My "nothing happened" assertions were not proofs. The tests read side effects from the server's stderr and decisions from its stdout. Those are two pipes with no ordering guarantee between them, so a call could return before its effect line had been read. I found it when the suite, run repeatedly under Node 24, failed a positive assertion in 2 of 8 runs (it had passed on Node 22 six times in a row, which was luck, not immunity). Probing it directly: after an executed call, the effect line was not yet visible for between 0.3% and 28% of calls across repeated 300-call probes on Node 22 and 24 (scheduling-dependent, so no single rate means much; every effect did arrive eventually). The dangerous half is the negative case: assert.deepEqual(effects, []) after a denied call passes just as happily when the effect line is late. A harness that can pass vacuously is worse than no harness in a lab whose claim is "denied means nothing happened". The fix is an ordering barrier, not a sleep. The mock server answers a lab-only lab/barrier request by writing a marker to stderr; stderr is a single ordered pipe, so a harness that has seen the marker has seen every effect written before it. The gateway exposes this as a test seam (upstreamStderrBarrier, a no-op without a stderr observer, not reachable from an agent), the test harness settles after every call, and the scenario runner settles before it measures each step. A dedicated test fails deterministically if the barrier is disabled (checked by disabling it: 6 of 6 runs failed that test, on Node 22 and 24). Residual limits: the barrier proves the harness has observed the server's stderr up to that point, not that the server reports every effect it causes. The mock only reports what its own code paths emit, which is why the effects are in-memory appends I can enumerate.

docs.title: The taint model is an assumption, and a conservative one
docs.text: A real gateway cannot know whether a model's argument was influenced by an injected sentence. The lab therefore taints at session level: any output from a tool marked taintsSession (here, anything reading notes) means later higher-risk calls are gated regardless of what the arguments look like. That is cheap and unforgeable by the model, and it is blunt: after one read, every ticket needs approval (the matrix's ambiguous case A1). Finer-grained provenance tracking would reduce that friction, but it requires the runtime to track data flow through the model, which this lab does not attempt and cannot validate.

docs.title: Optional integration with a real model (not executed)
docs.text:
Wiring a real client means calling gateway.callTool(ctx, name, args) wherever the client would call the server, building ctx from the authenticated session, and exposing visibleTools(ctx) as the tool list. The following is pseudocode for orientation; no real model, SDK or credential was used.

# pseudocode - not executed in this lab
ctx = { user: from_auth(session), agent: from_registry(agent_id), session: { id, tainted: false } }
tools = gateway.visibleTools(ctx)                 # hygiene only; enforcement is in callTool
loop:
    proposal = model.next(messages, tools)        # tool name + arguments, nothing else
    outcome  = gateway.callTool(ctx, proposal.name, proposal.args, approval_id_if_any)
    if outcome.decision == "approval_required": surface outcome.summary to a human, out of band
    messages.append(outcome.result or outcome.reason)   # reason codes, not internals

docs.title: Practical guidance and failure containment
docs.text:
• Decide authority outside the model, from identity the model cannot supply. Everything in this design follows from refusing to read a user, tenant or scope out of tool arguments.
  • Make the gateway the only path to a tool, and pin what you reviewed. A tool added or edited after review should be unreachable until someone reads the diff.
  • Gate by risk class and by provenance of content, and accept the friction: the cost of an unnecessary approval is a click; the cost of a missing one is an unrecorded exfiltration.
  • Fail closed, and say why. Unknown tool, malformed context, invalid policy, failed audit write, unreachable server: each denies or does not run, with a stable reason code.
  • Keep reasons stable and complete. A reason code with no test is a decision nobody has checked; the suite fails if one is added without a test.
  • Roll back by pin or policy, not by relaxing a check. A tool that breaks after a server update is quarantined until its new descriptor is reviewed; do not widen a scope to make a call succeed.

docs.title: What was not tested
docs.text:
• A real language model, real indirect prompt injection, or any measure of how often a model obeys one.
  • Authentication of the user, agent or approver; token validation; the MCP authorization flow; OAuth.
  • A conformant MCP server or client: only initialize, tools/list, tools/call and the list-changed notification are implemented. No pagination, resources, prompts, sampling or tasks.
  • Remote (HTTP) MCP transport and its authorization.
  • A compromised gateway host, a compromised approval UI, or an attacker with access to the audit store; anchoring the audit head.
  • Concurrency, load, and rate-limit behaviour under real traffic; approval fatigue in practice.
  • Sandboxing of the tool server itself; the server in this lab is trusted not to escape its own process.
  • Time to detect and contain, population false-positive rates, and cost: not measured in this article.

docs.title: Production considerations
docs.text:
Rollout. Start in observe mode: run the gateway in front of existing tool calls, log decisions, and enforce nothing, then review what would have been denied or gated. Onboard tools one at a time by reviewing the descriptor and pinning its hash; move a tool to enforcement only after its denial reasons have been triaged. Keep the first approval policy tight (egress and destructive) and widen the "needs a human" set only if you can staff it.

Detection. Alert on: descriptor drift or an unreviewed tool appearing (the rug-pull signal), repeated *_SCOPE_DENIED, PATH_INVALID or RECIPIENT_NOT_ALLOWED from one agent or session (probing), approval floods or TOO_MANY_PENDING_APPROVALS, a hash-chain verification failure, a gap in audit sequence, and OUTPUT_INVALID from a server that was previously quiet. The record holds identities, tool, an argument hash and a redacted preview, never raw bodies.

Operability. The gateway fails closed on an unavailable audit log, which makes the log's availability the tool's availability; size and monitor it accordingly, or accept read-only tools running unlogged by explicit policy. Approvals expire (120 s here); choose a TTL that matches how fast a human responds, and surface the approver queue. Policy and pins are files in version control; a policy change is a reviewed change with a version string that appears in every audit record.

False positives. Expect friction from taint gating: any workflow that reads then writes will ask for approval. Mitigate by narrowing which tools taint, by pre-approving narrow, low-risk write shapes, and by measuring approval volume per week; do not mitigate by removing the gate. Expect pin churn when a legitimate server updates a description. Expect legitimate multi-recipient mail to be rejected by the strict recipient parser and handle it with explicit tools, not looser parsing.

Blast radius. The worst case of a gateway bug is an unauthorized call executing. Keep per-tool rate limits and a destination allowlist as independent layers behind the scopes, keep destructive tools behind both approval and a clean session, and do not give an agent credentials the user does not hold.

Rollback. Set a tool's risk class to a stricter one or remove it from the policy; both take effect on the next call. Re-pin only after reading the descriptor diff. Preserve the audit log across rollback; it is the record of what the agent did while you decided.

docs.title: Limitations and what was not tested
docs.text:
The local experiment validates a decision model against a deterministic stand-in and one mock server. It does not validate the complete reference architecture, a real identity provider, live cloud enforcement, hosted CI, representative adversarial coverage or independent audit storage. Review status remains requires-review until a reviewer checks the claims above against validatedAgainst and the linked evidence.

Time to detect, time to contain, population false-positive and false-negative rates, pipeline overhead and cost are not measured in this article. Use the measurement contract to define clocks, denominators, repeated workloads and residual capabilities before claiming those outcomes.

docs.title: Threat-Driven Security Architecture for AI Agents
docs.text:
Application Security · Research

External authorization, action-bound approval, concurrent local consumption, and bounded tool execution.

The way I think about it: an AI agent is just an untrusted planner sitting inside a normal security system. The model can propose a tool, a target, some parameters, a whole workflow — but a deterministic control plane, not the model, decides whether that proposal is actually allowed. So every effect an agent can have on the outside world should go through a broker that pulls identity and tenant context from outside the model, applies its own resource limits, asks for approval when the stakes are high, and logs the decision before it ever calls a narrowly scoped tool.

System prompts and content filters are not authorization boundaries, and I don't treat them as one.

They're still worth having as defense in depth — they steer behavior and cut down on unsafe output — but neither one tells you who the user is, which tenant they belong to, what they're entitled to, or whether they actually agreed to a transaction. An injected instruction, a poisoned retrieval result, a model that regresses, or an unexpected tool response should never be able to grant a capability on its own.

docs.title: What's actually built here versus what's a design
docs.text:
I want to be upfront about what backs this write-up, because it's easy to blur "I designed this" with "I ran this":

  • The design: the end-to-end architecture, the operational procedures, the deployment patterns, and most of the evaluation cases below are engineering guidance I've worked through carefully — but I haven't validated any of it against a production agent, a real identity provider, a real model, a sandbox, a vector database, or an actual MCP implementation.
  • What I actually ran: the dependency-free labs/ai-agent-security lab, where I execute a local, fake tool through an external broker. I wrote tests that cover both cases that should succeed and cases that should fail — tenant checks, tool checks, amount limits, approval flow, replay, and the kill switch. It makes no network request and does nothing real.
  • Historical source-review record: the preceding revision recorded a primary-source check on 2026-07-23. The 2026-11-02 protocol audit retains that record and keeps implementationStatus: partially-tested, while setting reviewStatus: requires-review pending renewed review of the complete design. Local broker tests establish the bounded behavior described below.

docs.title: The core decision
docs.text:
Adopt a control-plane/data-plane split:

  1. Authenticate the human or workload before model invocation.
  2. Derive principal, tenant, purpose, and entitlements from trusted server-side state.
  3. Treat user input, retrieved content, model output, memory, tool descriptions, and tool results as untrusted data.
  4. Permit the model to emit only a proposed, typed action.
  5. Route every action through an external capability broker.
  6. Authorize the exact principal, tenant, tool, resource, constraints, and current policy version.
  7. Require separate, short-lived, single-use approval for high-impact effects.
  8. Give the selected tool a narrow downstream credential only after approval.
  9. Constrain execution with a sandbox, deny-by-default egress, resource limits, and an independently operated kill switch.
  10. Record the decision and outcome without placing credentials or unnecessary sensitive content in logs.

The point of designing it this way: the model's output is just one more input the broker has to check, never the thing that gets to decide.

docs.title: In scope
docs.text:
• LLM-backed assistants and agents that retrieve data, retain memory, call local or remote tools, use MCP, or coordinate subordinate agents;
  • direct and indirect prompt injection, retrieval and memory poisoning, cross-tenant access, confused-deputy behavior, unsafe output consumption, excessive agency, and model/software supply-chain compromise;
  • identity, authorization, approval, secret delivery, execution isolation, observability, staged rollout, evaluation, and incident response.

docs.title: Not established by this design
docs.text:
• that a model is truthful, deterministic, aligned, unbiased, or free of exploitable behavior;
  • that a content classifier detects every harmful instruction;
  • that a container alone safely executes arbitrary hostile native code;
  • that a generic control list satisfies a particular legal, regulatory, safety, privacy, or sector-specific obligation;
  • that using MCP makes a tool or server trustworthy;
  • that human approval is effective when the reviewer lacks context, time, or a trustworthy interface.

docs.title: Assumptions to validate per deployment
docs.text:
• The identity tier can authenticate users and workloads, resolve current tenant membership, and revoke access within a documented interval.
  • Each protected resource has an authoritative tenant owner and action-specific policy.
  • Downstream systems can enforce authorization again, support idempotency where effects may be retried, and return stable identifiers for audit.
  • The broker, policy store, approval service, secret manager, audit pipeline, and kill-switch path are outside the model's writable boundary.
  • Operators can isolate workloads, revoke credentials, stop queued work, and restore retrieval and memory from known-good versions.
  • Any exception to deny-by-default egress, tenant isolation, or bound approval is explicitly risk-accepted rather than silently delegated to the model.

docs.title: Assets, actors, and security invariants
docs.text:
Primary assets include tenant data, model and retrieval inputs, durable memory, tool credentials, financial or destructive authority, approval records, model artifacts, policy, prompts, audit evidence, and system availability.

Threat actors and fault sources include a malicious user, a tenant that can publish indexed content, a compromised document or website, a malicious tool server, a poisoned model or adapter, an overprivileged integration, a confused deputy, a compromised operator account, and an ordinary model or application failure.

The system should preserve these invariants:

  1. Missing or ambiguous principal, tenant, audience, purpose, tool, or policy context denies execution.
  2. Content cannot create authority. Instructions found in prompts, documents, memory, tool metadata, or tool results never add permissions.
  3. The model runtime never receives an omnibus credential or a credential for an action that has not been authorized.
  4. Every external effect is mediated by the same broker or by a downstream boundary with equivalent controls.
  5. Tenant isolation is enforced on ingestion, retrieval, memory read/write, tool execution, task state, audit access, and deletion.
  6. Approval is bound to the exact action displayed to the approver; a changed target, amount, tenant, tool, or payload requires new approval.
  7. Disabling execution, revoking capability, or isolating a tenant does not depend on cooperation from the model.

docs.title: Architecture and trust boundaries
docs.text:
flowchart LR
  subgraph UZ["Untrusted content zone"]
    U["User or calling service"]
    EXT["Web, email, files, and tool results"]
    R["Tenant-scoped retrieval"]
  end

  subgraph AZ["Agent reasoning zone"]
    C["Context builder with provenance labels"]
    M["Model: untrusted planner"]
    O["Orchestrator: typed proposed call"]
    MW["Memory write gate"]
  end

  subgraph CZ["Trusted control plane"]
    I["Identity gateway"]
    P["Policy and entitlement service"]
    A["Independent approval service"]
    B["Capability and tool broker"]
    K["Execution kill switch"]
    S["Secret manager"]
    L["Security audit pipeline"]
  end

  subgraph EZ["Constrained execution zone"]
    T["Pinned tool or MCP server"]
    E["Deny-by-default egress proxy"]
    D["Downstream resource"]
  end

  U --> I
  U --> C
  EXT --> R
  R --> C
  C --> M
  M --> O
  O -->|"proposal, never authority"| B
  O --> MW
  MW --> R
  I -->|"authenticated principal and tenant"| B
  P -->|"allowlist and constraints"| B
  A -->|"action-bound approval"| B
  K -->|"independent deny"| B
  S -->|"just-in-time narrow credential"| B
  B -->|"authorized typed call"| T
  T --> E
  E --> D
  B --> L
  T --> L
  R --> L
  MW --> L

The critical boundary is between the orchestrator's proposed call and the broker's authorization decision. Keep authenticated context on a protected server-side channel; do not ask the model to copy identity, scopes, or tenant claims into tool arguments. Tool parameters are still untrusted even when they match a schema.

docs.title: Threat model and required negative evidence
docs.text:
The OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications 2025 and OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications 2026 are living community risk catalogs, not authorization specifications. Use them as threat inputs and verify controls against the actual architecture.

Threat or abuse case Boundary and preventive controls Required negative evidence Direct prompt injection asks the agent to ignore policy or reveal data Treat the model as an untrusted planner; external authorization; typed outputs; least privilege Injection corpus cannot cause an unauthorized tool execution, tenant read, secret disclosure, or policy change Indirect injection in a document, website, email, image-derived text, or tool result Provenance labels; isolate retrieved data from trusted control data; tool broker; restricted rendering and egress Malicious retrieved instructions may alter text output but cannot create capability or escape allowed egress Retrieval poisoning promotes attacker content Controlled ingestion, source and version provenance, quarantine, deletion, re-indexing, quality review, and anomaly telemetry A poisoned fixture is traceable, removable, and cannot grant tool or memory authority Cross-tenant RAG or cache leakage Server-derived tenant filter at ingestion and query; storage authorization; deny missing tenant; tenant-bound cache keys Query tenant A with tenant B document IDs, embeddings, cache keys, filters, and deletion jobs; return no B content Tool misuse or excessive agency Tool allowlist; resource and amount constraints; rate, time, and step budgets; reversible-by-default actions Unauthorized tool, resource, amount, sequence, retry, and budget cases deny before executor invocation Confused deputy uses valid authority for the wrong client or target Validate issuer, audience/resource, subject, tenant, client, consent, and purpose; no token passthrough Tokens for another tool server, tenant, resource, client, or purpose are rejected Malicious or replaced MCP/tool server Registry allowlist, owner review, pinned version/digest, transport authentication, schema limits, isolation, and egress policy Unknown server, changed digest, tool-name collision, schema drift, and unsolicited capability all fail closed Improper output handling Treat model/tool output as tainted; structured validation; contextual encoding; parameterized APIs; URL/command allowlists XSS, template, SQL, shell, path, SSRF, header, and log-injection payloads do not reach an interpreter Durable memory poisoning Authenticate writer; bind tenant and subject; provenance, TTL, moderation/quarantine; approval for privileged memory Cross-user writes, injected policy claims, replayed memories, and malicious summaries cannot become trusted instructions Secret theft or exfiltration Secretless model context; broker-side just-in-time credential use; field redaction; deny egress; response minimization Fake canary values in documents, errors, environment, and tool output never leave approved destinations Model, adapter, tokenizer, dataset, or runtime compromise Approved registry; provenance; immutable digest; signatures where supported; isolated loading/conversion; evaluation and rollback Digest/signature mismatch, unsafe serialization, unapproved adapter, and unexpected dependency fail admission Unbounded consumption or agent loop Per-request token, cost, tool-call, wall-time, recursion, concurrency, and output limits Cycles, fan-out, oversized output, retry storms, and slow tools terminate within the configured budget Approval spoofing or fatigue Separate authenticated UI; exact diff and impact; action binding; expiry; one-time use; revalidation Missing, altered, expired, cross-tenant, or replayed approval denies; executor sees no call

Passing a model-level injection evaluation is useful evidence about behavior, but it is not evidence that authorization is correct. The deterministic boundary must reject forbidden actions even when the model proposes them every time.

docs.title: Keep instructions and authority separate
docs.text:
Classify every context item with origin, tenant, owner, version, retrieval time, and trust purpose. A "trusted source" may support an answer, but its prose still does not become executable policy. Place policy in code or a dedicated policy service with reviewed changes, explicit defaults, and versioned decisions.

For direct and indirect injection:

  • mark user, retrieval, memory, and tool-result segments as data;
  • minimize the content provided to the model and remove active markup when it is not needed;
  • do not expose unnecessary tools to the session;
  • require structured proposals and validate every field;
  • keep authorization, approval, credential use, and egress enforcement after the model;
  • measure content filters, prompt hardening, and injection classifiers as fallible detection or steering controls, never fail-open gates.

The prompt-injection and data-poisoning terminology used here aligns with the final NIST AI 100-2 E2025 adversarial machine-learning taxonomy. NIST also publishes a potential-updates notice for that final document; record the exact edition and errata state used by an evaluation.

docs.title: Isolate retrieval and prevent cross-tenant RAG
docs.text:
Derive the tenant from authenticated membership, not from a model-produced filter, request body, filename, or document metadata alone. Enforce that tenant at every data operation:

  • ingestion verifies the writer may add content to that tenant and records source URI/object ID, content digest, parser and embedding versions, owner, and time;
  • chunk and embedding records carry a non-null authoritative tenant key;
  • queries deny when tenant context is absent and apply the filter in the storage authorization layer, not only in the prompt or application post-processing;
  • post-retrieval checks verify every returned record belongs to the expected tenant before context assembly;
  • caches include tenant, principal or policy cohort, model, prompt template, and source versions in the key;
  • updates and deletion remove or tombstone derived chunks, embeddings, summaries, and caches;
  • shared indexes receive adversarial cross-tenant tests after schema, embedding, ranking, or library changes.

Embedding similarity and metadata supplied by an indexed document are not access control. Separate physical indexes may reduce some blast radius, but they do not remove the need for authenticated ingestion, query authorization, and deletion correctness. OWASP describes retrieval-specific risks under its living vector and embedding weaknesses material.

Treat retrieved content as potentially poisoned even after authorization. Quarantine newly ingested high-risk sources, maintain an emergency source denylist, and support re-indexing from a known-good corpus. Retrieval provenance should be visible to reviewers and carried into audit without logging entire sensitive documents.

docs.title: Authorize capabilities outside the model
docs.text:
The broker evaluates a capability tuple such as:

(principal, tenant, tool, action, resource, constraints, purpose, expiry, policy-version)

This tuple is an illustrative design, not a wire-format standard. Production policy should also account for environment, device or workload identity, separation of duties, risk tier, and downstream entitlements where relevant.

The broker should:

  • accept identity only from a validated gateway or workload channel;
  • allow only registered tool and action identifiers;
  • parse a closed, versioned schema and reject unknown or ambiguous fields;
  • constrain resource IDs, destinations, amount, data classification, time, frequency, and cumulative budget;
  • re-check current entitlement immediately before execution;
  • ask a separate approval service for high-impact calls;
  • mint, exchange, or retrieve a short-lived credential for only the selected downstream resource;
  • pass authoritative tenant and principal context independently of model arguments;
  • make downstream services authorize again;
  • apply idempotency keys and reconcile uncertain outcomes before retrying.

Do not hand the model a broad user access token. Do not let a tool server forward the client's bearer token to another API. The current MCP 2025-11-25 authorization specification requires resource indicators and prohibits token passthrough; its design builds on OAuth protected-resource metadata and related standards. Independently of MCP, follow OAuth 2.0 Security Best Current Practice, RFC 9700 and bind requested tokens to the intended resource using RFC 8707.

docs.title: Treat MCP and tool servers as security principals
docs.text:
MCP defines interoperability; it does not certify a server, tool, prompt, resource, or returned content. The MCP server specification describes tools as model-controlled, which makes the client/broker boundary especially important.

For each MCP or proprietary tool server:

  • register owner, business purpose, transport, endpoint, issuer, expected audience, permitted tenants, tool names, schema versions, artifact digest, network destinations, data classes, and incident contact;
  • authenticate both ends, negotiate only supported protocol versions, and reject unexpected capability or schema changes;
  • isolate local stdio servers because they inherit local process access; do not place a general cloud credential or an entire user environment in their process;
  • validate tool names and descriptions as untrusted metadata and prevent lookalike or collision-based selection;
  • cap input/output size, task duration, progress events, redirects, and resource fetches;
  • bind asynchronous task state and results to the authenticated principal and tenant, rather than relying on an opaque task ID alone;
  • prohibit inbound-token passthrough, validate the server audience, and obtain a separate downstream token;
  • run high-risk servers in separate identities and isolation domains so one server cannot read another server's secrets or network.

As of 2026-07-23, MCP's versioning page identifies 2025-11-25 as the current protocol. The project has announced 2026-07-28 as a release candidate, so it is a preview, not the baseline claimed by this article. Re-check the status before implementation because the specification is living material.

docs.title: Validate model and tool output at every sink
docs.text:
Model output, structured output, and tool output remain untrusted after parsing. A valid JSON object may still contain an unauthorized resource or an injection payload.

  • Use a closed schema with type, length, range, character, and enumeration constraints.
  • Encode text for its final HTML, Markdown, CSV, log, header, or template context.
  • Use parameterized database and API operations.
  • Never build shell commands, SQL, paths, URLs, templates, or policy expressions by concatenating model output.
  • Resolve object IDs through an authorized lookup; do not accept arbitrary filesystem paths or URLs.
  • Route outbound HTTP through an egress proxy that validates scheme, hostname, port, resolved destination, redirect target, and response size. Account for private addresses and DNS rebinding.
  • Strip credentials and unnecessary sensitive fields from errors and tool responses before they re-enter model context.

OWASP's improper output handling entry provides a threat catalog; the actual encoder and validator must be selected for each sink.

docs.title: Govern durable memory as a data store
docs.text:
Memory is a second retrieval system with a write path. A model-generated summary can preserve an attack after the original prompt disappears.

Separate conversation state, user preferences, factual records, and security policy. The model may propose a memory, but a memory gate should:

  • authenticate the writer and bind user, tenant, session, and purpose;
  • reject attempts to store credentials, hidden policy, or another tenant's data;
  • retain origin, source references, model and prompt version, confidence or review state, and expiry;
  • prevent a retrieved memory from overriding policy or becoming identity evidence;
  • require approval for durable memories that change workflow, destinations, permissions, or other high-impact behavior;
  • support inspection, correction, deletion, quarantine, version rollback, and tenant-scoped export;
  • detect unusual write volume, repeated injected phrases, cross-user reuse, and abrupt changes in influential memory.

Do not silently train on conversation or memory data. Training and retention decisions require their own documented authority, purpose, tenant handling, and deletion semantics.

docs.title: Sandbox execution, egress, and secrets
docs.text:
Use an ephemeral execution identity and filesystem per task or trust cohort. Depending on the runtime and threat model, controls may include a non-root user, read-only base image, minimal writable volume, syscall and capability reduction, no host or container-engine socket, no cloud instance-metadata access, CPU/memory/ process/file/output/time quotas, and a stronger virtual-machine boundary for hostile native code.

Network access should be denied by default. Send permitted traffic through an authenticated proxy with a destination and method allowlist, response limits, redirect validation, DNS and private-range protections, and attributable logs. Do not allow a generic "browse the internet" path from the same identity that can reach internal administration APIs.

Keep secrets out of prompts, retrieval, memory, environment dumps, command lines, and model-visible error messages. The broker should obtain a narrowly scoped, short-lived credential after authorization and expose it only to the selected tool process or make the downstream call itself. Secret scanning and output filters are backstops; the primary control is that the model never receives the secret.

docs.title: Require bound approval for high-impact actions
docs.text:
Classify high-impact operations before rollout. Typical candidates include:

  • transferring value or changing a financial commitment;
  • deleting or overwriting durable data;
  • granting permissions, creating credentials, or changing security policy;
  • deploying to production or modifying infrastructure;
  • exporting sensitive or cross-tenant data;
  • sending external communications or making a legally significant submission;
  • disabling a security control or expanding egress.

The approval interface should show the authenticated requester, tenant, exact tool and action, target, before/after change, amount and unit, data leaving the boundary, expected side effects, and expiry. Approval must be recorded through a separate authenticated channel, cryptographically or server-side bound to a canonical action digest, short-lived, single-use, and revalidated immediately before execution.

Any material change after approval creates a new action. Do not approve a plan that later allows the model to choose the target or amount. Rate-limit approval requests and measure reviewer overrides, abandonment, repeated prompts, and approval latency for signs of fatigue. A human click is not proof that the action was understood.

docs.title: Build an independent kill switch
docs.text:
Provide global, tenant, principal, model, tool-server, tool, destination, and action-level disablement. Enforce it in the broker and, for defense in depth, in credential issuance, queue consumption, egress, and downstream policy. The control must not require a prompt change, model response, normal deployment, or access to the affected agent.

Define and rehearse:

  • how pending and in-flight work is stopped or quarantined;
  • whether reads may continue while writes are disabled;
  • token revocation and secret rotation;
  • queue draining versus evidence preservation;
  • break-glass authentication and separation of duties;
  • how long it takes each check in the chain to actually pick up the change;
  • safe restoration and re-authorization after containment.

Failing to reach the kill-switch policy service should deny new high-impact actions. Any low-risk degraded mode must be explicit, bounded, observable, and tested.

docs.title: Failure modes and explicit semantics
docs.text:
Failure Required behavior Identity, tenant, or entitlement cannot be resolved Deny; never use model-, document-, or client-asserted fallback authority Policy service unavailable or policy version unknown Deny writes and high-impact actions; allow a read-only degraded mode only if separately designed and cached policy remains valid Approval service unavailable, evidence expired, or action changed Deny the high-impact action and require a new approval Audit pipeline unavailable Fail closed for high-impact actions; for explicitly low-risk actions, use a bounded durable local queue and alert before it fills Tool schema, owner, endpoint, certificate, version, or digest changes Quarantine the tool until registry review and compatibility/security tests pass Retrieval tenant filter missing or index returns mismatched tenant Drop the result, fail the request, alert, and investigate as a potential isolation incident Model provider or selected model unavailable Stop or use a separately evaluated equal-or-lower-capability fallback; never gain tools or permissions during fallback Egress proxy or destination validation unavailable Deny outbound traffic; do not bypass directly Downstream timeout leaves outcome uncertain Reconcile with an idempotency key or authoritative status endpoint before any retry Loop, recursive delegation, or budget exhaustion Stop scheduling, revoke task capability, persist minimal evidence, and return a bounded failure Kill-switch state cannot be read Deny new effects according to the last safe state and alert the control-plane owner

Availability pressure is not permission to weaken tenant or authorization boundaries. If an emergency bypass is genuinely required, handle it as a time-bound, approved, logged break-glass event and a security exception.

docs.title: Evaluation and release evidence
docs.text: The NIST AI RMF 1.0 organizes risk work around Govern, Map, Measure, and Manage. Its Generative AI Profile, NIST AI 600-1 calls for documented testing, red-teaming, monitoring, and risk tracking across the lifecycle. Use those outcomes to govern an engineering test program, not as a claim of certification.

docs.title: Deterministic boundary tests
docs.text:
For the broker, storage authorization, egress proxy, memory gate, and downstream service, make these release-blocking:

  • unknown principal, tenant, tool, action, schema version, resource, and policy deny;
  • cross-tenant read, write, cache, task, memory, audit, and deletion cases deny;
  • over-limit amount, rate, data class, destination, time, and cumulative budget deny;
  • missing, expired, altered, wrong-principal, wrong-tenant, wrong-tool, wrong-target, and replayed approvals deny;
  • changed tool-server digest, audience, issuer, redirect, schema, and capability deny;
  • private-network, metadata-service, redirect, DNS-rebinding, and oversized response egress cases deny;
  • executor invocation count remains zero for every rejected proposal;
  • kill switches prevent new invocation at each configured scope.

These tests require zero false allows for the cases encoded. A passing finite suite does not prove the policy complete.

docs.title: Model and system evaluations
docs.text:
Use versioned, access-controlled suites that include:

  • direct and indirect injections in user text, documents, email, web content, images converted to text, code comments, tool descriptions, errors, and tool results;
  • obfuscation, encoding, multilingual, multi-turn, delayed-trigger, and instruction-conflict variants;
  • poisoned retrieval ranking, forged provenance, cross-tenant document IDs, cache collisions, stale deletion, and malicious memory;
  • tool-name collisions, schema ambiguity, argument smuggling, approval spoofing, confused-deputy flows, asynchronous tasks, retries, and time-of-check/time-of-use changes;
  • output payloads for every interpreter or renderer and exfiltration attempts using unmistakably fake canary values;
  • long-horizon loops, multi-agent delegation, resource exhaustion, partial tool failure, and uncertain downstream outcomes;
  • model, prompt, adapter, embedding, parser, runtime, policy, and tool upgrades.

Run repeated trials because model behavior can vary. Record the entire tested configuration and distinguish:

  • proposal attack success: the model produced a forbidden proposal;
  • boundary false allow: a forbidden proposal reached the executor;
  • sensitive-output rate: fake canary or protected fixture appeared outside its allowed sink;
  • false deny and task success: legitimate work was blocked or failed;
  • budget containment: calls, time, tokens, output, and cost remained bounded;
  • detection and response: telemetry fired and containment completed within the rehearsed objective.

Do not average away a tenant-isolation or unauthorized-execution failure. Set explicit per-boundary release gates and document unmeasured risks. Keep held-out adversarial cases separate from prompt tuning and version both the corpus and expected policy decisions.

docs.title: Tested companion lab
docs.text:
Run:

node --test labs/ai-agent-security/tests/broker.test.js

The lab proves only that its small JavaScript broker:

  • allows an authorized tenant/tool/amount and calls a fake executor;
  • rejects an unauthorized tenant, tool, and over-policy amount;
  • requires approval above the configured impact threshold;
  • rejects approval bound to different action details or reused approval;
  • denies execution while its injected kill switch is active.

It does not implement token validation, cryptographic approval, a policy engine, MCP, network egress, a sandbox, durable audit, or a real external action.

docs.title: Staged rollout and rollback gates
docs.text:
Stage Capability Entry and exit evidence Rollback 0. Inventory and offline evaluation No production tools; synthetic or approved test data Threat model, data flow, tenant model, owners, tool registry, policy, failure semantics, and baseline eval recorded Stop evaluation and correct design or data handling 1. Read-only shadow Model proposes; broker evaluates; no external execution, or approved read-only duplicate path Negative boundary suite passes; proposal/denial telemetry and cost measured; no sensitive logs Disable model path; preserve conventional application 2. Read-only canary Narrow tenants/users, allowlisted sources and tools, strict budgets Cross-tenant and injection campaigns pass; on-call and kill switch rehearsed; user reporting available Disable tenant/model/tool scope and revoke credentials 3. Reversible writes with approval Small set of idempotent or reversible actions; every write approved Bound approval, reconciliation, rollback, audit, and downstream reauthorization tested Stop writes, reconcile in-flight work, undo through normal audited API 4. Bounded automation Selected low-impact actions may execute without per-action approval Sustained evidence for explicit false-allow, false-deny, task-success, cost, and incident objectives; risk acceptance recorded Return action to approval or read-only mode without model change

Expand one dimension at a time: tenant population, data class, tool, autonomy, model, or egress. Do not change all of them in one release. Rollback must preserve security policy and tenant isolation; "temporarily bypass the broker" is not a rollback.

docs.title: Observability and operations
docs.text:
Emit structured events at retrieval, memory, proposal, authorization, approval, credential issuance, tool invocation, egress, downstream result, and kill-switch transitions. Correlate them with a trace ID while minimizing content.

Useful fields include:

  • authenticated principal and workload, authoritative tenant, session, purpose, environment, and policy version;
  • model provider, model and adapter digest/version, prompt-template version, and orchestrator release;
  • retrieved source IDs, tenants, versions, digests, ranking metadata, and post-filter result counts;
  • proposed tool, registered server identity and digest, schema version, target class, amount/unit, risk tier, and budget;
  • allow/deny decision, stable reason code, evaluated constraints, approval ID and expiry, and kill-switch state;
  • credential audience and lifetime without the credential value;
  • executor start/finish, idempotency key, downstream status, bytes, duration, egress destination, and reconciliation result;
  • memory writer, subject, source, review state, version, expiry, and deletion.

Do not log bearer tokens, approval secrets, raw credentials, unnecessary prompt content, sensitive document bodies, or unrestricted model/tool output. Protect audit access with the same tenant and administrative separation applied to the source systems.

Alert on:

  • any deterministic boundary false allow;
  • cross-tenant retrieval/memory mismatch or missing tenant context;
  • unknown or changed tool server, schema, digest, issuer, or audience;
  • sharp changes in proposal denials, approval requests, reviewer overrides, memory writes, external destinations, loop termination, cost, or latency;
  • fake secret canary detection, blocked metadata/private-network access, or attempted credential disclosure;
  • kill-switch activation, failure to propagate, audit backlog, or repeated uncertain downstream outcomes.

Pre-deployment evaluation cannot represent all production conditions. NIST's final AI 800-4 report on deployed-system monitoring describes post-deployment monitoring practices as still nascent; keep claims about coverage and effectiveness bounded to measured evidence.

docs.title: Incident response
docs.text:
Add agent-specific actions to the normal incident plan:

  1. Detect and classify: identify affected tenants, principals, model/prompt/ adapter versions, retrieval sources, memory records, tools, credentials, egress destinations, approvals, and downstream effects.
  2. Contain: activate the narrowest reliable kill switch, stop queue consumption, deny credential issuance and egress, quarantine tool servers, freeze implicated ingestion and memory writes, and revoke affected tokens.
  3. Preserve evidence: retain policy versions, decision records, action digests, source and model artifact digests, tool results, task state, approval evidence, and downstream reconciliation IDs under the incident evidence policy. Avoid collecting unrelated tenant content.
  4. Eradicate: remove poisoned sources/memory, rebuild indexes and caches, rotate exposed secrets, patch or replace tools, restore approved artifacts, and close the authorization or sandbox gap.
  5. Reconcile and recover: determine which external effects actually occurred, reverse them through normal audited interfaces where possible, restore in read-only/canary mode, and re-run deterministic plus adversarial tests.
  6. Communicate and learn: follow applicable contractual, legal, regulatory, and tenant-notification processes; publish a bounded internal account; add regression tests and update the threat model, policy, playbooks, and risk register.

Do not delete suspicious memory or retrieval content before preserving the minimum evidence needed to understand derived chunks, caches, summaries, and effects. Do not re-enable automation solely because model output appears normal.

docs.title: Model and agent supply chain
docs.text:
Apply the final NIST SP 800-218A as an AI-specific community profile alongside SSDF 1.1. Maintain an inventory and provenance graph for:

  • base models, weights, adapters, tokenizers, embedding and reranking models;
  • training, tuning, retrieval, evaluation, and safety datasets;
  • system/developer prompt templates, policies, tool schemas, MCP servers, agent packages, plugins, and approval workflows;
  • parsers, converters, inference runtimes, native libraries, containers, build systems, and deployment manifests.

Acquire from approved sources; record licenses and use restrictions; pin immutable digests; verify signatures/attestations where the ecosystem supports them; scan ordinary dependencies; and isolate model loading and conversion. Treat executable or unsafe serialization formats as code and do not deserialize an untrusted artifact in a privileged environment. Preserve the exact artifact set used for evaluation and support rollback to a known-good set.

A provider name or model label is not a stable version. Contract and operational controls should address unannounced model changes, retention/training use, subprocessors, regional processing, incident notice, vulnerability handling, deprecation, export, and deletion. Re-run security and task evaluations before a new model, adapter, embedding, prompt, policy, runtime, or tool becomes eligible.

The SLSA provenance specification and CycloneDX machine-learning BOM are primary project materials that can represent parts of this evidence. Neither, by itself, proves an artifact safe or a deployed agent authorized.

docs.text:
Material Status used here How it is used NIST AI RMF 1.0, NIST AI 100-1 (January 2023) Final published framework; NIST states a revision is in progress Govern, Map, Measure, and Manage structure; not a certification NIST AI 600-1 (July 2024) Final Generative AI Profile Generative-AI lifecycle risk, evaluation, red-team, provenance, and monitoring outcomes NIST SP 800-218A (July 2024) Final SSDF Community Profile Secure development and acquisition practices for AI model/system producers and acquirers NIST AI 100-2 E2025 (March 2025) Final taxonomy with a published potential-updates notice Adversarial ML, poisoning, prompt injection, privacy, misuse, and mitigation terminology OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications 2025 Living community project material Threat discovery for prompt injection, supply chain, poisoning, output handling, agency, embeddings, and consumption OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications 2026 Published community project material, December 2025 Agent-specific threat discovery and mitigation prompts MCP 2025-11-25 Current protocol revision on the review date Protocol, server primitive, authorization, version negotiation, and task-boundary requirements MCP 2026-07-28 Release candidate on the review date Preview only; not the implementation baseline

docs.title: What's still not solved
docs.text:
Even with all of this in place, here's what can still go wrong:

  • novel model behavior and injection techniques that evade detection;
  • a compromised broker, policy administrator, identity tier, approval service, tool server, downstream service, or build pipeline;
  • legitimate but malicious insiders with authorized access;
  • authorization policy that is enforced correctly but models the wrong business rule;
  • side channels across shared inference, retrieval, caches, telemetry, or infrastructure;
  • sandbox escapes, kernel or runtime vulnerabilities, DNS and supply-chain compromise;
  • poisoned sources that are authorized and plausible enough to pass review;
  • approval fatigue, collusion, inaccessible context, and delayed revocation;
  • model-provider changes and incomplete visibility into hosted models or data handling;
  • finite evaluations that do not cover open-ended, long-horizon, multi-agent interactions.

The strongest mitigation is to reduce capability and blast radius: fewer tools, smaller data scopes, shorter credentials, reversible effects, lower budgets, tighter egress, narrower tenants, and less unattended autonomy. Some use cases should remain read-only, require approval permanently, or not use an agent.

docs.title: Engineering and operational checklist
docs.text:
Principal and tenant are authenticated outside the model and deny when missing.

User, retrieval, memory, tool metadata, model output, and tool output are all treated as untrusted.

Every effect crosses an external capability broker and downstream authorization.

Tool, resource, destination, amount, data class, rate, step, time, and cost constraints are explicit allowlists.

High-impact approval is separate, exact, short-lived, single-use, and revalidated before execution.

RAG ingestion, query, cache, derived data, and deletion each have a cross-tenant test that's supposed to fail.

MCP/tool servers have owners, pinned identities/versions/digests, schema limits, isolation, audience validation, and no token passthrough.

Model and tool output is validated and encoded for each final sink.

Memory writes have tenant binding, provenance, review state, TTL, and deletion/rollback.

Model context is secretless; credentials are just-in-time, narrow, and not visible to the model.

Execution is ephemeral and resource-limited; network egress is denied by default.

Kill switches exist at multiple scopes and are rehearsed independently of the model.

Deterministic authorization tests and stochastic model/system evaluations are both release evidence.

Observability distinguishes proposals, policy decisions, approvals, execution, egress, and downstream outcomes without logging secrets.

Incident response covers retrieval, memory, model artifacts, tasks, tools, credentials, approvals, and external-effect reconciliation.

Models, adapters, data, prompts, policies, runtimes, tools, and evaluations have provenance, immutable versions, admission checks, and rollback.

What's still not solved, what hasn't been measured, and the maximum autonomy permitted are all explicitly signed off by whoever owns that decision.

docs.title: Research question and hypothesis
docs.text:
Question: Can a model-proposed action acquire authority without independently bound approval and policy?

Falsifiable hypothesis (bounded experiment): Unauthorized principal/tenant/tool/amount/destination and approval replay never invoke the fake executor; concurrent replay admits at most one approved action.
