docs.title: Host Telemetry Detection Lab: Nine Linux Rules, Their False Positives, and What They Cannot See
docs.text:
Linux Security · Research

Nine high-signal host rules written as plain SQL, scored on a labeled synthetic corpus with benign look-alikes and known evasions, then run over real syscalls captured from a throwaway container.

This is a study of detection logic, not of a sensor. Nine rules turn host events (process starts, file reads and writes, permission changes, outbound connections) into alerts. The interesting questions are the ones a rule's author usually skips: what legitimate activity does it also flag, what malicious activity does it miss, who owns each exception, and what does it say when its data source is gone?

Synthetic data, stated plainly. Every event produced by the generator carries "synthetic": true and "origin": "synthetic-generator". Nothing here records, simulates or reproduces a real intrusion; there is no malicious code in the lab. The one dataset with "origin": "strace-capture" is real kernel-observed syscalls from harmless placeholders inside a throwaway container. The corpus was written by the rule author, so its numbers describe the rules' logic, not field accuracy.

Evidence labels: tested locally (executed here; output in the lab's evidence/), policy model (a rule evaluated by a local test, not by a production sensor), source-reviewed (read in the named primary source), requires-review (no independent reviewer yet). They map to T2/T3, T1, T0 and review status in the evidence standards. This article builds on, and does not repeat, the process-identity argument in Linux Host Analysis Without Invented Attack Paths.

docs.title: Scope
docs.text: In scope: the behaviours below, expressed as queries over normalized events; their false positives and misses; exception ownership; missing-telemetry reporting; deduplication; and a cross-check of the same rules on real kernel-observed syscalls. Out of scope: fleet-scale collection, kernel sensors (auditd, eBPF, Falco, Tetragon, osquery), a SIEM, enrichment, and response automation. Response guidance is written for people and was never executed.

docs.title: What I built
docs.text:
The code lives in the linux-host-telemetry lab. The shape:

flowchart LR
  subgraph SRC["Telemetry sources"]
    GEN["generator.py<br/>seeded, synthetic: true"]
    CAP["capture.sh<br/>host strace on a throwaway container"]
  end
  GEN --> VAL["engine.validate<br/>schema, origin, clocks"]
  CAP --> NRM["normalize_strace.py<br/>strace lines to events"] --> VAL
  VAL --> DB[("SQLite events table")]
  DB --> RULES["rules/*.sql<br/>nine readable queries"]
  AL["allowlist.json<br/>owner, reason, expiry"] --> RULES
  COV{"required sources and fields present?"} --> RULES
  RULES --> DED["deduplicate<br/>rule, host, subject, 5 min"]
  DED --> ALERT["alerts with count, clocks, response text"]
  LAB["scenario labels"] -.->|"offline scoring only"| SCORE["confusion matrix per rule"]
  ALERT --> SCORE

The labels reach the scorer only; a test asserts that no rule's SQL mentions scenario, synthetic or origin, so a rule cannot read the answer key.

Process ancestry, the one place SQL needs care, is a recursive query keyed on process identity (host, boot, pid, start time), not on pid:

flowchart TD
  EV["event arrives"] --> OK{"valid schema, known origin,<br/>ingest_ts not before ts?"}
  OK -->|"no"| REJ["reject the event, do not guess"]
  OK -->|"yes"| NEED{"rule's sources and fields present?"}
  NEED -->|"no"| BLIND["rule is BLIND: reported, not scored, not 'clean'"]
  NEED -->|"yes"| Q["run the rule's SQL"]
  Q --> ALLOW{"matches an unexpired allowlist entry?"}
  ALLOW -->|"yes"| SUP["suppressed, entry owner on record"]
  ALLOW -->|"no"| DEDUP{"same rule, host, subject within 5 minutes?"}
  DEDUP -->|"yes"| FOLD["fold into the open alert, count + 1"]
  DEDUP -->|"no"| NEW["new alert, evaluated in the next 5 s batch"]
  NEW --> TRI["triage: read-only first, then the rule's response text"]

Status: tested locally; every box maps to a function in engine.py and at least one test.

docs.title: The rules
docs.text:
Each rule is one SQL file whose header states severity, required telemetry and response guidance. Scenario counts are from the pinned table below.

Rule Looks for Why it is high-signal Known false-positive sources LNX-001 A shell or interpreter whose ancestor within 3 levels is a network-facing service Services rarely need a shell; the ancestry catches a helper in between App code that shells out (git, image conversion); supervisors LNX-002 A write under /etc/cron.d, /etc/cron.*, /etc/crontab by a non-package-manager System cron is mostly managed by packages and configuration management Manual edits; config-management tools not allowlisted LNX-003 A systemd unit written by a non-package-manager whose ExecStart is under /tmp, /dev/shm, /var/tmp, /home or /root A service pointing at a writable directory is persistence-shaped Developer user units under /home LNX-004 A process executing from /tmp, /var/tmp or /dev/shm connecting to a public address Legitimate services do not run from world-writable directories CI tooling unpacked in /tmp LNX-005 A read of /etc/shadow, SSH host/user keys, cloud credentials by anything but the designed readers Few programs have a reason to read these Backup agents, audit scanners LNX-006 A write to sudoers, passwd/shadow/group, PAM, sshd_config, ld.so.preload by anything but the designed tools Direct changes to authorization are rare and consequential Approved manual changes (tee, editors) LNX-007 chmod setting setuid/setgid on a file by a non-package-manager New setuid binaries are a classic local-escalation precondition None observed; directories are excluded on purpose LNX-008 Execution from /memfd:…, /proc/self/fd/…, or a path ending (deleted) A process with no file on disk is unusual A binary replaced mid-upgrade (rare) LNX-009 Truncating or deleting under /var/log by a non-rotation tool, or auditctl -e 0 Removing evidence is rarely routine Emergency disk clean-ups

Design decisions worth defending:

  1. SQL, not a DSL. A reviewer can read the query that fired. The cost is that SQL cannot express "this process, then that one within 60 seconds" cleanly; LNX-001 needs a recursive CTE, and anything with ordered sequences would need a second engine.
  2. Exceptions are data with an owner and an expiry. The engine refuses an allowlist entry missing either, and ignores an entry after its date. Exercised: the backup agent (S43) is suppressed; the legacy sync tool (S45), whose exception expired 2026-06-30, alerts again with the same behaviour.
  3. Package-manager and designed-tool exclusions live in the rule, not the allowlist. They are part of what the rule means; environment-specific exceptions are not.
  4. Path-based egress (LNX-004) is a deliberate simplification. It is cheap and quiet, and it misses a reverse connection from a system bash (S34). A behavioural version needs socket-to-stdio correlation that this telemetry model does not carry.

docs.title: Research question and hypothesis
docs.text:
Question: Can a small set of SQL host rules separate designed behaviour from suspicious behaviour on labeled telemetry while reporting a missing sensor or field as blind rather than clean?

Falsifiable hypothesis (bounded experiment): Every scenario's outcome matches its documented expectation, including seven named residual false positives and two named misses; background activity produces no alerts; a rule whose source or field is absent is reported blind and excluded from scoring. Any silent change in the confusion matrix, an alert on background noise, or a missing-source rule scored as a true negative refutes it.

docs.title: Research threat model
docs.text: Element Declared scope Actor A local process on a Linux host with the privileges of a web service account or an interactive session, trying persistence, credential access, privilege change or log removal Assets The host's authentication and authorization files, cron and systemd persistence points, credential files, and the audit trail Entry points Process starts, file writes/reads/chmods/truncates, outbound connections as seen by an assumed sensor Trust boundaries Kernel events → sensor → normalization → rule → alert → human; the rules assume the sensor reports faithfully Impact under investigation A rule that alerts on everything, nothing, or only on what its author expected, and a telemetry gap that looks like a quiet host Trusted assumptions The sensor delivers accurate exe, path and process-identity fields; the host kernel is not compromised; an attacker who knows these rules is out of scope (two evasions are shown, not a bypass analysis)

docs.title: Method and evidence requirements
docs.text:
Follow the evidence standards (Detection row: labeled fixtures, parser and query, TP/FP/FN/TN counts, a missing-source case, event/ingest/alert clocks, deduplication and response limits). The lab owns setup, prerequisites, expected output, safety, evidence collection and teardown. From repository root:

python3 labs/linux-host-telemetry/tests/test_detections.py

This command is a tested local check of detection logic, with the scope below. The full run (bash labs/linux-host-telemetry/scripts/run-lab.sh) additionally generates the corpus, scores it, removes the network sensor, and, where Docker and strace exist, captures real syscalls. A passing run does not show that the rules work on a real fleet; it shows that they do what this article says on the data it describes.

docs.title: Validation
docs.text:
Recorded run, 2026-11-05 (evidence/versions.txt): Python 3.13.18, SQLite 3.53.1, Linux 6.18.44, strace 6.8, Docker 29.9.2. All tested locally.

Command Observed python3 labs/linux-host-telemetry/tests/test_detections.py Ran 23 tests ... OK bash labs/linux-host-telemetry/scripts/run-lab.sh --publish-evidence 9 assertions passed, 0 failed generator 855 synthetic events, 42 labeled scenarios (seed 20261105); byte-identical on a second run engine over the corpus 27 deduplicated alerts; 0 alerts on 400 iterations of background noise engine, network sensor removed (--sources exec,file) LNX-004 blind (missing source net), no LNX-004 alert, no LNX-004 score capture 176 strace lines, 28 normalized events engine over the capture alerts from exactly LNX-002, 005, 006, 007, 009; LNX-004 silent; LNX-003 blind (missing field exec_start)

docs.title: Scenario-level results on the synthetic corpus
docs.text:
42 scenarios: 17 malicious-pattern, 17 benign look-alike, 6 control, 2 evasion. Counted per rule per scenario; totals over the nine rules are TP 19, FP 7, FN 2, TN 216.

Rule TP FP FN TN Precision Recall LNX-001 4 1 0 24 0.80 1.00 LNX-002 2 1 1 23 0.67 0.67 LNX-003 1 1 0 24 0.50 1.00 LNX-004 2 1 1 23 0.67 0.67 LNX-005 3 1 0 24 0.75 1.00 LNX-006 3 1 0 24 0.75 1.00 LNX-007 1 0 0 25 1.00 1.00 LNX-008 2 0 0 25 1.00 1.00 LNX-009 1 1 0 24 0.50 1.00

These are a regression guard and a statement of documented behaviour, not a population estimate: the author wrote both the rules and the corpus, small per-rule denominators make the ratios unstable, and the 216 true negatives are mostly scenarios that have nothing to do with a given rule. The table is pinned in the tests so a change is a deliberate edit.

Claim class Evidence tier and boundary Rule logic does what the SQL says on labeled input T2/T3, tested locally, 23 tests over the synthetic corpus The seven look-alikes alert and the two evasions stay silent, as documented T3, pinned confusion matrix Real kernel events reach the same rules through a normalizer T2, one capture, five rules positive, one negative, one blind Time to detect, field false-positive rate, adversary resistance Not established; synthetic latency only A rule's recommended response is right for your environment T0 judgment; never executed here

docs.title: Residual false positives, and what resolves each
docs.text:
The seven benign look-alikes that alert are the point of the exercise. Each needs context the telemetry does not carry:

Scenario Rule Why it alerts What resolves it Owner action S04 gunicorn runs git rev-parse HEAD LNX-001 Real service, real shell The exact command and parent are known Allowlist parent_exe + command regex with an owner and expiry, or have the app read its version at build time S13 vim edits /etc/cron.d/backup LNX-002 A manual change by a human A change record Ask; prefer configuration management as the only writer S23 developer user unit under /home LNX-003 /home is in the writable set Host role (developer workstation vs server) Scope the rule to server roles S33 CI toolchain in /tmp connects out LNX-004 Executes from a writable directory The binary's hash or a dedicated build directory Run builds elsewhere; allow by hash, never by path S44 nightly audit scanner reads /etc/shadow LNX-005 Designed reader not on the list Inventory of scanners Allowlist with owner and expiry S54 tee /etc/sudoers.d/dev-team, approved LNX-006 Legitimate, approved write The approval Attach a change reference; do not allowlist tee S82 truncate -s 0 /var/log/syslog LNX-009 Emergency clean-up Asking the person; confirming the shipper holds the data Respond by asking, not by isolating

Ten other look-alikes (S03, S11, S12, S21, S22, S43, S52, S53, S61, S62) are correctly quiet: three because of an unexpired exception, the rest because the rule excludes the designed tool or the specific shape (for example S62: setgid on a directory).

docs.title: What the lab found that I did not plan for
docs.text:
1. Deduplication can hide a distinct action. The key (rule, host, subject) with a 5-minute window folds any second hit with the same subject into the first alert's count. When I tested a pid-only ancestry join, the benign S06 hit was folded into S01's alert (subject nginx > sh), so my first scorer attributed the alert only to S01 and S06 looked silent. The scorer now tracks the folded scenarios (evaluation-only metadata; a real pipeline sees only the count). The production lesson: choose the key deliberately. A coarse key reduces noise and also means a second, different shell started by the same service inside the window is not a second alert.
  2. Python's ipaddress.is_private is true for the RFC 5737 documentation ranges the lab uses as stand-ins for "somewhere on the Internet". The first normalizer classified them as private and a test caught it. Classification now treats only loopback, RFC 1918, link-local and ULA as internal.
  3. A source can be present while a needed field is not. The first engine reported LNX-003 as evaluated on the strace capture, although strace can never provide a unit's parsed ExecStart. Coverage is now checked per source and per field: LNX-003 is blind on the capture. A silent rule and a blind rule look identical in an alert list; they must not be treated alike.
  4. PID reuse is a real attribution risk, and identity prevents it. In S06 a benign shell reuses the pid of a former nginx child. The identity-aware ancestry (pid and start time, the latter being /proc/[pid]/stat field 22, source-reviewed) attributes it correctly; the same query with the start-time condition removed alerts on it. Both outcomes are asserted.
  5. Ingestion lag, not rule logic, dominates detection time. Synthetic latency was a median of 3.6 s, but S91, whose events reach the pipeline 125 s late, alerts after 125-127 s. These are synthetic clocks (a 5 s evaluation batch plus a generated lag), not a measurement of any real pipeline.

docs.title: The real-kernel cross-check
docs.text:
capture.sh runs a busybox container whose script performs harmless analogs: a comment-only file in /etc/cron.d, a read of the container's own /etc/shadow, a comment-only sudoers.d drop-in, chmod 4755 on a copy of /bin/true, a truncated log file, and a connection from a copy of wget in /tmp to a private canary. The host attaches strace -f to the container's PID 1. 176 raw lines became 28 events and exactly the five matching rules alerted. LNX-004's negative control (a /tmp executable talking to a private address) stayed silent.

Two caveats are part of the finding. The first-attached process has no execve in the trace, so its exe comes from /proc/<pid>/exe at attach time. And strace is a capture convenience: it perturbs timing, records only the syscalls it is asked for, and supplies host PIDs without start times (the normalizer substitutes a per-trace ordinal, which keeps identity within one capture but is not a kernel start time).

docs.title: Practical guidance and failure containment
docs.text:
• Treat blind as an incident in the pipeline. A rule whose source or field is gone should page the telemetry owner, because its silence is not evidence of a clean host.
  • Exceptions need an owner and an expiry, and the engine should enforce both. An exception without an expiry is a permanent hole nobody remembers granting.
  • Respond read-only first. Every rule's response text starts with capture and attribution; containment follows evidence. LNX-008 in particular: the deleted or in-memory file is only recoverable while the process lives.
  • Never auto-isolate a host on a single rule. Seven of nine rules have a documented legitimate source; automation without the context that resolves it turns a false positive into an outage.
  • Roll back by disabling the rule or its exception, not by loosening the pattern. Rules are files; the previous version is in version control.

Failure containment: a bad rule is bounded by its blast radius, an alert (a person reads it), not by an action. The first automated action added to any rule should be reversible and rate-limited, and I did not build one.

docs.title: What was not tested
docs.text:
• Production sensors (auditd, eBPF, Falco, Tetragon, osquery) and their fidelity, drops, and overhead. strace is not a representative sensor.
  • Real fleet data. False-positive rates here are properties of a hand-written corpus. A real environment will have more sources of both noise and evasion.
  • Rules LNX-001, 003, 004 and 008 on real kernel data. The capture exercises 002, 005, 006, 007, 009 and one negative for 004; the rest are tested on synthetic events only.
  • A knowing adversary. Evasion is two hand-written cases (a per-user crontab, an outbound connection from system bash). There is no bypass analysis.
  • Time to detect and time to contain against a real pipeline; the latency in this lab is synthetic.
  • Response actions. They are written guidance and were never executed.
  • Container and Kubernetes context (namespaces, cgroups, image provenance as fields) and multi-host correlation.

docs.title: Production considerations
docs.text:
Rollout. Run every rule report-only on a few hosts of each role (web, build, bastion, workstation) for at least one full change cycle. Record each alert's disposition; the list of dispositions is the first draft of the allowlist and tells you which rules need a host-role scope (LNX-003 and LNX-004 almost certainly do). Promote a rule to paging only when its residual false-positive sources are known and owned.

Detection. Alert on pipeline health as seriously as on the rules: a falling event rate per host, a rule reported blind, an allowlist entry about to expire, and a rule that has not fired in a long time all deserve a signal. Log the rule version, the allowlist version and the evaluation batch on every alert so a disposition can be reproduced.

Operability. Keep rules in version control as plain files and review them like code, including the exclusions. Give each exception a named owner and an expiry date and notify the owner before the date. Choose the deduplication key per rule, not globally, and state the window in the alert so an analyst knows a count of 50 means 50 hits.

False positives. Expect the seven families above plus whatever your environment adds (CI runners, backup and EDR agents, developer tooling, configuration management). Resolve each by adding context to the rule (host role, a change reference, a binary hash), not by widening exclusions. Never allowlist a generic tool such as tee, sh or python3.

Blast radius. A detection rule's worst case is an unnecessary investigation or, with automation, an unnecessary isolation. Keep the response step manual until the rule's disposition history justifies otherwise, and make any automated step reversible.

Rollback. Disable the rule file or the exception; both are one-line changes and both leave the history intact. Keep the corpus in the repository and re-run the tests when a rule changes so a fix for one false positive cannot silently open a new miss.

docs.title: Limitations and what was not tested
docs.text:
The local experiment validates detection logic on a corpus its author wrote and on one small real capture. It does not validate the complete reference architecture, a production sensor, live cloud enforcement, hosted CI, representative adversarial coverage, or independent audit storage. Review status remains requires-review until a reviewer checks the claims above against validatedAgainst and the linked evidence.

Time to detect, time to contain, population false-positive and false-negative rates, pipeline overhead and cost are not measured in this article. Use the measurement contract to define clocks, denominators, repeated workloads and residual capabilities before claiming those outcomes. Report local fixture counts separately from live coverage.

docs.title: Attack Path Analysis: Preconditions, Reachability and Evidence-Backed Control Breaks
docs.text:
Threat Intelligence · Research

An attack path is a conditional argument, not a line in a graph. Each edge needs a starting capability, reachable target, accepted credential or trust relationship, satisfied policy conditions, and a consequential action. Missing evidence leaves an unknown edge; it does not justify colouring the edge exploitable.

docs.title: The core decision
docs.text: Prioritize paths by preconditions you've actually verified, impact, and how many independent, good controls would have to fail for it to go through. For each edge, name the exact principal or asset, credential, network route, identity transition, policy conditions, runtime requirement, data source, and the checkpoint that's supposed to stop it. Then test the case that should actually break the edge. Recompute after changes, and treat how stale the graph is as part of your confidence, not an afterthought.

docs.title: Scope and non-goals
docs.text:
This reference specifies three representative paths:

  1. CI workflow → federated cloud role → sensitive deployment;
  2. compromised Kubernetes workload → workload identity → cloud data plane; and
  3. cross-tenant application flaw → data-store authorization boundary.

These are design scenarios, not incident claims. The article does not assert a vulnerable named organization, a successful container escape, a production tenant breach, or a complete scanner. It does not treat a CVE, ATT&CK technique, IAM allow, route, or graph edge as proof of exploitability.

docs.title: Graph reachability versus exploitability
docs.text:
Question Evidence Common overstatement Network reachability Resolved destination, route, DNS, security group/NACL/firewall/CNI decision, listener and protocol “Same VPC/cluster means reachable” Identity reachability Credential issuance/presence, issuer, audience, subject, trust and session conditions “Workload can get a token, therefore it can use the target” Authorization reachability Identity/resource/session/boundary/SCP policy and application object decision “An allow statement proves access” Exploitability Vulnerable behavior, controllable input, required state/version/configuration and successful negative/positive test “A route, CVE or technique ID proves compromise” Impact Specific action/resource/data and recovery consequence “Cloud access means administrator”

Model network and identity reachability separately. A resource can be routable but reject identity, or an identity can be authorized while no route exists. Application data APIs may be reachable through an authorized service while the caller is still denied at tenant/object policy.

docs.title: Evidence, time and unknowns
docs.text:
Attach provenance and observation time to every node and edge:

  • Configuration evidence: workflow at commit/digest, IAM and resource policies, trust relationships, deployment manifest, service account, route tables, security rules, database policies.
  • Runtime evidence: resolved artifact digest, issued token claims, pod UID, live route/listener, CloudTrail or audit event, admission decision, application authorization decision.
  • Conditional evidence: branch/environment, OIDC subject/audience, principal/session tags, source ARN/account/VPC endpoint, time, MFA, object/tenant state.
  • Freshness: collection timestamp, maximum age, change event and last successful verification.
  • Unknowns: data not visible in IaC, generated policies, runtime mutation, emergency exceptions, cached permissions, manual console changes and provider-side state.

IaC shows intended managed configuration, not all live state. Graph data can become stale between collection and response. Conditional policies cannot be flattened to an unconditional allow without evaluating the request context. Record “unknown” rather than assuming allow or deny.

docs.title: Scenario 1: CI workflow → federated cloud role → sensitive deployment
docs.text:
Initial foothold

Attacker can modify or execute a specific repository workflow context, or controls a dependency/action that executes in that context. A generic repository read token is insufficient.

Required preconditions

The job receives an OIDC token; the cloud trust policy accepts its issuer, exact audience and subject/claim conditions; the job can request the target role; session/boundary/SCP policy permits deployment; environment approvals do not block; and the deployment target accepts the role's action.

Edge-by-edge path

  1. Workflow control → OIDC request: job has id-token: write and reaches the token endpoint. Enforcement: workflow permissions and protected workflow review.
  2. OIDC token → role session: AWS validates the GitHub issuer and trust-policy audience/subject conditions. Enforcement: role trust policy.
  3. Role session → deployment API: identity policy, permission boundary, session policy, SCP and resource policy permit the exact action/resource/conditions. Enforcement: IAM policy evaluation.
  4. Deployment API → sensitive runtime: artifact, environment and target controls accept the change. Enforcement: protected environment, signer/provenance policy, deployment service and admission controls.

Evidence source

Workflow file at reviewed commit; action pins; environment rules; OIDC token claims from an authorized diagnostic run; role trust/permission/boundary/SCP/resource policies; CloudTrail STS and deployment events; artifact digest and admission/deployment record.

Preventive controls

Untrusted PR jobs without credentials; minimal workflow permissions; full-SHA action pins; exact OIDC audience and subject; environment approval; dedicated deploy role; permission boundary/SCP; artifact attestation with expected signer workflow/source; deployment target authorization.

Detection evidence

Unexpected workflow dispatch/ref, OIDC token issuance context, AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity principal/session, novel source/workflow, role use outside expected deployment API, artifact digest change, failed/overridden admission.

Test that should fail

Run an authorized fixture from the wrong repository, branch, environment and audience. Each must fail role assumption. A valid role session attempting an out-of-scope resource/action must also fail.

What's still not solved

Compromised approved maintainer, protected workflow, identity provider, runner or cloud control plane; validly signed malicious source; review collusion; overly broad emergency role; telemetry delay.

Control classification: workflow permissions, trust conditions, IAM and admission are preventive; OIDC/STS/deployment telemetry is detective; artifact rollback, role disablement and environment recovery are recovery controls.

docs.title: Scenario 2: compromised Kubernetes workload → workload identity → cloud data plane
docs.text:
Initial foothold

Attacker executes code in the specific application container. This does not imply node, cluster-admin, or another pod's identity.

Required preconditions

The pod can obtain or use a projected service-account/workload token; the token has the expected issuer/audience/subject; cloud federation trusts that exact identity; network/DNS can reach the token and data endpoints; cloud policy permits a consequential data action; and no tenant/object guardrail denies it.

Edge-by-edge path

  1. Code execution → workload credential: projected token, metadata/identity socket or SDK credential path is available to the compromised process. Enforcement: pod spec, token automount, file permissions and workload identity agent.
  2. Credential → cloud session: federation validates issuer, audience, subject/service account and configured trust. Enforcement: cloud trust/federated-credential object.
  3. Session → service endpoint: DNS, route, endpoint and security controls permit connection. Enforcement: CNI/node egress, VPC routes, endpoints and security rules.
  4. Cloud API → data operation: identity/resource/endpoint/SCP policy and service-specific conditions permit the exact resource action. Enforcement: cloud IAM and data-plane resource policy.

Evidence source

Pod/deployment and resolved image digest; service account UID; projected-token configuration and decoded non-secret claims; workload-federation trust; CNI/VPC path; effective cloud policies; CloudTrail/data-access logs; runtime process/network telemetry.

Preventive controls

No token automount where unnecessary; one bounded service account per trust class; exact audience/subject trust; least-privilege cloud role; resource/endpoint policy; CNI/node egress control; read-only/non-root/seccomp/capability controls; separate node/cluster boundary for hostile tenants.

Detection evidence

Unexpected token exchange, cloud session name/tags, API calls outside workload baseline, access from new pod/node, denied endpoint/resource-policy calls, unusual process lineage, data-volume anomaly.

Test that should fail

Wrong namespace/service account/audience must fail federation; pod without the identity must not receive credentials; valid session must be denied another bucket/table/key/tenant; blocked egress path must prevent endpoint access.

What's still not solved

Compromised authorized workload can exercise its legitimate permissions; in-memory token theft within validity; node/identity-agent compromise; mis-scoped wildcard policy; side channels; missing data events; provider or policy-evaluation defects.

Control classification: pod identity, federation trust, egress and cloud policy are preventive; audit/runtime/data-access telemetry is detective; token/role disablement, workload quarantine and data recovery are recovery controls.

docs.title: Scenario 3: cross-tenant application flaw → data-store authorization boundary
docs.text:
Initial foothold

Attacker is a valid user or client in tenant A and can control an object identifier, filter, route tenant, job message or cache key. No infrastructure compromise is assumed.

Required preconditions

The API accepts the request; application identity is authorized to query the data store; tenant/user context is missing, mutable, stale or inconsistently propagated; query/cache/queue/storage authorization fails to bind the object to tenant A; and the returned data or side effect is observable.

Edge-by-edge path

  1. Valid tenant-A identity → API request: authentication succeeds but supplies attacker-controlled object input. Enforcement: route/request schema and authenticated tenant binding.
  2. API → application authorization: service fails to decide subject, tenant, object and action, or trusts a mutable header. Enforcement: centralized policy or service-owned object authorization.
  3. Application → data query: shared database credential can access rows beyond tenant A and the query omits tenant predicate/context. Enforcement: tenant-scoped query/repository and database row-level policy where appropriate.
  4. Data result → response/cache/job: cross-tenant result is returned, cached under a non-tenant key, or delivered to a queue/object path without tenant binding. Enforcement: response filtering, tenant-scoped cache/queue/storage namespace and downstream authorization.

Evidence source

API route/auth policy; data-flow and trust-boundary model; authorization decision log; query/repository code; database role and row-security policy; pool/session-context behavior; cache key; queue envelope; object-storage resource policy; positive/negative tenant fixtures.

Preventive controls

Server-derived tenant context; object lookup by tenant plus ID; deny-by-default authorization; forced database row security for the application role where used; transaction-local tenant context; scoped cache/queue/object keys; service-side reauthorization; least-privilege data role.

Detection evidence

Cross-tenant authorization denials, mismatched route/token/object tenant, unusual object enumeration, database rows returned across context, cache-key collisions, queue tenant mismatch, support/emergency path use.

Test that should fail

Tenant A cannot read/update/delete tenant B's object by ID, alternate route, batch/filter, cache, queue replay or object-storage key. Missing tenant context fails closed. Reused pooled connection does not retain the previous transaction's tenant context.

What's still not solved

Policy/query defects shared across all layers, privileged database roles that bypass row policy, table owner/superuser/BYPASSRLS behavior, stale relationship data, support impersonation, backup/analytics copies, cache/queue consumers not covered by the tested API path.

Control classification: application/data-store/cache/queue authorization is preventive; decision/query anomaly telemetry is detective; cache invalidation, data correction, credential rotation and tenant incident response are recovery controls.

docs.title: Control breaks and prioritization
docs.text:
Priority signal Higher confidence/urgency Lower confidence or unknown Starting point Observed compromised principal/asset with timestamp Hypothetical “internet attacker” without a reachable interface Edge evidence Current config plus authorized runtime decision IaC-only, stale graph or name-based inference Conditions Exact request context satisfies all known conditions Conditions discarded during graph ingestion Impact Specific tested read/write/deploy action Generic “admin” or “data access” label Control breaks No independently tested denial before impact Multiple boundaries, each recently confirmed to actually deny it

Pick the earliest reliable point in the chain that removes the required capability without unacceptable operational impact. I'd rather delete an unnecessary trust relationship, route, or permission than bolt on another detector. Keep detective and recovery controls around anyway, because preventive configuration drifts or gets bypassed.

docs.title: Testing what should get denied
docs.text:
For every graph build, test:

  • wrong issuer, audience, subject, branch, repository, namespace, service account and tenant;
  • route absent while identity is valid, and identity denied while route is present;
  • explicit deny, permission boundary, session policy, SCP and resource-policy effects;
  • stale collection after policy/workflow/deployment changes;
  • runtime-only state absent from IaC, including resolved digest, token claims, session tags, emergency exception and pooled tenant context;
  • valid identity without target action/object authorization; and
  • recovery: revoke/disable, quarantine, roll back artifact/configuration, restore data and preserve evidence.

Version the graph schema and collectors. Record collection errors and permissions; a least-privilege collector may legitimately leave unknowns. Alert when a high-impact edge exceeds its maximum age, when a preventive control is removed, and when a case that's supposed to be denied stops actually being denied.

docs.title: MITRE ATT&CK mappings
docs.text: ATT&CK describes observed adversary behaviors; it is not an attack-path proof system. Add a technique only when the scenario actually contains that behavior and cite the current Enterprise or Containers technique page. Do not infer exploitability from the existence of a technique ID, and do not force a cloud/IAM/application authorization edge into a technique that describes something else. This article intentionally leaves scenario-specific technique IDs out until an observed or tested behavior warrants them.

docs.title: What's still not solved
docs.text: A compromised trusted maintainer or identity provider, runtime state the collectors never see, stale or incomplete graphs, bugs in conditional-policy evaluation, ephemeral credentials stolen and used within their validity window, policy exceptions, cloud-provider and application bugs, business operations that are valid but still malicious, telemetry loss, and recovery actions that destroy the evidence or availability you needed — all still real. A graph helps with investigation and prioritization; it never replaces checking each edge yourself.

docs.title: Research question and hypothesis
docs.text:
Question: Does a policy-backed graph path correspond to an admitted sequence of authority transitions?

Falsifiable hypothesis (bounded experiment): A wrong trust context or explicitly denied persistence API breaks the local path; reporting it as executable despite that denial refutes the path-evidence contract.

docs.text: Element Declared scope Actor Compromised CI job or low-privilege tenant Assets Role transition, artifact authority, application object and retained evidence Entry points Federation subjects, update APIs, object IDs and graph edges Trust boundaries Configured relation → authenticated transition → authorized action → observed consequence Impact under investigation False-positive exploit chain or missed viable privilege transition Trusted assumptions Owned test host, reviewed fixture/code and independently established identity context; deployment administrators remain outside the local attacker model

docs.text:

Attach preconditions and evidence time to every edge. Prioritize the earliest independently governed break and retest downstream capability after removing it.

Count exercised allow/deny cases against the declared corpus, keeping structural, native-policy and runtime results separate. Preserve failure, unknown and missing telemetry states. Roll back the exact reviewed control change while retaining evidence; broad privilege or global bypass is not an automatic recovery path.

docs.title: Cloud Incident Case Studies: Evidence, Chronology, and Control Lessons
docs.text:
Threat Intelligence · Research

Incident lessons are useful only when chronology and evidence are honest. This review uses affected-organization disclosures and competent-authority records, separates confirmed facts from engineering inference, and avoids judging an organization for a control that did not exist at incident time.

docs.title: Evidence method
docs.text:
For each case:

  • Confirmed means directly stated by the organization or a government/court source cited below.
  • Engineering inference connects confirmed facts to a control design but is not a claim about the victim's undocumented environment.
  • Retrospective control was released or became available later and is useful for current defense, not a contemporaneous missed requirement.

Public reports do not expose every root cause, architecture detail, detection signal, or corrective action. Absence from a disclosure is not proof a control was absent.

docs.title: Confirmed chronology and scope
docs.text:
Capital One says unauthorized access occurred on March 22 and 23, 2019. The company determined unauthorized access had occurred on July 19 and announced the incident on July 29, 2019. It reported approximately 100 million people in the United States and 6 million in Canada were affected. The disclosed categories and counts vary by data type; the company's facts page is the authoritative scope reference rather than the shorthand "100 million records."

The US Department of Justice described a misconfigured web application firewall that enabled commands to reach and obtain credentials for data access. The prosecution and later court materials provide case-specific evidence; they should not be expanded into an unsupported claim that every S3 bucket or the entire AWS environment was exposed.

docs.title: Control analysis
docs.text:
Engineering lessons for current systems:

  • constrain the application/WAF instance role to exact required actions/resources;
  • prevent server-side request forgery through URL allowlists, parser-safe validation, egress controls, and removal of generic fetch/proxy behavior;
  • segment sensitive data and use data-access/audit detections independent of the web tier;
  • monitor unusual metadata/credential access, role sessions, object enumeration, and bulk reads;
  • treat application-layer compromise plus reachable workload credentials as a compound threat and test it.

AWS launched IMDSv2 on November 19, 2019 - months after the March incident. Requiring IMDSv2 and limiting metadata hop behavior are strong retrospective defense-in-depth recommendations for current EC2 designs. They must not be described as a control Capital One failed to enable at incident time.

docs.title: Residual caution
docs.text: IMDSv2 reduces important SSRF/metadata attack paths but does not repair an overly privileged role, arbitrary command execution, compromised host, exposed credentials, or sensitive-data access that the role is authorized to perform.

docs.title: Uber, September 2022
docs.text: Source continuity: the former Uber newsroom URL returned 404 during this audit. The linked SEC Exhibit 99.1 preserves Uber’s September 19 statement and was consulted on 2026-11-02. This changes source availability, not the incident scope.

docs.title: Confirmed chronology and access path
docs.text:
Uber's September 19 security update said an external contractor's account was compromised. Uber reported it was likely the attacker purchased the contractor's corporate password after the contractor's personal device was infected with malware. The attacker repeatedly attempted to log in, generating two-factor approval requests, and the contractor accepted one. Uber said the attacker then accessed other employee accounts and tools and posted a message to a company-wide Slack channel. The company identified the activity on September 15 and responded by restricting affected systems and access.

Use Uber's update for the organization's stated impact. Avoid summaries such as "the attacker controlled all infrastructure" unless a primary source establishes that scope. Password possession plus an approved MFA prompt explains an authenticated session; it does not by itself prove every subsequent privilege path or dataset.

docs.title: Control analysis
docs.text:
Engineering inference for present-day programs:

  • use phishing-resistant authentication (for example device-bound/passkey/security- key mechanisms appropriate to the workforce platform) for privileged access;
  • reduce MFA push fatigue with number matching, context, rate limits, risk signals, help-desk controls, and user reporting;
  • prevent an ordinary contractor session from becoming an administrative platform session through tiered identities, just-in-time privilege, device health, network/ application access policy, and separate privileged workstations;
  • restrict and monitor credential stores, scripts, shared drives, PAM tools, service credentials, and administrative remote-management systems;
  • correlate identity, endpoint, SaaS, source-control, secrets, and cloud audit events.

docs.title: Failure mode lesson
docs.text: MFA success is an authentication signal, not proof of legitimate intent. Repeated denials followed by approval, new device/location, contractor privilege use, and rapid movement across administrative tools should create high-confidence containment and human-verification paths.

docs.title: Confirmed chronology and mechanism
docs.text:
CircleCI's incident report states that malware on an employee laptop enabled a threat actor to steal a valid, two-factor-authenticated session cookie. CircleCI reported the initial laptop compromise on December 16, 2022, reconnaissance on December 19, and data exfiltration on December 22. The employee had privileges that enabled generation of production access tokens, and the attacker extracted encryption keys from a running process, enabling access to encrypted customer credentials. CircleCI alerted customers in early January 2023 and instructed rotation.

The event is best described as a December 2022 compromise discovered/disclosed in January 2023, not simply a "2023 breach." The primary report should govern detailed scope, token rotation, and remediation claims.

docs.title: Control analysis
docs.text:
Engineering lessons:

  • session cookies for privileged SaaS/control-plane access are bearer credentials; protect endpoints, bind sessions/device context where supported, shorten privileged lifetimes, and reauthenticate for critical actions;
  • separate ordinary engineering sessions from production token-generation authority;
  • reduce standing privileges and require just-in-time, approved, attributable access;
  • design encryption so a single long-running process and its identity cannot expose every customer's credential without additional scoped authorization/audit;
  • make customer-secret rotation fast, automatable, and inventory-driven;
  • provide customers with exact affected secret categories, time windows, audit evidence, and verification steps.

Encryption at rest did not make the decrypted data inaccessible to an authorized running process. This is a general envelope/key-access design lesson, not a reason to discard encryption at rest.

docs.title: Cross-case engineering patterns
docs.text: Pattern Capital One Uber CircleCI Current design response Trusted workload/user session abused workload credentials reached from web tier contractor session accepted after MFA prompts stolen authenticated session cookie constrain session privilege and continuously evaluate context Privilege compounded impact data-access role capabilities movement into other internal tools/accounts ability to mint production tokens/read keys eliminate standing privilege; separate trust tiers and duties One control was insufficient perimeter/WAF did not contain data role MFA approval did not establish legitimate intent encryption did not protect from authorized process/key access layer preventive, detective, and recovery controls Credential lifecycle mattered workload credential scope/session password/session/admin secrets customer secrets required rotation inventory, scope, short lifetime, revocation and rehearsed rotation Detection/reconstruction required multiple planes web, STS/cloud, data access IdP, endpoint, SaaS/internal tools endpoint, identity, production, customer credential access normalize/correlate control-plane and data-plane telemetry

docs.title: Validation questions for architectures
docs.text:
1. Can a server-side request or code-execution flaw reach a credential endpoint or data plane, and what exact authorization would that credential have?
  2. Does a successful MFA/session event permit privilege escalation without independent device, role, approval, and risk controls?
  3. Which identities can mint production/customer credentials or read encryption keys from memory/control planes?
  4. Can the organization identify every credential/artifact/data object touched by one compromised session and revoke/rotate it quickly?
  5. Are controls evaluated as of incident date, and are later mitigations labeled retrospective?

docs.title: Operational checklist
docs.text:
Incident timelines use occurrence, detection, containment, and disclosure dates.

Record counts and access scope retain the source's precision and caveats.

Confirmed fact, inference, and retrospective control are visibly separated.

Identity/session privilege is correlated with endpoint, SaaS, cloud, and data access telemetry.

Workload/user credentials are narrow, short-lived, and revocable.

Break-glass, bulk-secret rotation, and customer notification evidence are tested.

New vendor/court disclosures trigger review rather than silent narrative drift.

docs.title: Limitations
docs.text: These are public-source case studies, not forensic reports. They do not assign legal liability, evaluate controls unavailable in private evidence, or claim that listed recommendations would certainly have prevented the incidents.

docs.title: Research question and hypothesis
docs.text:
Question: Can public incident disclosures support control lessons without inventing the missing exploit details?

Falsifiable hypothesis (bounded experiment): Every incident-specific statement maps to an owner/court source; a detail supported only by an analogous lab must remain a hypothesis rather than incident fact.

docs.title: AI Agent External Tool-Broker Lab
docs.text:
Application Security · Lab

Exercises action-bound approval, replay resistance, kill-switch behavior, and unknown-argument denial in a local tool broker.

Status: tested teaching implementation. The surrounding production architecture in appsec/ai-agent-security.md is conceptual and partially tested.

This dependency-free Node.js lab demonstrates one narrow security boundary: a model may propose an action, but a broker outside the model decides whether a fake executor receives it. The executor stores an in-memory record and returns status: simulated; it performs no network, filesystem, financial, cloud, or other external action.

docs.title: Security properties exercised
docs.text:
The broker receives authenticatedContext separately from proposedCall and then:

  • resolves a static server-side policy for the authenticated principal;
  • rejects an unauthorized principal, tenant, tool, destination, or amount;
  • accepts only a closed argument schema;
  • requires approval at or above the configured impact threshold;
  • asks an injected approval verifier for the authoritative approval record;
  • binds approval to principal, tenant, tool, amount, and destination;
  • consumes approval before execution to reject replay;
  • checks an independently injected execution kill switch;
  • emits sanitized decision and outcome events to an in-memory audit sink;
  • invokes a fake executor only after all controls allow the call.

The tests assert that the fake executor's invocation count stays zero for denied actions. This distinction matters: a model may still propose a forbidden action, but it must not acquire authority by doing so.

docs.title: Run
docs.text:
From the repository root with Node.js 22 or newer:

node --test labs/ai-agent-security/tests/broker.test.js

No package installation, environment variable, credential, service, container, or network connection is required.

docs.title: Files
docs.text:
• broker.js contains the broker and stable denial codes.
  • tests/broker.test.js has tests for both what should work and what should get denied, plus the fake policy, approval store, audit sink, kill switch, and executor.

docs.title: Deliberate limitations
docs.text:
This is not a production authorization library. In particular:

  • authenticatedContext is assumed to come from a trusted gateway. The lab does not validate a session, workload certificate, issuer, signature, audience, freshness, revocation, or tenant membership source.
  • The policy is an in-process fixture. It has no administrative authorization, durable version, distribution, cache, or outage behavior.
  • The approval verifier reads an in-memory map. It does not authenticate an approver, verify a signature, enforce separation of duties, or persist single-use state across processes.
  • Replay state, audit events, and fake execution records are memory-only.
  • The broker validates one teaching schema for a simulated payment-like action. A real broker needs a reviewed, versioned schema and constraints per tool.
  • The lab does not implement MCP, OAuth, token exchange, downstream reauthorization, idempotency reconciliation, a sandbox, secret delivery, egress control, rate limiting, or durable incident evidence.

For production, derive identity and tenant outside the model, use a maintained authorization implementation, bind short-lived credentials to the selected resource, make the downstream service authorize again, and test fail-closed behavior at every boundary.

docs.text:
Element Bounded experiment Actor Model controlling tool proposal and approval ID Assets tool authority, tenant/action binding and approval consumption Entry points JSON call and replayed approval Boundary Authenticated context → external broker → atomic in-memory consume → fake executor Safety Owned synthetic fixtures; no production data or cloud credentials; no cloud deployment 
flowchart LR
  I[Controlled input] --> B[Tested boundary]
  B --> A[Expected allowed case]
  B --> D[Expected denied case]
  A --> E[Assertions and sanitized evidence]

docs.title: Complete local setup
docs.text:
Use a fresh repository checkout and the prerequisites above. From repository root:

npm ci --ignore-scripts
node --test labs/ai-agent-security/tests/broker.test.js

This is a local decision experiment, so the complete implementation is its tracked code, fixtures and policy files. It needs no Terraform deployment, service account or publicly exposed server. Never relocate fixture workflows into an active CI directory without a separate environment review.

docs.title: Evidence, expected output and interpretation
docs.text:
The documented command exits zero only when its assertions pass; an unexpected allow/deny, schema or state result is a failure. Preserve the full command output under ignored .artifacts/research/ with runtime/tool versions and exit status. Use the specific expected markers above rather than inventing example output. The lab audit records the validation run.

No model, MCP transport, durable approval store or real downstream tool is executed. Local finite-case coverage is not a production false-positive or false-negative estimate. TTD/TTC, representative pipeline overhead and monthly cloud cost are not measured in this lab.

docs.title: Teardown and resources
docs.text:
The processes exit and remove their temporary test files. There is no cloud destroy command. Retained evidence, optional provider downloads and local Docker image cache are your only persistent outputs; remove them after review. Node dependencies can remain for subsequent runs.

Local CPU, memory, dependency downloads and optional image disk space are the resource cost. There is no measured cloud bill. Related research links above define which claims the experiment supports.

docs.title: Azure landing-zone hierarchy and policy lab
docs.text:
Cloud Security · Lab

Validates pinned-provider Terraform hierarchy, policy, identity and logging assumptions without deploying cloud resources.

docs.title: Terraform objective and evidence boundary
docs.text: Partially tested: the pinned AzureRM 4.50.0 provider validates the Terraform schema and three mock-plan tests. No Azure token exchange, policy evaluation, resource creation, subscription move or log delivery was executed. The older Bicep example below is retained as an alternative compilation exercise.

docs.title: Threat model and architecture
docs.text:
A workload contributor must not change inherited policy or audit ownership. Assets are hierarchy, policy, evidence identity and log coverage. Entry points are parent moves, policy effects, federated subject and diagnostic configuration. Bootstrap administration is trusted separately from a read-only evidence identity.

flowchart TD
  P[Existing isolated parent management group] --> R[Lab root]
  R --> F[Platform]
  R --> W[Landing zones]
  R --> S[Sandbox]
  R --> A[Audit-first location policy]
  U[Existing disposable subscription, not moved] --> D[Activity diagnostics]
  D --> L[Lab Log Analytics workspace]
  G[Exact GitHub lab subject] --> I[Read-only evidence identity]
  I --> L

docs.title: Prerequisites and complete local validation — tested
docs.text:
Terraform >=1.7,<2, internet to initialize AzureRM 4.50.0, and about 1 GiB disk for provider code. No Azure login or credential is needed for mocked tests.

bash labs/azure-landing-zone/validate.sh

Expected: schema validation succeeds and three runs pass: audit-first/scoped identity, Disabled-policy rejection and wildcard-subject rejection. Mock plans use all-zero synthetic UUIDs and never call Azure. Keep the generated provider lockfile in version control. Source is terraform/main.tf.

docs.title: Management-group, identity, logging and guardrail assumptions
docs.text:
• The existing parent is an isolated lab parent in a dedicated tenant. A bootstrap identity would need narrowly reviewed hierarchy/policy rights there and resource, identity, diagnostic and role-assignment rights in the disposable subscription. This module deliberately does not grant its own bootstrap permissions.
  • The subscription is not moved beneath the new hierarchy. Runtime policy inheritance for that subscription is not established. Never infer inherited enforcement from a hierarchy diagram or mock plan.
  • Default policy effect is audit; it records noncompliance and does not block it. deny is an explicit input for a later impact-reviewed experiment. Disabled is rejected. Tenant-specific aliases and actual policy evaluation remain untested.
  • The evidence identity receives Log Analytics Reader at the workspace only. Its exact issuer/audience/subject trust and GitHub environment must be separately checked with an actual non-production token exchange before use.
  • Subscription activity categories Administrative, Policy and Security are sent to a lab workspace in the design. Data-plane services, Entra logs, independent log-archive protection and source freshness are outside it. The workspace is in the lab subscription and is not an independent production archive.
  • Retention is 30 days and daily quota is 1 GiB. A quota is not a guaranteed bill cap and can cause monitoring gaps. No public service/network resource is created by the template, but workspace private connectivity is not configured here.

docs.title: Evidence, cost and cleanup
docs.text:
mkdir -p .artifacts/research
bash labs/azure-landing-zone/validate.sh > .artifacts/research/azure-terraform.txt 2>&1

No cloud resources exist to destroy. Remove local .terraform/ downloads and retained evidence after review, keeping .terraform.lock.hcl. A later authorized cloud run would incur workspace ingestion/retention and possibly related service charges; costs and policy/logging effectiveness are not measured. It requires separate state, plan review and a reviewed destroy plan that first removes only lab policy/diagnostic/role assignments, then lab identities/workspace/groups, then empty child and root management groups. Never delete the existing parent, move subscriptions, or weaken production inheritance as cleanup.

Read the maintained landing-zone research and lab audit. The Azure experiment does not establish AWS Organizations/SCP behavior.

docs.title: Historical alternative: Bicep compilation
docs.text: This lab compiles a small tenant-scope Bicep design for a management-group hierarchy and an audit-first custom policy assignment. It demonstrates deployment shape, federated CI identity, and a reviewable what-if boundary; it does not deploy during repository validation.

docs.title: Architecture decision
docs.text: The sample separates platform, landing-zone, and sandbox subscriptions beneath an organization root. The policy begins with audit, because changing a broad management-group policy to deny before impact analysis can interrupt workloads. Production design still needs connectivity, identity, security, decommissioned, and workload-archetype management groups based on the organization's operating model.

docs.title: Prerequisites and compile
docs.text:
• Azure CLI 2.83.0 or later with Bicep support.
  • No Azure login is needed to compile.
az bicep build --file labs/azure-landing-zone/main.bicep

Expected result: Bicep returns a compiled ARM template without diagnostics. The repository code validator performs this compilation when Azure CLI is available and reports an explicit limitation otherwise.

docs.title: What-if, not deployment
docs.text:
After replacing every angle-bracket placeholder, an authorized reviewer may inspect:

az login --tenant <tenant-id> --allow-no-subscriptions
az deployment tenant what-if \
 --name landing-zone-review \
 --location canadacentral \
 --template-file labs/azure-landing-zone/main.bicep \
 --parameters '@labs/azure-landing-zone/parameters.example.json'

The included workflow uses GitHub OIDC and a protected environment. Configure the federated credential with an exact repository/environment subject, constrain the service principal to the required tenant/management-group operations, and require a human review of the what-if artifact. Do not add a client secret.

docs.title: Deployment and rollback considerations
docs.text: Management-group and policy changes have a wide blast radius. Roll out new policy in audit mode, inventory noncompliance, assign named exemption owners with expiry, pilot a narrow management group, then move to deny only with tested break-glass and rollback procedures. Removing a policy assignment does not undo resource mutations performed by deployIfNotExists or modify; this sample deliberately uses audit.

docs.title: Negative cases to review
docs.text:
• placeholder or duplicate management-group IDs;
  • an OIDC subject broader than the protected environment;
  • policy enforcement before exemptions and regional dependencies are inventoried;
  • a hierarchy move that changes inherited role and policy scope;
  • subscription vending without ownership, budget, network, logging, and lifecycle metadata;
  • a tenant-level deployment identity with permanent credentials or excessive roles.

docs.title: Cleanup and limitations
docs.text: Compilation creates main.json; remove that generated file after inspection. This lab does not execute what-if in CI because it has no authorized tenant, and it does not deploy, move subscriptions, create role assignments, configure networking, or validate tenant-specific Azure Policy aliases. What-if itself is predictive output, not proof of runtime correctness.

docs.title: Docker image and runtime hardening lab
docs.text:
Cloud Security · Lab

Runs an insecure and a hardened configuration of the same small service, measures the difference from inside the containers, and exercises a static policy gate, a derived seccomp profile, image scanning, SBOM generation and local-only signing.

Status: partially tested. The static policy gate runs anywhere and is part of npm run validate. The runtime, scanning, SBOM and signing steps ran on one disposable VM on 2026-11-05 (85 of 85 assertions passed) and are not wired into CI. AppArmor, rootless Docker, user-namespace remapping and a production signing trust root were not executed (see What was not tested).

Evidence labels used on this page:

Label Meaning Closest tier in the evidence standards tested locally I ran it in this lab and kept the output in evidence/ T2/T3, T4 where the same case ran on both stacks source-reviewed I read it in the named primary source; not executed here T0 policy model A rule set evaluated by a local test, not enforced by the real system T1 requires-review No independent reviewer has checked it against its sources review status of this page

docs.title: Scope
docs.text:
One service, two configurations, one question: what can code running inside the container do, and what changes when the controls are on? The service is a Go program of about 730 lines (standard library only) (app/main.go) with an HTTP endpoint and a probe subcommand that tries a fixed list of benign operations (write the root filesystem, chown, mknod, open a raw socket, mount, create a user namespace, reach the Docker socket, write a bind-mounted directory, open a TCP connection) and reports the errno the kernel returned. Observing denials from inside the container is the point; reading a Compose file and assuming it took effect is how hardening claims go wrong.

In scope: image build, base-image choice, user, filesystem, capabilities, no-new-privileges, seccomp, resource limits, network topology, image scanning, SBOM, signing and verification by digest.

Out of scope: Kubernetes (see the Kubernetes lab), runtime detection tooling, registry operations, host hardening and anything that targets systems I do not own. Nothing here contacts a real cloud account, production system or third-party service other than downloading base images and the Trivy vulnerability database.

Safety. The insecure stack runs privileged: true, pid: host and mounts the Docker socket on purpose. Run run-lab.sh only on a throwaway VM or CI runner. The probe sends one read-only GET /_ping to the socket and nothing else; it creates no containers and changes no host state outside a temp directory the script owns.

docs.title: What I built
docs.text:
Path Purpose app/ Go (stdlib only) service with probe, healthcheck, forktest, memtest subcommands, plus k8sprobe and tcpcheck, which the Kubernetes lab reuses insecure/Dockerfile, insecure/compose.yaml Deliberately bad baseline; every line maps to a rule the gate must report hardened/Dockerfile, hardened/compose.yaml Same service, controls on hardened/seccomp.json Allowlist profile derived from strace of the shipped binary scripts/gen-seccomp.sh Derives the profile; prints which syscalls were service, harness, hand-off or removed scripts/run-lab.sh Builds, runs both stacks, runs controls, scans, signs, asserts, optionally publishes evidence scripts/scan.sh, scripts/sign-verify.sh Trivy + Syft; local registry + cosign with an ephemeral key tests/policy-check.js (+ .test.js) Static Dockerfile/Compose gate; 38 tests, a positive and a negative case per rule tests/runtime_check.py, inventory.py, summarize_scan.py Assertions on observed output, image attack-surface inventory, scan dedup evidence/ Sanitized output of the run described below

    SRC["app source"] --> B1["builder stage<br/>digest-pinned Go image"]
    B1 --> IMG["static binary on<br/>distroless nonroot"]
  end
