Every box except "verify digest before run" was executed by run-lab.sh; verification was executed as a command (cosign verify) but nothing in this lab refuses to start an unsigned image. Enforcement at deploy time needs an admission controller or a deploy wrapper; the Kubernetes lab models that decision.

docs.title: Attack surface and threat model
docs.text:
Element Declared scope Actor Code running as the container's main process: a compromised dependency, an RCE in the service, or a malicious image layer Assets The host kernel and filesystem, the Docker daemon, neighbouring containers, the service's own data Entry points Anything the process can call: syscalls, mounted paths, sockets, network Trust boundary Container process → kernel (namespaces, capabilities, seccomp, cgroups) → host Not in scope A kernel vulnerability or runc escape; hardening reduces reachable kernel surface but cannot make a shared kernel a hard multi-tenant boundary

The insecure configuration is built to expose each of these at once: root, full capability set, no syscall filter, host PID namespace, Docker socket, writable bind mount, writable root filesystem, no limits, all-interface port.

docs.title: Control decisions
docs.text:
Each row names what the control prevents and what it does not. The last column is the cost I would expect to pay.

Control Insecure Hardened Stops Does not stop Cost / false-positive risk Base image golang:1.27-alpine (toolchain, apk, shell ship in runtime), tag only distroless static-debian12:nonroot, tag + digest Post-exploitation tooling: no shell, package manager or compiler Vulnerable code in the binary itself No shell means no docker exec sh; debug with an ephemeral debug container or a separate debug image User root (uid 0) 65532:65532 Writing root-owned files, binding <1024 without caps Kernel bugs reachable by unprivileged users Bind-mounted volumes must be writable by that uid; fails at start, visibly Capabilities 40 effective (privileged) cap_drop: ALL, CapEff=0 chown, mknod, raw sockets, mount via CAP_* checks Anything that needs no capability Needs NET_BIND_SERVICE for port 80/443 unless you remap ports; ping needs NET_RAW no-new-privileges NoNewPrivs: 0 NoNewPrivs: 1 setuid/file-capability privilege gain on execve A process that is already privileged Breaks legitimate setuid helpers (sudo, ping on some images) Seccomp none (Seccomp: 0) allowlist, default ERRNO Namespace creation via clone, mount, ptrace, bpf, module loading, open_by_handle_at Abuse of syscalls that remain allowed Highest false-positive risk of any control here; see Seccomp profile Root filesystem writable read_only: true + 8 MiB noexec tmpfs on /tmp Persisting a payload or tampering with binaries in the image layer Memory-only attacks; writes to any mounted volume Every writable path must be enumerated; apps that write to /var/cache break at runtime Resource limits none 128 MiB (no swap), 64 PIDs, 0.5 CPU Memory exhaustion, fork exhaustion, CPU starvation of neighbours Network or disk-bandwidth exhaustion An undersized limit is an availability incident, not a security event; size from measured peaks Namespaces pid: host own PID namespace Enumerating and signalling host processes — None for this app Socket / mounts Docker socket, writable host dir none Daemon API access (host-root equivalent), host file tampering — CI runners and reverse proxies often want the socket; give them a socket proxy or a rootless daemon instead Network default bridge, 0.0.0.0:8080 internal: true, no published port Egress to anything outside the network; reachability of the canary Abuse of what the app is allowed to talk to An internal-only service needs a second hop for ingress (a proxy on both networks) Supply chain unpinned tag, no signature digest pins, SBOM, cosign signature + attestation Tag substitution; unverified bytes A compromised build pipeline that signs bad bytes Digest pins stop receiving base-image fixes until bumped (observed below)

docs.title: Seccomp profile
docs.text:
I did not copy a profile. scripts/gen-seccomp.sh extracts /app/posture from the built image, runs it under strace -f for the service workload and the lab-harness subcommands, removes a fixed deny list the probe attempts on purpose (strace records an attempt even when the kernel refuses it, so without this step the profile would learn the attacks), and emits a default-ERRNO allowlist. Observed on this run:

service syscalls allowed : 41
runtime hand-off allowed : 3  ['fstatfs', 'statfs', 'statx']
harness-only allowed     : 9  ['dup3', 'mkdirat', 'newfstatat', 'pidfd_open', 'pidfd_send_signal', 'pipe2', 'readlinkat', 'unlinkat', 'waitid']
observed but removed     : 4  ['fchownat', 'mknodat', 'mount', 'umount2']

Status: tested locally. The output above is from the run that generated the committed hardened/seccomp.json.

Three things I learned the hard way, all observed:

  1. An application trace is not enough. The first profile left the container unable to start: runc init itself issues syscalls after the filter is loaded and before execve. On runc 1.5.2 the failure walked from fstatfs to statx before the container came up. That "hand-off" set is runtime-version dependent; re-derive it when runc changes.
  2. clone needs an argument filter, not an allow. The profile allows clone only when flags & 0x7E020000 == 0 (the namespace flags) and returns ENOSYS for clone3, because seccomp cannot inspect the clone3 flags struct and libc/Go fall back to clone. This matches the structure of Moby's default profile (source-reviewed: moby/profiles seccomp/default.json, which uses the same 2114060288 mask and errnoRet: 38 for clone3 when CAP_SYS_ADMIN is absent).
  3. A denial is only evidence if you know which layer produced it. mount, chown, mknod and raw sockets are refused by capability checks as well, so they cannot show that seccomp works. User-namespace creation through clone(CLONE_NEWUSER) needs no capability (Docker's seccomp documentation calls this out), so it is the discriminating probe. I also tried unshare(CLONE_NEWUSER) first and got EINVAL even with every restriction off (tested locally). unshare(2) documents EINVAL for CLONE_NEWUSER when the caller is multithreaded (source-reviewed), and a Go program is always multithreaded. A probe that fails for an unrelated reason would have looked like a pass.

The default action is ERRNO, not KILL. A missed syscall then degrades one request instead of killing PID 1 and restart-looping the service. The cost is that a blocked syscall can be swallowed by code that ignores errors.

docs.title: Image scanning: what the numbers say, and what they do not
docs.text:
This is where my expectation was wrong, so I am recording it as found. tested locally, Trivy 0.76.1, vulnerability DB updated 2026-11-04 19:02 UTC, both images built from golang:1.27-alpine (Go 1.27.3):

Measure insecure (alpine 3.24.3 + toolchain) hardened (debian 12.15 distroless) Unique CVE/package findings 0 4 (all UNKNOWN severity: Debian LTS advisories against ca-certificates and tzdata; fixed versions exist) SBOM-only scan (trivy sbom on the Syft CycloneDX file) 0 4 (agrees with the image scan) SBOM components by type 39 library, 213 file, 1 application, 1 OS 7 library, 950 file, 1 OS Executable files in the image 86 10 Shell / package manager / compiler ash+sh / apk / go none / none / none Image content size 356,984,047 bytes 9,404,585 bytes

Reading it correctly:

  • A CVE count did not rank these images by risk. The image with a shell, a package manager and a compiler had no known vulnerabilities on the day it was scanned; the hardened image had four. The hardened image's attack surface is far smaller, which is why the lab measures it directly (tests/inventory.py walks the exported filesystem) instead of trusting scan counts.
  • The hardened image is older on purpose, and that is a trade. Pinning the distroless base by digest makes the build reproducible and stops a registry-side tag move from changing what you run. It also freezes the base at the digest I pinned, so Debian updates that landed afterwards show up as findings. Digest pinning only works with automation that bumps the digest (Renovate/Dependabot or a scheduled rebuild) and re-scans. I did not build that automation here.
  • Raw counts mislead; deduplicate. An earlier scan of the same two images built from golang:1.24-alpine reported 976 raw findings for the insecure image, which collapse to 116 unique CVE/package pairs because the same Go standard-library CVEs repeat for every Go binary in the toolchain. The hardened image, then, carried 23 HIGH findings from the toolchain's standard library. Those two scans are kept as a clearly-labeled one-off record, observation-go124-toolchain-scan.json, and cannot be regenerated: the images no longer exist and the DB moves daily. Moving the builder to a supported toolchain removed them. The lesson is that "distroless" does not mean "no findings": a statically linked Go binary carries its toolchain's standard library.
  • SBOM totals are not comparable. 958 vs 254 components looks like the opposite of the truth; file-level components (every zoneinfo file in tzdata) dominate. Compare package-level components.
  • Trivy's Dockerfile checks agreed with my gate on the big items. It flagged the insecure Dockerfile for root user (DS-0002, HIGH), no HEALTHCHECK (DS-0026) and the secret-shaped ENV (DS-0031, CRITICAL) and reported nothing for the hardened one. My gate reports 30 findings vs 0 because it also covers Compose.

docs.title: Signing: what local-only signing proves
docs.text:
scripts/sign-verify.sh runs a registry:2 container on loopback, generates an ephemeral key pair with a random one-time password (never written to disk or committed), and signs with an empty signing config (no Fulcio, Rekor or TSA). cosign v3 deprecates --tlog-upload=false; an explicit empty signing config is the supported way to say "no transparency service". Results (tested locally, evidence/signing__summary.json):

Case Expected Observed Verify the signed hardened digest, right key accept accepted Verify the unsigned insecure digest reject rejected (no signatures found) Verify the signed digest with an unrelated key reject rejected Verify by tag, then re-point the tag at different content and verify again accept, then reject accepted, then rejected Verify the SBOM attestation (cyclonedx) accept accepted Verify the same digest as slsaprovenance reject rejected

This proves the mechanics: a signature binds to a digest, so tag substitution fails verification. It does not prove: who signed (the key is anonymous), when (no transparency log or timestamp), or that the signer was your pipeline. Production needs keyless signing bound to a CI workload identity or a KMS/HSM key, a transparency log, and verification at admission against a pinned identity. The existing Kubernetes lab contains the admission-side ImageValidatingPolicy and its offline model; neither is exercised against a real signature here.

docs.title: Validation
docs.text:
All commands run from the repository root. Environment for the recorded run (evidence/versions.txt): Linux kernel 6.18.44, Docker Engine 29.9.2 (overlayfs snapshotter, cgroup v1), Compose 5.6.1, runc 1.5.2, Trivy 0.76.1, Syft 1.56.0, cosign v3.1.4, strace 6.8. docker info listed only seccomp under security options.

node --test labs/docker-security/tests/policy-check.test.js     # no Docker needed
bash labs/docker-security/scripts/run-lab.sh --publish-evidence  # needs a disposable Docker host

docs.title: Static gate (tested locally, no Docker)
docs.text: node labs/docker-security/tests/policy-check.js labs/docker-security/insecure → 30 findings, exit 1. ... hardened → 0 findings, exit 0. 38 unit tests pass: one positive and one negative case per rule, plus the cases below. Writing them found a real defect in my own rule: docker.sock:ro evaded the socket rule because the regex anchored on end-of-string. A read-only mount of a socket file does not restrict API calls, so the rule now matches :ro, containerd.sock, podman.sock and crio.sock as well.

docs.title: Runtime comparison (tested locally)
docs.text:
Observed from inside the running service containers via docker compose exec ... probe (evidence/runtime__*-probe.json):

Observation Insecure Hardened Effective uid 0 65532 CapEff 000001fffeffffff (40 capabilities, no SYS_RESOURCE because this VM drops it) 0000000000000000 NoNewPrivs / Seccomp 0 / 0 (off) 1 / 2 (filter, 1 filter) Root filesystem writable read-only Memory / PIDs / CPU unlimited / unlimited / unlimited 134217728 / 64 / 50000 µs per 100000 Visible processes, PID 1 96, the VM's init (host PID namespace) 2, posture write_root_filesystem allowed EROFS write_tmp_scratch allowed allowed (the app still works) chown_to_other_uid, mknod_char_device, raw_socket, mount_tmpfs allowed EPERM each clone_new_user_namespace allowed EPERM Docker socket present, GET /_ping → HTTP/1.0 200 OK ENOENT Bind-mounted host directory read and write allowed; file written by the container is owned by uid 0 on the host ENOENT TCP to the canary service allowed blocked, name does not resolve (different network)

Seccomp attribution controls (same user, caps dropped, no-new-privileges, read-only; only --security-opt seccomp varies, evidence/runtime__hardened-seccomp-*-probe.json):

seccomp setting Seccomp mode clone(CLONE_NEWUSER) unconfined 0 allowed Docker default profile 2 EPERM this lab's derived profile 2 EPERM

With capabilities already empty, the only thing that changes between rows is the seccomp setting. That is what makes the denial attributable to the filter.

Resource limits:

Test Insecure Hardened forktest 200 (bounded: sleeping children, then exit) 200 started 13 started, EAGAIN (Go runtime threads count against the 64-PID limit) memtest 512 (touch 512 MiB) exit 0 killed, exit 137; last progress line touched_mib: 112

After the hardened OOM kill, Docker reported running oom_killed=true health=healthy. The kernel killed the exec'd test process, not PID 1, so the service stayed up. That is OOM victim selection, not a guarantee: a leak in the service itself would be the victim, and Docker's own documentation notes the kernel kills processes in a container when it hits its limit. Treat limits as availability controls.

docs.title: What the lab asserts
docs.text: run-lab.sh ends by running tests/runtime_check.py, which exits nonzero when any observed value differs from the claims above: 85 passed, 0 failed on the recorded run. Supply-chain assertions print SKIP with the recorded reason when Trivy, Syft or cosign are absent, never a silent pass.

docs.title: What was not tested
docs.text:
• AppArmor / SELinux profiles. docker info showed name=seccomp only; /sys/kernel/security/lsm does not exist on this VM kernel, so no LSM profile could be loaded. Not executed. Docker's security documentation describes AppArmor and SELinux as an additional layer; whatever a production host adds on top of the controls measured here is unmeasured.
  • Rootless Docker and userns-remap. Not executed. These change what "uid 0 in the container" means and are the control I would add for workloads that must run as root.
  • cgroup v2. The run was on cgroup v1. The probe reads both layouts, but the v2 paths were not exercised.
  • Windows, macOS/Docker Desktop, Podman, containerd-direct.
  • Hosted CI. run-lab.sh is not part of npm run verify:native-labs; adding a privileged-container job to the gating workflow without a hosted-runner trial would risk blocking publication. Static tests are in npm run validate.
  • Keyless signing, Rekor, a transparency-log-backed verification, KMS keys. Local ephemeral key only.
  • Runtime detection (Falco, Tetragon, auditd) for the behaviours the probe exercises. See the Linux telemetry lab for synthetic detection logic.
  • Escape techniques. The lab does not attempt container escapes, and a passing run is not a claim that none exist.
  • Reproducible builds. The two images rebuild with different digests each time; -trimpath and a pinned builder narrow the gap but I did not verify bit-for-bit reproducibility.

docs.title: Production considerations
docs.text:
Rollout. Do not enable everything at once. Order by blast radius and ease of rollback: (1) digest pins and non-root, (2) no-new-privileges and cap_drop: ALL with a measured add-back list, (3) read-only root with a tmpfs inventory, (4) resource limits from observed peaks plus headroom, (5) seccomp last, in a lower environment first. For seccomp, ship SCMP_ACT_LOG (needs auditd/journald) for at least one full release cycle and review the denied syscalls before switching to ERRNO; this lab went straight to ERRNO because its workload is fully enumerated.

False positives. The things that break first are exactly the things hardening removes: apps that write outside declared paths (EROFS), images that expect root-owned volumes (EACCES), services that silently ignore EPERM from a blocked syscall, setuid helpers, JIT runtimes and anything calling clone3. A seccomp profile learned from a bounded workload will miss rare paths (a reload handler, a crash dumper, a TLS renegotiation path); mitigate with staged LOG mode, a regression test that exercises every code path, and a per-service exception process.

Detection. Alert on the configuration, not only the behaviour: privileged, cap_add, docker.sock mounts, pid: host, seccomp=unconfined and writable host bind mounts at CI/admission time (this lab's gate is a starting point). At runtime, a container that performs mount, namespace creation or writes to a read-only path is a signal only if you collect the denial; EPERM from seccomp is silent unless you configure logging. I did not test a runtime sensor.

Operability. Debugging a shell-less image needs a documented procedure (ephemeral debug container sharing the PID namespace, or a debug tag of the image that is never deployed to production). Health checks must not assume curl. Exit 137 after a limit change is the OOM killer, not a crash loop. Track image age: a digest-pinned base that nobody bumps becomes the scan finding you are paying to avoid.

Blast radius. Even fully hardened, containers share the host kernel. The controls here shrink reachable kernel surface and what an attacker can do post-exploit; they do not make this safe for hostile multi-tenant code. For that, add a user-namespaced or VM-isolated runtime (gVisor, Kata, Firecracker) and say so in the threat model.

Rollback. Everything is declarative: revert the image digest or the Compose file. Keep the previous profile versioned beside the image tag. The break-glass setting seccomp=unconfined is dangerous precisely because it works; make it a time-boxed exception that alerts, never a default fix for a failing deploy.

docs.title: Terraform plan and Rego policy lab
docs.text:
DevSecOps · Lab

Exercises secure, insecure, unknown, and deleted-control Terraform plan states through local policy fixtures.

This lab demonstrates why source scanning, plan evaluation, provider-side controls, and drift monitoring are separate layers. It does not deploy infrastructure.

docs.title: Tested scope
docs.text:
• Terraform CLI 1.14.6 for formatting and offline initialization/validation.
  • Open Policy Agent 1.17.0 for Rego v1 unit tests and fixture evaluation.
  • Terraform plan JSON fixtures use format_version: "1.2" and intentionally model only the resource shapes consumed by the policy.

Run the dependency-free structural tests:

node labs/iac-policy/tests/run-tests.js

Run the native policy tests against each positive or negative serialized-plan fixture:

opa test labs/iac-policy/policy/terraform.rego labs/iac-policy/policy/secure_fixture_test.rego labs/iac-policy/fixtures/secure_plan.json -v
opa test labs/iac-policy/policy/terraform.rego labs/iac-policy/policy/insecure_fixture_test.rego labs/iac-policy/fixtures/insecure_plan.json -v
opa test labs/iac-policy/policy/terraform.rego labs/iac-policy/policy/unknown_fixture_test.rego labs/iac-policy/fixtures/unknown_plan.json -v
opa test labs/iac-policy/policy/terraform.rego labs/iac-policy/policy/deleted_fixture_test.rego labs/iac-policy/fixtures/deleted_control_plan.json -v

Validate the two backend examples without contacting AWS:

terraform -chdir=labs/iac-policy/terraform/insecure init -backend=false
terraform -chdir=labs/iac-policy/terraform/insecure validate
terraform -chdir=labs/iac-policy/terraform/hardened init -backend=false
terraform -chdir=labs/iac-policy/terraform/hardened validate

docs.title: Evidence and negative cases
docs.text:
fixtures/secure_plan.json is accepted. The negative fixtures demonstrate:

  • public object-storage configuration and absent public-access controls;
  • absent encryption and access logging;
  • unrestricted network ingress;
  • a public, unencrypted database;
  • wildcard IAM permissions;
  • missing authorization-driving tags;
  • security-relevant values that are unknown at policy-evaluation time; and
  • deletion of a public-access control.

The Rego policy fails closed for the modeled unknown values. That is a policy choice: some organizations instead defer a decision until values are known. If you defer the decision, whatever checks it later still has to block until it's actually known.

docs.title: Backend comparison
docs.text:
The insecure example embeds a deprecated DynamoDB lock table and does not opt into S3 lockfile locking, version recovery, or KMS encryption. The hardened example uses use_lockfile = true, an explicit KMS key, and documents the S3 permissions required for the state and .tflock objects. Bucket versioning, access logging, and the KMS key are bootstrap controls outside the backend block and must be enforced separately.

sensitive = true affects CLI/UI display; it does not remove a value from state. State readers should therefore be treated as readers of potentially sensitive data.

docs.title: Limitations
docs.text:
• The plan fixtures are reviewed test inputs, not output from a live cloud account.
  • This policy covers a deliberately small AWS resource set. It is not a complete cloud security baseline.
  • Terraform validation checks syntax and internal consistency. It does not prove that backend permissions, KMS policy, provider behavior, or runtime state match the design.
  • OPA plan evaluation cannot replace service control policies, cloud configuration rules, posture management, or drift investigation.

docs.title: IAM and workload-identity decision lab
docs.text:
Cloud Security · Lab

Exercises issuer, audience, subject, delegation, boundary, PassRole, and external-ID decisions against local fixtures.

This dependency-free offline lab tests exact workload-identity trust fixtures and a small, explicit subset of authorization semantics. It exists to prevent four different decisions from being collapsed into “the token worked”:

  1. SIGNATURE_INVALID - an external cryptographic-verifier boundary did not authenticate the token signature.
  2. CLAIMS_REJECTED - the signature boundary succeeded, but issuer, audience, or lifetime checks failed.
  3. TRUST_POLICY_REJECTED - the token/caller was authenticated and its protocol claims were accepted, but the role trust policy or federated credential rejected the principal, subject, external ID, or requested session tags.
  4. PERMISSIONS_DENIED - federation/role assumption succeeded, but the resulting session was not authorized for the requested API/resource.

AUTHORIZED means only that the deliberately small local model accepted the tested request. It is not evidence that a cloud provider issued credentials or allowed a real API call.

docs.title: Prerequisites and run command
docs.text:
• Node.js 24.12.0 (a compatible Node.js 22+ runtime is also supported).
  • No npm packages, credentials, network access, cloud subscription, or AWS account.

From the repository root:

node labs/iam-oidc/tests/run-tests.js

Expected output:

PASS: 45 IAM/OIDC structural and policy-model evaluations completed.

The command exits nonzero on any unexpected decision or structural regression.

docs.title: Tested fixture coverage
docs.text:
Area Positive fixture Negative fixtures AWS GitHub OIDC Exact provider, issuer, sts.amazonaws.com audience, repository, and main branch Invalid signature; wrong issuer/audience/repository/branch/provider; expired token AWS GitHub environment Exact repository and production environment Branch subject presented to an environment trust; wrong environment Microsoft Entra federation Exact GitHub issuer, subject, audience, action, and resource-group scope Invalid signature; wrong issuer/audience/environment; denied action/scope EKS IRSA Exact cluster OIDC provider, issuer, audience, namespace, and service account Wrong cluster issuer/audience/namespace/service account; denied downstream API Third-party AssumeRole Exact vendor role, customer external ID, and constrained session tags Wrong principal/external ID/tag; extra tag; missing sts:TagSession authorization Permission-boundary delegation Create a role in the delegated path with the approved boundary Missing/alternate boundary; outside path; boundary removal/replacement Restricted iam:PassRole Exact role, ECS service principal, and task-definition family Wrong role, destination service, or associated resource

The readable GitHub subject examples are exact fixture values. A branch subject and an environment subject are alternatives: when a job references an environment, the default subject uses the environment rather than the branch. GitHub also documents immutable owner/repository-ID subject formats for repositories created after July 15, 2026, repositories that opt in, and qualifying renamed/transferred repositories. Inspect the actual token claims for the repository, then make the cloud trust configuration match that format exactly.

docs.title: Files and evidence boundary
docs.text:
• policies/ contains illustrative AWS trust/permissions policies and a Microsoft Entra federated-credential object.
  • fixtures/ contains positive and negative requests. Every mutation declares its expected stage.
  • evaluator.js implements only the condition operators and policy behavior used by these fixtures.
  • tests/run-tests.js performs structural assertions and evaluates all fixtures using Node.js built-ins.

The fixture field "signatureVerified": true represents output received across a trusted in-process boundary from a real JWT/JWS verifier. Setting the field does not verify a signature. Production integration must discover and pin the intended issuer, select keys by kid, validate the allowed algorithm and signature, reject malformed tokens, enforce time and audience rules, and handle key rotation and outage behavior. An attacker-controlled build must not be able to supply or replace the verifier result.

The permission evaluator models explicit deny, identity-policy allow, resource/action matching, selected condition operators, and the intersection with one permissions boundary. It intentionally does not claim full AWS IAM semantics.

docs.title: Production validation sequence
docs.text:
1. Inspect provider-issued claims from a protected, non-production workflow or workload and record the exact issuer, audience, and subject format.
  2. Validate policy documents with provider tooling and review their deployment plan/change set.
  3. Run negative exchanges in a disposable test account/subscription: wrong repository/ref/environment/service account/audience/external ID and unapproved session tags must fail.
  4. After a successful exchange, call one explicitly allowed and one explicitly denied API on disposable resources. Capture provider audit evidence without recording bearer credentials.
  5. Test revocation/rollback, environment protection, permission-boundary immutability, and PassRole changes through the same governed path used in production.

These are documented production-validation steps, not actions performed by this lab.

docs.title: AWS simulator limitations
docs.text:
The IAM Policy Simulator is useful for identity policies and one permissions boundary, but AWS documents material limitations: it does not simulate role/user cross-account access, resource-based policies for IAM roles, RCPs, or SCPs that contain conditions. It also does not perform GitHub or EKS OIDC discovery/signature validation, exchange a token through STS, or prove that a role trust policy admits a real federated principal. SimulatePrincipalPolicy/SimulateCustomPolicy results therefore cannot replace a negative AssumeRole or AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity test in a disposable AWS account. AWS recommends checking behavior in the live environment after simulation.

IAM Access Analyzer policy validation and external-access findings are valuable static checks, but they likewise do not establish successful end-to-end token verification or downstream authorization.

docs.title: Failure modes and limitations
docs.text:
• No cloud resource is created and no AWS, Azure, GitHub, or Kubernetes endpoint is called.
  • No JWT/JWS cryptography, JWKS retrieval, certificate path, key rotation, clock-skew policy, replay cache, or bearer-token handling is implemented.
  • The evaluator is not a general IAM interpreter. It omits resource policies, SCPs, RCPs, session policies, service-specific authorization, principal-ID transforms, policy variables, NotAction/NotResource/NotPrincipal, and most condition operators.
  • Microsoft Entra action/scope evaluation is a pedagogical allow-list, not the Azure RBAC engine. The fixture uses the baseline exact-match federated-credential model, not the separate flexible federated identity credential preview.
  • EKS fixtures cover IRSA. EKS Pod Identity uses a different trust model and should have separate tests when selected.
  • An external ID mitigates cross-account confused-deputy risk; AWS does not treat it as a secret. It does not replace a narrow principal or least-privilege role policy.
  • iam:PassRole authorization must be evaluated together with the destination API, the passed role's trust policy, and the passed role's permissions. This lab checks the exact PassRole dimensions and destination service trust, but does not call ECS.

docs.text: The test reads tracked JSON and starts one Node.js process. It creates no temporary files, credentials, containers, or cloud resources, so no cleanup is required.

docs.title: Kubernetes admission, network, and image-policy lab
docs.text:
Cloud Security · Lab

Runs an insecure and a hardened workload on a real local kind cluster and measures workload identity, RBAC, admission control, network reachability and runtime constraints before and after, with four policy engines compared on one case corpus.

Status: partially tested. Two layers of evidence live here:

  1. Offline (runs in CI): Kyverno CLI 1.18.2 over the pod-hardening policy and the admission case corpus, OPA/Rego unit and manifest tests, kubeconform, and Node tests that pin the manifests' structure. The Node tests are part of npm run validate; the Kyverno tests and the new Rego check (validate-rego.sh, which has not yet run on a hosted runner) are part of npm run verify:native-labs; kubeconform was run locally only.
  2. Live (one disposable kind cluster, run once on 2026-11-05, 83 of 83 assertions passed): Kubernetes v1.37.0 with a policy-enforcing CNI, real API calls from inside pods, real Pod Security Admission and ValidatingAdmissionPolicy decisions, real connectivity tests. Not wired into CI.

The image-verification policy remains a schema-validated example with an offline decision model (see Existing offline fixtures); signature, certificate, registry, transparency, mutation and live admission of signed images were not executed.

Evidence labels: tested locally (executed here, output kept in evidence/), source-reviewed (read in the named primary source, not executed), policy model (a rule set evaluated by a local test, not enforced by the real system) and requires-review (no independent reviewer has checked it). They map to T2/T3 and T4, T0, T1 and review status in the evidence standards.

docs.title: Scope
docs.text:
One question: what can a compromised workload do, as seen from inside the cluster, and which control changes the answer? Four properties are measured on an insecure baseline and a hardened equivalent, using the same application image family as the Docker lab:

Property How it is measured Workload identity A k8sprobe subcommand in the pod calls the API with the pod's own token and records HTTP status codes and item counts only (never names or values), plus SelfSubjectAccessReview for write permissions so it changes nothing Permissions kubectl auth can-i as the ServiceAccount, cross-checked against the in-pod result Network reachability tcpcheck from inside each pod to a data-tier canary, another tenant's canary, and the API server endpoint Runtime constraints The Docker lab's probe run inside the pod: uid, capabilities, NoNewPrivs, seccomp, read-only root, cgroup limits, denied syscalls

Out of scope: multi-node scheduling, node hardening, etcd encryption, API-server audit logging, service mesh, cloud IAM, and any cluster that is not the kind cluster this lab creates and deletes. A namespace, a PSA label or a NetworkPolicy is not a hostile multi-tenant boundary; see the Kubernetes multi-tenancy research.

docs.title: What I built
docs.text: Path Purpose cluster/ kind config (portable and a compatibility variant), up.sh (kind + Calico with a pinned manifest SHA-256 + preloaded images), down.sh baseline/ Insecure manifests: over-granted ServiceAccount, privileged root container with hostPID and hostPath, no NetworkPolicy, no admission labels, plus the two canary fixtures hardened/ PSA restricted namespace, least-privilege RBAC, restricted workloads, default-deny NetworkPolicies, a CEL ValidatingAdmissionPolicy admission-cases/ 16 pods, each differing from a compliant pod in one property; expectations.json (predictions written before the engines ran); a Kyverno CLI test policies/rego/ workload.rego (pod, RBAC, namespace and NetworkPolicy rules) and 12 unit tests scripts/ np-smoke.sh, admission-matrix.js, run-cluster-lab.sh, manifests-to-input.js, publish_evidence.py tests/ manifests.test.js (16 structural tests), cluster_check.py (assertions on observed output), existing run-tests.js evidence/ Sanitized output of the run described below, plus two labeled one-off observations policies/hardened-pods.yaml, verify-release-images.yaml, fixtures/ Existing; unchanged

docs.title: Pod identity to the Kubernetes API
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
  autonumber
  participant K as kubelet
  participant P as api-reader pod
  participant N as Calico egress policy
  participant A as kube-apiserver
  K->>A: TokenRequest for ServiceAccount api-reader, bound to the pod, 3600 s
  A-->>K: signed JWT with sub, aud, exp and pod binding
  K->>P: project token, cluster CA and namespace into the pod
  P->>N: connect to the API server endpoint on 6443
  N-->>P: allowed, the only egress rule for api-reader besides DNS
  P->>A: GET configmaps/app-config with the bearer token
  A->>A: authenticate, then authorize with RBAC
  A-->>P: 200 for app-config
  P->>A: LIST secrets in kube-system
  A-->>P: 403 Forbidden

Status: tested locally. The last four steps are the hardened-apireader-k8sprobe.json result: a GET of the one named ConfigMap returned 200; every list and the write and escalation reviews were denied. The token was bound to the pod with about 3594 s remaining.

docs.title: RBAC decision flow
docs.text:
flowchart TD
  R["API request with bearer token"] --> AU{"Authenticate:<br/>signature, audience, expiry"}
  AU -->|"fails"| E401["401 Unauthorized"]
  AU -->|"ok: system:serviceaccount:NS:NAME"| B{"Any RoleBinding in the request namespace<br/>or ClusterRoleBinding naming this subject?"}
  B -->|"none"| E403["403 Forbidden<br/>permissions are additive, so no match means deny"]
  B -->|"yes"| M{"Does a rule in a bound role match<br/>verb, apiGroup, resource, subresource<br/>and resourceNames?"}
  M -->|"no"| E403
  M -->|"yes"| W{"Is it a write to roles or bindings?"}
  W -->|"no"| ADM["Admission chain, then persist or return"]
  W -->|"yes"| X{"Does the caller already hold the permissions being granted,<br/>or the escalate or bind verb?"}
  X -->|"no"| E403
  X -->|"yes"| ADM

Status: source-reviewed against the RBAC reference (permissions are purely additive; role and binding writes are limited by privilege escalation prevention) and consistent with the live results: the baseline identity could list secrets in kube-system and create pods/exec, yet escalate and impersonate were denied, because the over-grant was deliberately not cluster-admin.

docs.title: Admission control flow
docs.text:
flowchart LR

docs.title: Admission control: four engines, one corpus
docs.text:
16 pods, each differing from the compliant pod in exactly one property. Decisions come from the live API server (--dry-run=server; nothing persisted) for PSA and VAP, run in isolation by using two namespaces (lab-hardened has the PSA labels; lab-vap-only has only the VAP selector label) and then together; Kyverno and OPA ran offline on the same file.

Case PSA restricted (live) VAP (live) PSA+VAP together (live) Kyverno hardened-pods (offline) OPA workload.rego (offline) compliant-app allow allow allow allow allow compliant-api-reader allow allow allow allow allow finding-pod-level-only-run-as-non-root allow allow allow deny allow finding-sa-level-automount-false allow allow allow deny deny rejected-privileged deny allow deny deny deny rejected-hostpath deny allow deny deny deny rejected-host-namespaces deny allow deny deny deny rejected-run-as-root deny allow deny deny deny rejected-capability-add deny allow deny deny deny rejected-no-seccomp deny allow deny deny deny rejected-privilege-escalation deny allow deny deny deny gap-no-limits allow deny deny deny deny gap-latest-tag allow deny deny allow deny gap-writable-rootfs allow deny deny deny deny gap-automounted-token allow deny deny deny deny gap-projected-token-unapproved allow deny deny allow deny

What the matrix shows:

  • No single control covers the corpus. PSA restricted denies 7 cases the VAP allows (host namespaces, privileged, hostPath, non-root, capabilities, seccomp, privilege escalation); the VAP denies 5 cases PSA allows (missing limits, :latest, writable root filesystem, an automounted token, an unapproved projected token). Together they deny 12 of 16 and admit exactly the 4 acceptable pods. With no admission control (lab-baseline) all 16 were admitted.
  • PSA does not enforce on Deployments. The documentation says enforce mode applies to the resulting Pods, and that is what happened: the Deployment was accepted with a warning and its ReplicaSet could not create a single pod. The failure shows up as FailedCreate events, not as a rejected kubectl apply. Alert on those events; do not rely on the apply error.
  • Engines disagree on equivalent configurations, and I got two predictions wrong. The cases marked finding- exist because of misses:
  • The existing hardened-pods Kyverno policy rejects finding-pod-level-only-run-as-non-root, which PSA and OPA accept: it reads runAsNonRoot at the container level only. I predicted the compliant pods would pass; the CLI failed all four, and adding only the container-level field made them pass (tested locally). The policy is unchanged; my workloads set the field at both levels, and the finding is pinned by a test.
  • gap-automounted-token was allowed in lab-hardened but denied in lab-vap-only. The cause was the ServiceAccount: in lab-hardened it sets automountServiceAccountToken: false, which protects a pod that merely omits the field. The offline engines see only the Pod, treat omission as true, and are therefore conservative (finding-sa-level-automount-false: live allow, Kyverno and OPA deny). The case now sets the field explicitly.

admission-cases/expectations.json keeps the original predictions and the history; a mismatch is a finding, not a value to overwrite. - A real gap in the existing Kyverno policy. gap-projected-token-unapproved and gap-latest-tag pass hardened-pods: the policy checks automountServiceAccountToken but not an explicitly projected token volume, and does not look at image tags. Setting automountServiceAccountToken: false and projecting a token yourself satisfies it. PSA restricted also allows that volume type. The VAP and the Rego rule close it. - The "approved" label is a review marker, not authorization. The VAP lets a pod project a token only if it carries lab.example/api-access: approved and a non-default ServiceAccount, but whoever can create the pod can set the label. A real control binds approval to something the pod author cannot set: a VAP parameter resource listing permitted ServiceAccounts, or a platform-owned namespace label. I did not build that.

docs.title: NetworkPolicy enforcement is a property of the CNI
docs.text:
Writing NetworkPolicy objects proves nothing; the API server accepts them whether or not anything enforces them. The Kubernetes documentation says so directly (source-reviewed): a policy without a controller that implements it "will have no effect".

I observed this. With kind's default CNI on this VM, a default-deny Ingress+Egress policy changed nothing: the client kept reaching the server 30 seconds later. The CNI's policy controller logged netlink receive: no such file or directory while programming nftables, which I believe means this kernel lacks an nftables capability it needs. That was a manual experiment, not part of the scripted run, so it is kept as a labeled one-off (observation-kindnet-no-enforcement.txt). On a kernel with full nftables support kindnet may enforce policy; I did not test that.

The lab therefore disables the default CNI, installs Calico v3.33.0 (manifest pinned by SHA-256) and runs scripts/np-smoke.sh before anything else: the same request must succeed, then time out after a default-deny policy. The orchestrator aborts if it does not. Every "blocked" result above is conditional on that test having passed (np-smoke.json: before_policy_reachable: true, after_default_deny_reachable: false).

docs.title: Existing offline fixtures (kept unchanged)
docs.text:
The following is the original content of this README, preserved because the tests that back it still run.

Native Kyverno v1.18.2 testing exercised the hardened-pod policy. The image policy is a schema-validated example; signature, certificate, registry, transparency, mutation, and live admission were not tested.

This lab validates a narrow Kubernetes security baseline with positive and negative fixtures. It does not claim that a namespace, admission policy, or NetworkPolicy is a hard hostile-tenant boundary.

docs.title: Pinned validation scope
docs.text:
• Kubernetes API shapes reviewed for Kubernetes 1.34.
  • Kyverno CLI 1.18.2.
  • Kyverno policies.kyverno.io/v1 ValidatingPolicy and ImageValidatingPolicy, stable in Kyverno 1.18.

Run the dependency-free structural and identity-policy tests:

node labs/kubernetes-security/tests/run-tests.js

Run the native Kyverno tests:

kyverno test labs/kubernetes-security --remove-color

For a complete copy-and-run setup without an installed CLI, use bash labs/kubernetes-security/validate-kyverno.sh. The script downloads the pinned 1.18.2 platform archive, compares its SHA-256 with the reviewed release checksum, runs the seven-case suite and removes its temporary binary. It supports Linux and macOS ARM64/x86-64 and requires Python, curl and tar. This verifies a checksum, not the release's Sigstore signature. No cluster is contacted or modified.

On 2026-07-23, the official Kyverno v1.18.2 Windows CLI asset (SHA-256 b5c9d1cb75587a312dc8334537a5773bdedb1a985deae9d89a5251385afb831f) ran the native hardened-pod suite: 7 tests passed and 0 tests failed. This native run does not include verify-release-images.yaml.

docs.title: Enforcement demonstrated
docs.text:
policies/hardened-pods.yaml denies:

  • privileged containers and privilege escalation;
  • host PID, IPC, or network namespaces;
  • hostPath volumes;
  • added Linux capabilities or failure to drop ALL;
  • writable root filesystems;
  • missing non-root and seccomp configuration;
  • missing CPU/memory requests or limits; and
  • service-account token automount unless explicitly disabled.

The accepted Pod is tested alongside privileged, host-namespace, hostPath, capability, missing-resource, and token-automount negative fixtures.

policies/verify-release-images.yaml uses the stable Kyverno 1.18 policies.kyverno.io/v1 ImageValidatingPolicy. It constrains repository, keyless issuer, full workflow-and-branch subject, SLSA provenance predicate type, required verification, digest verification, and failurePolicy: Fail. Separate :* and @sha256:* globs make tagged and digest references to the exact repository eligible for evaluation while excluding lookalike repositories.

On 2026-07-23, the manifest conformed to Kyverno v1.18.2's official ImageValidatingPolicy CRD v1 schema. The downloaded CRD asset SHA-256 was 3528151f3717c9946ee56d60866f2cf6c29a4b1a7e759c72af60451147b995c2. The Node harness separately evaluates eleven synthetic, already-resolved evidence claim sets. It returns false for unsigned, wrong repository/workflow/branch/issuer/predicate, missing or malformed provenance, verifier/transparency failure, and digest mismatch.

The twelfth case proves only that a tag such as :latest matches the reviewed tag selector. Its admission result is deliberately null: the harness does not model registry resolution or Kyverno's mutateDigest behavior and therefore makes no accept/deny claim for tag-only input. This is a schema-validated example; no live enforcement test. Signature, certificate, registry, transparency-log, mutation, webhook failure, and controller behavior were not executed.

docs.title: Network boundary
docs.text: fixtures/network-policies.yaml contains namespace-wide default-deny ingress and egress plus an explicit DNS exception. NetworkPolicy has an effect only when the selected CNI implements it. DNS labels, ports, node-local DNS paths, dual-stack behavior, and required application egress must be verified in each cluster. NetworkPolicy does not control all host-network, node, service-mesh, or cloud-network paths.

docs.title: Operational rollout
docs.text: Use observe → audit → warn → enforce → measure bypasses. Track policy evaluation errors, denials, exceptions and expiry, unsigned-image attempts, registry/rekor availability, admission latency, and workloads that require a separate runtime class or cluster. Keep a reviewed break-glass path outside tenant administrator control.

docs.title: Validation
docs.text:
Environment of the recorded live run (evidence/versions.txt): kernel 6.18.44 (cgroup v1), kind v0.33.0, node image kindest/node:v1.37.0 (containerd 2.3.4), kubectl v1.37.0, Calico v3.33.0, Kyverno CLI 1.18.2, OPA 1.22.0, kubeconform v0.8.0.

npm ci --ignore-scripts
node labs/kubernetes-security/tests/run-tests.js                 # existing decision-model tests
node --test labs/kubernetes-security/tests/manifests.test.js     # 16 structural tests, no cluster
kyverno test labs/kubernetes-security --remove-color             # 23 tests: 7 existing + 16 new, offline
opa test labs/kubernetes-security/policies/rego                  # 12 unit tests
bash labs/kubernetes-security/scripts/run-cluster-lab.sh         # live: creates and deletes a kind cluster

Observed on the recorded run:

Check Result manifests.test.js 16 passed kyverno test 23 passed, 0 failed (the 16-case corpus plus the 7 existing cases) opa test 12 of 12 OPA over baseline/ plus fixtures 35 violations across 15 rules (privileged, hostPath, host namespaces, root, seccomp, limits, PSA, default-deny, RBAC secrets/exec/bindings, token) OPA over hardened/ 0 violations kubeconform, Kubernetes 1.37.0 schemas, strict 45 resources, 45 valid, 0 skipped Live assertions (tests/cluster_check.py) 83 passed, 0 failed

The live run took 2 min 21 s from nothing to deletion. run-cluster-lab.sh deletes the cluster on exit; --keep-cluster and --use-existing exist for iteration, and --use-existing resets the lab namespaces first.

Two facts about the sandbox the run needed, both recorded as one-offs in observation-sandbox-kubelet-failures.txt: the kubelet refused to start on cgroup v1 (failCgroupV1: false fixes it), and runc could not lower oom_score_adj because the VM's capability bounding set lacks CAP_SYS_RESOURCE (containerd restrict_oom_score_adj fixes it; the capability is documented in capabilities(7), source-reviewed). cluster/up.sh selects kind-config.compat.yaml automatically when it detects either condition. On a cgroup v2 workstation the portable config is used.

docs.title: What was not tested
docs.text:
• A multi-node cluster, scheduling constraints, node-to-node policy paths, and NetworkPolicy behaviour across nodes.
  • Kyverno or OPA Gatekeeper running as live admission controllers. Both ran offline only. Webhook latency, failurePolicy behaviour under outage, background scans and exceptions were not exercised. The ValidatingAdmissionPolicy is the only non-PSA live admission control.
  • Signed-image admission. The ImageValidatingPolicy and its model are unchanged; no signature was verified in a cluster.
  • Other CNIs, and kindnet on a kernel where it works, NetworkPolicy features beyond L3/L4 allow rules (named ports, SCTP, endPort, FQDN or L7 policy), IPv6, and egress to cloud metadata endpoints.
  • API-server audit logging. The Audit action on the VAP binding was set but no audit sink was configured, so I cannot show the records.
  • Token theft and replay. The lab shows what an identity can do; it does not test token exfiltration, TokenReview of a deleted pod's token, or revocation timing.
  • Pod Security Admission exemptions and cluster-wide defaults (an AdmissionConfiguration), and PSA at versions other than v1.37.
  • seccomp Localhost profiles (the Docker lab's profile on a node). The hardened pods use RuntimeDefault.
  • Cloud-managed Kubernetes (EKS, AKS, GKE) and their identity federation. Nothing here contacts a cloud provider.
  • Hosted CI. run-cluster-lab.sh is not part of any workflow.
  • Measured time to detect, time to contain, false-positive rates over real workloads, and cost are not measured in this lab.

docs.title: Production considerations
docs.text:
Rollout. Do not turn on enforce first. For PSA: warn and audit at restricted per namespace, read the warnings for a release cycle, fix or exempt, then enforce; keep the version label pinned and bump it deliberately after a cluster upgrade. For a ValidatingAdmissionPolicy: bind with Warn or Audit before Deny. For RBAC: start from what the workload was observed to call, not from a built-in role. For NetworkPolicy: introduce default-deny last per namespace, after the allow rules for DNS and the real dependencies are in place and tested; the failure mode is a silent timeout.

False positives. Observed here: the Kyverno policy rejecting pod-level runAsNonRoot; offline engines denying a pod whose ServiceAccount already disables the token. Expected in practice: :latest and digest-only references tripping naive tag rules, init containers and sidecars with legitimate NET_BIND_SERVICE or NET_ADMIN, and operators that need hostPath. Give exceptions an owner and an expiry; the allow-list is where the policy is actually decided.

Detection. The denial is the signal, but only if you collect it: a rejected Pod created by a controller appears as a FailedCreate event on the ReplicaSet, not at kubectl apply. Alert on those events, on new ClusterRoleBindings, on pods/exec use, and on any pod that projects a token. I did not test an audit pipeline or a runtime sensor here.

Operability. failurePolicy: Fail is correct for a security control and an outage for the control plane if the policy cannot be evaluated; the built-in VAP removes a webhook as a failure domain, which is its main operational advantage over a webhook engine. Default-deny egress needs DNS and API-server rules that depend on the CNI's view of the destination (Calico matched the post-DNAT node IP, so the policy needed the endpoint address); re-check after control-plane changes. Short-lived projected tokens are refreshed by the kubelet, so applications must re-read the file.

Blast radius. A namespace is a policy scope, not an isolation boundary: pods share the node kernel, and the controls above shrink what a compromised pod can reach, not whether a kernel bug is exploitable. For hostile tenants, add a sandboxed runtime or separate clusters.

Rollback. Everything is declarative. Remove the VAP binding or set its action back to Warn, relabel the namespace to warn, or delete the NetworkPolicy. Do not roll back by granting a broader role to make a deploy work; that is how the baseline was created.

docs.title: Teardown and resources
docs.text: run-cluster-lab.sh deletes the cluster on exit and removes nothing else. Docker images, the base-image cache and Node dependencies remain. Resource cost is local only: about 2 min 21 s of wall time and one kind node on a 4-CPU, 16 GiB VM; no measured cloud cost.

docs.title: Complete local setup
docs.text:
Use a fresh repository checkout and the prerequisites above. From repository root:

npm ci --ignore-scripts
node labs/kubernetes-security/tests/run-tests.js
kyverno test labs/kubernetes-security --remove-color

Native policy testing needs Kyverno CLI 1.18.2; the dependency-free structural check can run without it. The complete policy and pod/network manifests are tracked beside this README. No existing cluster is used or modified.

This is a local decision experiment, so the complete implementation is its tracked code, fixtures and policy files. It needs no Terraform deployment, service account or publicly exposed server. Never relocate fixture workflows into an active CI directory without a separate environment review.

docs.title: Evidence, expected output and interpretation
docs.text:
The documented command exits zero only when its assertions pass; an unexpected allow/deny, schema or state result is a failure. Preserve the full command output under ignored .artifacts/research/ with runtime/tool versions and exit status. Use the specific expected markers above rather than inventing example output. The lab audit records the validation run.

Native CLI pod-policy tests do not prove live cluster admission, signature verification, image mutation or CNI packet enforcement. Local finite-case coverage is not a production false-positive or false-negative estimate. TTD/TTC, representative pipeline overhead and monthly cloud cost are not measured in this lab.

docs.title: Teardown and resources
docs.text:
The processes exit and remove their temporary test files. There is no cloud destroy command. Retained evidence, optional provider downloads and local Docker image cache are your only persistent outputs; remove them after review. Node dependencies can remain for subsequent runs.

Local CPU, memory, dependency downloads and optional image disk space are the resource cost. There is no measured cloud bill. Related research links above define which claims the experiment supports.

docs.title: Linux host telemetry detection lab
docs.text:
Linux Security · Lab

Runs nine SQL detection rules over a deterministic synthetic corpus with labeled benign look-alikes and known evasions, then over real syscalls captured with strace from a throwaway container.

Status: partially tested. The engine, the nine rules and the 23 unit tests run anywhere with Python 3 and are part of npm run validate. The real-kernel capture ran once on 2026-11-05 on a disposable VM and is not in CI. The analysis, false-positive reasoning, response actions and diagrams are in the article: Host Telemetry Detection Lab.

Every event the generator produces is synthetic. Nothing in this lab records, simulates or reproduces a real intrusion. Events are data: a path, an executable name, a destination in a documentation address range. No malicious code exists here, no payload is executed, and the real-kernel capture runs only harmless placeholders inside a throwaway container.

Evidence labels: tested locally (executed here, output in evidence/), policy model (a rule evaluated by a local test, not by a production sensor), source-reviewed, requires-review.

docs.title: Scope
docs.text: Detection logic over host telemetry: process ancestry, file writes, file reads, permission changes and outbound connections. Not in scope: collecting telemetry at fleet scale, kernel sensors (auditd, eBPF, Falco, Tetragon), a SIEM, enrichment, or any response automation. Rules are tested on labeled data the rule author wrote, so the numbers describe the rules' behaviour on that corpus, not how they would perform on a real fleet.

docs.title: What I built
docs.text: Path Purpose generator.py Deterministic (seeded) synthetic corpus: 855 events in 42 labeled scenarios; every event has "synthetic": true engine.py Loads events into SQLite, validates the schema, runs rules/*.sql, applies the allowlist, deduplicates, reports missing sources and fields as blind, scores against labels rules/ Nine rules, each a readable SQL file with a header: id, title, severity, required sources, response guidance allowlist.json Exceptions; the engine refuses an entry without an owner, a reason and an expiry, and ignores an entry after it expires capture/ workload.sh (harmless analogs in a busybox container), capture.sh (host strace), normalize_strace.py scripts/ run-lab.sh (everything), summarize.py (assertions and the scored table) tests/test_detections.py 23 tests: determinism, schema rejection, pinned confusion matrix, PID reuse, exception expiry, deduplication, blind coverage, clocks, label leakage, parser evidence/ Sanitized output of the run below

docs.title: Validation
docs.text:
Recorded run (evidence/versions.txt): Python 3.13.18, SQLite 3.53.1, Linux 6.18.44, strace 6.8, Docker 29.9.2.

python3 labs/linux-host-telemetry/tests/test_detections.py        # 23 tests, standard library only
bash labs/linux-host-telemetry/scripts/run-lab.sh                 # corpus + rules + (if available) real capture
Check Observed Unit tests 23 passed Synthetic corpus 855 events, 42 scenarios (17 malicious-pattern, 17 benign look-alike, 6 control, 2 evasion), 27 deduplicated alerts, 0 alerts on 400 background-noise iterations Scenario-level totals over nine rules TP 19, FP 7, FN 2, TN 216 Documented residual false positives 7 look-alikes (S04, S13, S23, S33, S44, S54, S82) alert by design and are pinned in the tests Documented misses 2 (S14 per-user crontab, S34 outbound from system bash) stay silent and are pinned Network sensor removed LNX-004 reported blind, no alert, and not scored as a true negative Real capture (strace, busybox container) 176 trace lines → 28 events → alerts from exactly LNX-002, 005, 006, 007, 009; LNX-004 silent on a private-address connect from /tmp; LNX-003 blind (strace cannot supply ExecStart)

Full per-rule table, residual-false-positive analysis and response actions: see the article.

docs.title: What was not tested
docs.text:
• Any production sensor: auditd, eBPF, Falco, Tetragon, osquery. The schema is inspired by what they emit; none was run.
  • Detection on real fleet data, real adversary tradecraft, or adversaries who know the rules. Evasion is represented by two hand-written cases.
  • strace as a sensor: its overhead and blind spots were not measured; it is a capture convenience.
  • Rules LNX-001, 003, 004 and 008 against real kernel data (the capture exercises 002, 005, 006, 007, 009 and one negative for 004).
  • Time to detect and time to contain: the lab reports synthetic latency from synthetic clocks only.
  • Response actions: they are written guidance, never executed.

docs.title: Production considerations
docs.text: See the article for rollout, detection, operability, false positives, blast radius and rollback. In short: ship rules to a few hosts in report-only mode, own every exception (owner + expiry), page on nothing until the residual false-positive sources for your environment are known, and treat a blind rule as an incident in the telemetry pipeline, not as a quiet host.

docs.title: MCP tool-authorization gateway lab
docs.text:
AI Security · Lab

A policy gateway between an agent runtime and a mock MCP-style stdio server, tested against a deliberately compromised stand-in agent for allowlists, scoped identity, taint, approval gates, descriptor pinning, output validation and tamper-evident audit.

Status: partially tested. Dependency-free Node.js; the tests run in npm run validate. The analysis, diagrams and the mapping to the MCP specification are in the article: MCP Tool Authorization Lab.

There is no language model here. The "agent" is a deterministic stand-in that obeys any CALL tool {json} line found in a tool result: the worst case of a compromised planner. It shows that the gateway's decisions do not depend on model behaviour. It cannot show whether a real model is injectable or how often. No LLM API is contacted, no credential is used, and every tool effect is an in-memory array append in a local child process. The .test domains are reserved for testing; all data is synthetic.

Evidence labels: tested locally (executed here; output in evidence/), policy model (decision logic evaluated against a stand-in, not a real model or identity provider), source-reviewed, requires-review.

docs.title: Scope
docs.text: The authorization decision for an agent-proposed tool call: which tools exist, whose authority applies, when a human must decide, what the tool may return, and what is recorded. Out of scope: authenticating users or agents (the context is a trusted input here), token issuance and exchange, the MCP authorization flow, transport security, sandboxing the tool server, and any real model behaviour. This extends the AI-agent external tool-broker lab (action-bound approval, replay resistance) to an MCP-shaped server with taint, descriptor pinning, output validation and an audit chain; it does not replace it, and the SSRF lab covers URL-fetching tools.

docs.title: What I built
docs.text: Path Purpose mock-server.js Newline-delimited JSON-RPC 2.0 over stdio: initialize, tools/list, tools/call; five tools on in-memory data; modes normal, rugpull, hostile_output, slow, crash; side effects reported on stderr so tests observe them independently; plus a lab-only lab/barrier method (not MCP) that orders stderr against stdout for the test harness gateway.js The single enforcement point: allowlist, descriptor pin, closed-schema check, path/recipient validation, user-AND-agent scope intersection, destination allowlist, risk gating with taint, approval verification, execution rate limit, audit-before-execute, timeout, output validation policy.json Deny-by-default policy; each tool's reviewed descriptor is pinned by SHA-256 audit.js Hash-chained append-only log with verifyChain lib/ Canonical hashing, a closed JSON-Schema subset, strict scope and path matching agent-sim.js NaiveAgent, the compromised-planner stand-in tests/gateway.test.js 35 tests against a real spawned server process scripts/run-scenarios.js 16 scenarios, expectations declared before each step, decision matrix written to JSON and Markdown scripts/pin.js, scripts/run-lab.sh Pin check/update; run everything

docs.title: Validation
docs.text:
Recorded run (evidence/versions.txt): Node.js v22.23.4, Linux 6.18.44, policy version 2026-11-05.1.

node --test labs/mcp-tool-authorization/tests/gateway.test.js     # 35 tests
node labs/mcp-tool-authorization/scripts/run-scenarios.js         # 16 scenarios, 31 proposed calls
bash labs/mcp-tool-authorization/scripts/run-lab.sh               # pins + tests + scenarios
Check Observed Descriptor pins all five match the benign server Mechanism tests 35 passed, 0 failed (includes a check that every reason code the gateway can emit was exercised) Scenario matrix 16 scenarios, 31 proposed calls: 11 allow, 5 approval required, 15 deny; every expectation met; every audit chain verifies Side effects observed on a channel separate from the protocol: nothing happened for any denied or unapproved call. Reads are ordered by a stderr barrier; without it the assertion could pass because a line was late (see the article, finding 8) Reproducibility decisions, reasons, effect counts and audit sequence numbers are identical across runs. The audit-chain head hashes in decision-matrix.json are not: approval ids are random, so they change on every run and are not a regression signal

The matrix, with a read-across to reasons and audit sequence numbers, is in the article.

docs.title: What was not tested
docs.text:
• A real language model, real prompt injection, or any measure of how injectable a model is. The stand-in obeys every injected instruction by construction.
  • Authentication of the user, the agent or the approver; token validation; the MCP authorization specification; OAuth flows.
  • A conformant MCP server or client: the mock implements four MCP methods (initialize, notifications/initialized, tools/list, tools/call) plus the lab-only barrier, and no pagination, capabilities negotiation, resources, prompts or sampling.
  • Remote (HTTP) MCP transport; only stdio.
  • A compromised gateway host, a compromised approval UI, or an attacker with access to the audit store. The audit chain's tail-truncation gap is demonstrated, not closed.
  • Concurrency, performance and rate-limit behaviour under load; approval-fatigue effects on real reviewers.
  • Cloud, production data or credentials. None is used.

docs.title: OAuth/OIDC token-boundary lab
docs.text:
Application Security · Lab

Exercises issuer, audience, time, nonce, state, redirects, PKCE, and key rotation against local boundary fixtures.

Tested locally on 2026-07-23 with Node.js 24.12.0 and Go 1.26.1. The JavaScript suite supports Node.js 22 or newer.

This dependency-free lab turns the most important OAuth/OIDC resource-server boundaries into executable acceptance and rejection checks. It is deliberately a small verifier model, not a replacement for a maintained JOSE/OIDC library.

docs.title: What the lab proves
docs.text:
tests/oauth-security.test.js generates trusted, rotated, and attacker RSA keys and checks that the resource-server validator:

  • accepts a correctly signed RS256 access token for the configured issuer, API audience, tenant, and required scope;
  • rejects a bad signature, issuer, audience, expiration, not-before time, tenant, or scope;
  • accepts the configured audience in either the string or array form;
  • accepts old and new trusted keys during a bounded rotation overlap, then rejects the retired key;
  • rejects an unknown kid without turning it into a network location; and
  • compares web redirect URI requests to registered strings exactly, including case, port, path, query, and fragment differences.

The tid and scope/scp names are an explicit example contract. Real providers can use different claims, token profiles, and authorization semantics. Configure those from trusted provider documentation. The API must still enforce current object, tenant, and business authorization after token validation.

docs.title: Run
docs.text:
From the repository root:

node labs/oauth-oidc/tests/oauth-security.test.js
go -C appsec/scripts/oauth-pkce test ./...

Expected results are 14 passing Node.js checks and 8 passing Go checks. The Go program covers the RFC 7636 Appendix B vector, generated-verifier round trip, wrong verifier, plain downgrade, method case, length, syntax, and malformed challenge. It never prints verifier or challenge values.

docs.title: Security boundaries and limitations
docs.text:
• The lab trusts only keys supplied in the configured Map; it performs no discovery or network fetch. Production metadata/JWKS retrieval needs a configured HTTPS issuer, bounded caching, rate limits, controlled redirects and egress, and a last-known-good rotation strategy.
  • Only RS256 with typ=JWT is modeled. A maintained library should be configured for the provider's exact asymmetric algorithm and token profile.
  • The clock is injected so time tests are deterministic. Deployed code needs a narrow documented skew and synchronized clocks.
  • Exact matching is shown for a confidential web client's HTTPS redirects. Native loopback redirects have the port exception defined by RFC 8252 and are intentionally outside this matcher.
  • The lab does not implement authorization-code redemption, nonce/state persistence, DPoP, mTLS, introspection, revocation, or refresh-token rotation.
  • Neither raw tokens nor PKCE verifiers should be written to logs.

docs.title: PostgreSQL row-level security isolation lab
docs.text:
Application Security · Lab

Exercises row-level security, transaction-local tenant context, pooled connections, and negative cross-tenant cases.

This disposable lab tests a transaction-scoped tenant context, complete USING and WITH CHECK policies, forced row security, and role properties that prevent ordinary application identities from bypassing the boundary.

docs.title: Prerequisites and tested versions
docs.text:
• Docker Engine or Docker Desktop with Compose v2.
  • PowerShell 7+ on Windows or a POSIX shell on Linux/macOS.
  • Node.js 22+ and npm for the application integration test.
  • Maintained PostgreSQL client: pg 8.22.0, lockfile pinned.
  • Image: postgres:18.4-alpine3.24, pinned to the PostgreSQL 18.4 patch release checked on 2026-07-21. For a long-lived environment, pin the image digest in the deployment's own dependency process.

docs.title: Run
docs.text:
PowerShell:

./labs/postgresql-rls/run-tests.ps1

POSIX shell:

./labs/postgresql-rls/run-tests.sh

The scripts generate an ephemeral local password, install the lockfile-pinned pg client, start the service, run SQL runtime/boundary/catalog suites plus the pooled-client suite, and remove containers and volumes. The password is not persisted in a tracked file. Pass -Keep or --keep to retain the service for inspection.

Expected output includes PASS messages for cross-tenant reads and writes, mutation of a visible row's tenant key, missing and malformed context, connection reuse, forced RLS for the table owner, catalog flags, non-bypass role attributes, policy count, policy roles, and complete policy expressions. Any SQL error or failed assertion returns a nonzero status.

docs.title: Security properties exercised
docs.text:
• Tenant identity is set with transaction-local set_config(..., true); it does not leak into the next transaction on a pooled connection.
  • Missing context matches no rows and fails writes. Malformed UUID context raises an error instead of falling back to a broader scope.
  • Both row visibility and new row values are constrained, including an attempted update that moves a visible row into a different tenant.
  • FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY is exercised while running as the table owner.
  • Catalog tests reject missing RLS flags, bypass-capable application roles, extra policies, unexpected policy roles, and absent or trivially true expressions.

docs.title: Application integration boundary
docs.text: Every request and background job must establish the tenant inside the same database transaction as the protected queries. A background worker is not implicitly a system-wide tenant: it should process one explicit tenant per transaction, or use a separate narrowly scoped maintenance role and separately reviewed policy. Do not place a connection in a pool after a session-scoped tenant setting.

docs.title: Limitations
docs.text: The test connects as the local database administrator and uses SET ROLE to exercise non-bypass identities. It does not model managed-service administrator roles, network controls, connection-pool middleware, migration orchestration, replication, backups, side channels, or application authorization. PostgreSQL superusers and roles with BYPASSRLS bypass RLS by design; they require separate administrative controls and monitoring.

docs.title: Event context and secret-cache lifetime lab
docs.text:
Cloud Security · Lab

Exercises producer context, tenant scope, duplicate events, warm-process reuse, and fail-closed cache refresh in a local model.

Tested teaching model. This is not a Lambda, event-source, Vault or Secrets Manager implementation. Context authentication is injected, not cryptographically verified. No cloud resource or real secret exists.

docs.title: Objective and threat model
docs.text:
An event sender controls IDs, tenant and payload. The model trusts a separately verified producer context, derives execution tenant from it, and rejects stale, foreign or schema-invalid input. A duplicate must not repeat a simulated side effect. A long-lived process must not reuse another request's tenant context.

flowchart LR
  E[Untrusted event] --> H[Verified-context handler]
  C[Trusted producer and tenant context] --> H
  H --> I[Serialized local idempotency ledger]
  I --> S[Versioned secret cache]
  S --> X[Fake executor]

docs.title: Prerequisites, setup and validation
docs.text:
Node.js 22+; no package install, container, network, credential or cloud account. From repository root:

node --test labs/request-lifecycle/lifecycle.test.js

Expected: six passing methods. Negative producer/tenant/schema/time cases assert zero executor calls; the concurrent duplicate case asserts one call; warm reuse asserts separate tenants. Cache tests inject a clock: old version at 999 ms, new version at 1000 ms, refresh failure after expiry rejects without a stale fallback. This measures the model's exact timer contract, not provider rotation latency.

docs.title: Evidence, cost and teardown
docs.text:
mkdir -p .artifacts/research
node --test labs/request-lifecycle/lifecycle.test.js > .artifacts/research/lifecycle.tap

The process exits and all memory state disappears. Delete the evidence after review. There is no service, persistent state, infrastructure, cloud cost or destroy step. CPU/memory are small local test-process costs; production overhead is not measured.

docs.title: Failure modes and limitations
docs.text: The ledger intentionally retains event data in memory to compare payload reuse; it has no retention cap, durable transaction or distributed reconciliation. A failure after an external side effect but before ledger completion could duplicate work. Do not treat this serialization as production exactly-once execution. Secret material remains in process memory; the cache cannot revoke already issued values or existing downstream sessions. A real provider, queue and storage system need separate tests and lifecycle controls. Audit is memory-only and omits error events when the secret provider throws; detection coverage for that path is incomplete.
