docs.title: Secure CI/CD boundary and fail-closed gate lab
docs.text:
DevSecOps · Lab

Exercises untrusted workflow boundaries and fail-closed scanner evidence against local positive and negative fixtures.

The local tests evaluate fixture structure and fail-closed gate behavior; they do not execute a hosted workflow, authenticate to Azure, or inspect repository environment settings.

This lab makes CI/CD trust-boundary decisions reproducible. It keeps untrusted pull- request code away from privileged workflow context, rejects unsafe workflow patterns, and blocks when scanner evidence is missing, malformed, incomplete, or above policy.

docs.title: Prerequisites and run commands
docs.text:
• Node.js 24.12.0 (the tests also support a compatible Node.js 22+ runtime).
  • Locked repository dependencies installed with npm ci --ignore-scripts for the existing YAML/gate suite.

The security-policy suite uses Node.js built-ins only:

node labs/secure-cicd/tests/policy-tests.js

Run the existing gate and YAML fixture suite after installing locked dependencies:

node labs/secure-cicd/tests/run-tests.js

Expected output ends with PASS. The gate test asserts exit code 0 only for a completed scanner report within policy. Critical findings and secret findings return 3; invalid or failed scanner input returns 2. A pipeline should treat every nonzero code as blocking.

docs.title: Covered boundaries
docs.text:
Boundary Accepted evidence Rejected evidence Immutable dependencies Every remote action in hardened fixtures uses a full 40-character commit SHA Mutable major tags such as actions/cache@v4 Least privilege Read-only default token and narrowly scoped job permissions permissions: write-all Untrusted PR isolation Ordinary pull_request, no secrets/OIDC/environment, credential-free checkout pull_request_target plus attacker-head checkout and shell execution Artifact integrity Revision-bound artifact name and sha256sum --check before cloud authentication; this detects corruption but is not an independent trust anchor Privileged execution of an artifact without digest verification Provenance GitHub attestation creation and verification constrained to repository, signer workflow, protected source ref, and source digest before cloud authentication Privileged artifact use without provenance verification or with repository-only signer constraints Release approval boundary Release job binds to the production environment Privileged consumer with no environment binding Cloud authentication Azure workload federation via job-scoped id-token: write; identifiers come from non-secret variables Stored long-lived cloud credential references Cache isolation Privileged release consumes no dependency/tool cache Untrusted producer and privileged consumer share and execute a predictable cache

The tests deliberately exercise both sides. A negative fixture passing as hardened - or a hardened fixture matching a prohibited condition - fails the suite.

docs.title: Checksum and attestation trust
docs.text:
release.txt.sha256 travels beside release.txt. It can detect corruption, but an attacker who can replace both files can generate a matching checksum. The external trust decision is the GitHub attestation: the fixture requires the expected repository, the exact .github/workflows/trusted-build-release.yml signer, protected refs/heads/main source ref, and the triggering GITHUB_SHA source digest.

GitHub CLI 2.96.0 accepts the fixture's signer syntax as owner/repository/path/to/workflow. The local suite asserts that all four constraints appear before Azure authentication; it does not fetch a live attestation or prove that a hosted workflow produced one. Predicate data remains partly under the originating workflow's control. A trusted reusable builder can provide stronger isolation when its inputs, permissions, build, and signing steps are themselves designed as a protected boundary.

docs.title: Fixtures
docs.text:
• safe-pr.yml uses the ordinary pull_request event, read-only content permission, credential-free checkout, full-SHA action pins, lockfile installation without lifecycle scripts, and an environment variable for untrusted PR text.
  • trusted-build-release.workflow.yml builds only a protected main revision, records a digest, creates provenance, downloads the revision-bound artifact into a separate release job, verifies digest and provenance, binds the job to the production environment, and only then exchanges GitHub OIDC identity for an Azure session. Attestation verification constrains repository, signer workflow, source ref, and source digest. Its final command validates the session and does not deploy resources.
  • unsafe-pr-target.workflow.yaml.txt combines pull_request_target, write-all token, mutable action tag, untrusted head checkout, and expression injection into shell.
  • unsafe-privileged-consumer.workflow.yaml.txt downloads and executes an unverified artifact with stored cloud credential references and no protected environment.
  • unsafe-shared-cache.workflow.yaml.txt lets untrusted code populate a predictable cache that a privileged job restores and executes.
  • azure-pipelines.safe.yml shows a credential-free PR validation stage. A separate protected release stage and workload-federated service connection are still required for deployment.

Files ending in .workflow.yaml.txt are intentionally non-runnable negative fixtures. The positive GitHub workflow files live outside .github/workflows, so repository validation cannot authenticate or deploy.

docs.title: Required platform configuration
docs.text:
The environment: production declaration creates a binding, not an approval by itself. Configure required reviewers, branch/tag restrictions, and environment secrets/variables in GitHub repository settings. Configure the Azure federated credential to accept only the intended repository and protected-environment subject, then grant the resulting identity only the required Azure role. Those settings are outside this offline lab and require separate review and a non-production exchange test.

Do not move untrusted artifacts or caches into the release boundary merely because a later workflow is privileged. Bind an artifact to its producer, repository, revision, digest, and expected provenance identity; parse reports as data and never execute untrusted artifact or cache content.

docs.title: Failure modes and limitations
docs.text:
The gate validates a small normalized report; production integrations must authenticate report provenance, bind it to the commit and tool configuration, handle waivers with expiry/ownership, and preserve evidence. Thresholds are an example, not an assertion of acceptable organizational risk.

The policy suite is intentionally dependency-free static analysis over controlled fixtures. It does not replace a general YAML parser or platform policy engine, prove the safety of pinned third-party actions, verify GitHub/Azure configuration, exercise environment approval, or validate a real cloud role. GitHub-hosted runner behavior, artifact service authorization, and attestation verification must be tested in the target repository before release is enabled.

docs.title: Artifact provenance and SBOM verification lab
docs.text:
DevSecOps · Lab

Exercises offline artifact digest, provenance identity, source, builder, and SBOM policy decisions.

SLSA v1.2 uses tracks and track-specific levels, not one universal maturity score.

This offline lab demonstrates policy checks across four deliberately separate inputs:

  1. the artifact bytes;
  2. a SLSA v1 provenance statement;
  3. the trusted output of an external cryptographic verifier; and
  4. organization policy.

The policy independently constrains predicate.runDetails.builder.id, predicate.buildDefinition.buildType, the canonical source URI, and the attestation issuer. The external verifier result must return the authenticated statement, which must deep-match the separately supplied provenance. The statement subject must then match the locally calculated artifact digest.

docs.title: Prerequisites and run command
docs.text:
• Node.js 24.12.0 (compatible Node.js 22+ should also work).
  • Repository dependencies installed using npm ci --ignore-scripts.
node labs/supply-chain/tests/run-tests.js

Expected output ends in PASS. Cases the policy should reject:

  • wrong builder ID;
  • wrong build type;
  • missing runDetails;
  • wrong source;
  • wrong issuer;
  • failed cryptographic-verification result;
  • a verifier result bound to another statement;
  • a provenance subject with the wrong digest; and
  • modified artifact bytes.

docs.title: SLSA field model
docs.text:
SLSA v1.2 assigns different meanings to fields that must not be conflated:

  • buildDefinition.buildType identifies the parameterized build template/process;
  • runDetails.builder.id identifies the trusted build platform for that invocation;
  • subject[].digest binds provenance to output bytes; and
  • signature, certificate, issuer, and transparency checks happen on the attestation envelope before provenance policy is applied.

policy.json therefore uses explicit expectedBuilderId, expectedBuildType, expectedSourceUri, and expectedIssuer fields.

docs.title: External verifier boundary
docs.text:
verifier-result.valid.json is a tested pedagogical adapter contract, not a Sigstore, Cosign, or GitHub-defined file format. It represents data returned over a trusted in-process boundary after a real verifier has checked the signed envelope, certificate chain or key, signer identity, and any required transparency evidence. I create separate temporary verifier results to test wrong issuer, failed verification, and statement mismatch. Neither the tracked fixture nor temporary results can establish cryptographic validity merely by containing "verified": true.

Production code must invoke and authenticate a supported verifier, consume its result without allowing the build under test to forge or replace it, and then enforce the same statement and policy constraints. The fixture carries the statement returned by the external verifier; the harness requires it to deep-match the policy-evaluated statement, so a successful result cannot be replayed for modified provenance.

Example production commands, not executed by this offline lab:

cosign verify-attestation \
 --type slsaprovenance \
 --certificate-oidc-issuer=https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com \
 --certificate-identity-regexp='^https://github.com/jasonachkar/cybersecurity-writeups/' \

gh attestation verify <artifact-path> \

Pin the expected artifact digest and narrow workflow identity; do not treat a valid signature from any identity as authorization.

docs.title: Failure modes and limitations
docs.text:
An SBOM is an inventory, not evidence that components are vulnerability-free. Provenance describes a build path, not developer intent or source safety. This lab does not implement DSSE parsing, certificate/key validation, transparency-log checks, certificate revocation semantics, reusable-workflow delegation, private-repository identity, key-compromise response, or the production attestation envelope. Those belong to the selected external verifier and platform integration.

The lab binds source in both the GitHub workflow external parameters and resolvedDependencies; it also requires the external workflow repository, path, and ref to reconstruct the authorized builder ID. A production GitHub build-type policy should additionally reject every unexpected or unrecognized external parameter.

docs.title: Evidence, expected output and interpretation
docs.text:
The documented command exits zero only when its assertions pass; an unexpected allow/deny, schema or state result is a failure. Preserve the full command output under ignored .artifacts/research/ with runtime/tool versions and exit status. Use the specific expected markers above rather than inventing example output. The lab audit records the validation run.

The JSON external-verifier result is a fixture, not a cryptographic signature-verification result. No registry or signing service is contacted. Local finite-case coverage is not a production false-positive or false-negative estimate. TTD/TTC, representative pipeline overhead and monthly cloud cost are not measured in this lab.

docs.title: Evidence standards
docs.text: This is the portfolio's proposed review contract. It describes how to assess the work here; it is not an industry certification or a claim of independent review.

docs.title: Evidence tiers
docs.text:
Tier Evidence What it cannot establish T0 Assertion, documented capability, or engineering guidance; cite the primary source Local configuration or behavior T1 Versioned configuration, compiled template, static policy/schema result Enforcement, reachability, or successful authentication T2 Observed allowed behavior with exact input, output, version, and command Rejection of hostile inputs T3 Negative/adversarial cases against an owned isolated target, with state assertions Untested bypass resistance or production effectiveness T4 Matched vulnerable/remediated comparison over the same cases and initial state General superiority outside the tested conditions

Every major claim must identify its tier, artifact, and scope, either inline or in a claim ledger. Tiers describe evidence strength for that claim, not article rank. A compiled deny policy remains T1 until behavior is exercised. A local interpreter's T3 result is evidence about that interpreter, not about AWS, Azure, or a cluster.

docs.title: Uncertainty language
docs.text:
Label Use Observed Directly produced by the linked lab; give the case and result Likely An inference from stated evidence; describe the missing experiment Assumed A prerequisite not established here, such as independent log ownership Not established Evidence is insufficient; do not imply successful exploitation Not tested The method was not executed in the declared environment

Separate sourced product behavior (T0 in this portfolio) from locally reproduced behavior. A vendor document can be authoritative without being a local experiment. Never promote a boolean verifier fixture to a cryptographic-verification result. Maintain requires-review until an evidence reviewer completes the source check.

docs.title: Required artifacts by research type
docs.text:
Type Minimum review artifacts Cloud Terraform/provider locks, scope diagram, privilege assumptions, plan/validation, allowed/denied API matrix, audit event, teardown and cost model; mark cloud execution absent when absent Application Seed state, auth/session contract, endpoint × actor × object matrix, requests/responses, before/after state assertions, denied-attempt logs AI agent Principal/delegation map, untrusted-input entry, tool schema/authorization, denied tool invocation, egress decisions, bounded evidence retention; distinguish simulated tool calls from a real model run Detection Synthetic fixtures with labels, parser/query, true/false positive and negative counts, missing-source case, event/ingestion/alert clocks, deduplication and response limits Supply chain Artifact digest, provenance, expected identity/source/builder, trusted verifier boundary, tamper cases, missing/failed evidence and promotion decision

Do not collect live credentials as evidence. Use generated local sessions, synthetic records and mock metadata. Redact authorization headers, cookies, URL queries and bodies before persistence. Keep only fields needed to reproduce a decision.

docs.title: Measurement contract
docs.text:
Declare the corpus, denominator, seed/reset strategy, repetitions, and exclusions. Publish machine-readable case results; a failing security assertion returns nonzero. Distinguish a test failing from an attack being correctly denied.

Outcome Measurement Coverage Exercised threat cases / enumerated threat cases; list omissions False positives Benign cases denied / benign cases exercised False negatives Hostile cases allowed / hostile cases exercised Time to detect Alert creation minus event occurrence, with clock and ingestion uncertainty Time to contain Independently verified access loss minus containment decision; distinguish token expiry from revocation Pipeline impact Repeated elapsed times with/without gate on the same runner and inputs; report sample size Operational cost CPU, memory, requests, storage/retention, operator effort and cloud rates; do not infer a monthly bill from static code Residual risk Remaining actor capability after each control fails; include ownership and recovery boundary

When clocks, live integrations, billing, or representative workloads are absent, write not measured in this lab and specify the future experiment. Fixture accuracy is not a population estimate of detection effectiveness.

docs.title: Research methodology
docs.text: This site treats security research as an evidence-producing discipline. Its labs use owned local targets; architecture guidance is not production-test evidence.

docs.title: Research, documentation, and tutorials
docs.text: Research asks a falsifiable question and produces evidence that could disprove its hypothesis. Documentation explains a sourced capability or design. A lab tutorial makes a procedure repeatable. A page can combine these forms, but must identify which conclusions come from experiments and which are proposals.

docs.title: Research model
docs.text:
Each deep-dive follows: Question, Hypothesis, Threat model, Method, Evidence, Findings, Practical guidance, Limitations, and Open questions.

Start with an actor, asset and disputed boundary. Define the success and failure conditions before implementing a fix. Run the same cases against vulnerable and remediated paths, reset state between cases, and test allowed behavior as well as denials. Preserve useful historical explanation with an explicit historical label.

docs.title: Article contract
docs.text:
Section Review question Question Which decision is this investigation intended to inform? Hypothesis What observable result would refute the proposed control? Threat model What can the actor control, and what remains trusted? Method Which commands, versions, fixtures and state resets reproduce the test? Evidence Which input, output, log and state assertion support each claim? Findings What was observed, separately from interpretation? Practical guidance Which boundary should enforce the decision, and who operates it? Limitations What was not tested, and where does the claim stop? Open questions Which next experiment could change the conclusion?

Every major claim carries a T0–T4 tier using the evidence standards. Every research article states what was not tested. A link to a lab does not imply that the full architecture was exercised.

docs.title: Multi-tenant BOLA: One Authorization Predicate Across Every Data Path
docs.text:
Vulnerability Research · Research

An owned session-authenticated API compares cross-tenant CRUD, export, mass assignment, and agent refunds before and after data-access enforcement.

docs.title: Executive summary
docs.text:
Observed, T4: an authenticated synthetic user can read, change and delete a foreign tenant's document through the vulnerable API. Export trusts a client tenant header, and an agent wrapper replaces the caller with the target object's owner. The remediated API rejects the tested foreign-object operations, preserves state on denials, scopes export to the session, and permits the user's intended work.

This is an owned teaching API. It is not a finding against a named SaaS platform. OWASP API1:2023 provides the class context: authentication alone does not establish object-level authority (T0). The lab provides behavioral evidence separately.

docs.title: Research question and hypothesis
docs.text:
Does a common data-access predicate prevent tenant and owner confusion across read, update, delete, export, sensitive action and agent-invocation paths?

Hypothesis: deriving tenant/user from a valid server session and applying row.tenant == actor.tenant AND row.owner == actor.user at the repository boundary, plus operation-specific role and field checks, rejects the enumerated misuse without breaking the five positive cases. Any unauthorized disclosure or mutation in the remediated corpus refutes this hypothesis.

docs.title: Threat model
docs.text:
Element Scope Assets Synthetic tenants, users, customer links, documents and refund records Actor Alice has her own valid session; knows synthetic document IDs; controls method, path, JSON fields and X-Tenant-ID Entry points /documents/{id}, /documents/{id}/refund, /export, /agent/refund Boundaries Cookie → server session; session → data-access context; object → customer; user → agent wrapper; permitted fields → stored row Trusted Session map, seed state, server process and code; no client-supplied tenant authority Impact tested Foreign read/update/delete, selected-field reassignment, foreign export and recorded refund Out of scope Login, stolen-session defense, payment processor, SQL, real model behavior and administrative compromise 
flowchart TD
  U[Authenticated user with untrusted IDs and JSON] --> A[HTTP API]
  A --> S[Server-side session context]
  A --> W[Agent refund wrapper]
  W --> S
  S --> R[Repository: tenant and owner predicate]
  R --> O[Document]
  O --> C[Customer relationship]
  R --> E[Tenant-scoped export]
  R --> F[Role-checked synthetic refund]
  R --> L[Minimal authorization event]

docs.title: Affected component and vulnerability class
docs.text: api.py contains two repository paths over the same seed model. The vulnerable object lookup uses only an ID. Update binds arbitrary fields, export accepts a tenant header, and the agent uses object-owner authority. Those are distinct defects: BOLA, unsafe property assignment, context confusion, and excessive delegation. They interact but should not be counted as one generic “authentication failure.”

docs.title: Prerequisites and isolation requirements
docs.text:
Python 3.13+ runs the complete suite. Docker Compose additionally runs the same HTTP tests in a container with no external network. Both API servers listen only on loopback at OS-assigned ports. No secrets, users or JWTs are copied from a real system. The server generates opaque 256-bit session material at runtime, stores only its digest, checks expiry and deletes all state when the process exits.

This is session-based authentication, not a JWT implementation. The test bootstrap creates sessions directly inside the owned process. It does not model user login.

docs.title: Method and controlled misuse
docs.text:
Every case starts from fresh state and a generated Alice session. The runner performs real HTTP requests, checks status and selected returned content, and independently inspects state. In the secure path every denied matrix call must leave the entire seed state unchanged. A separate case tests role denial for the reader Aaron on his own refund action.

Tested commands, from the repository root:

python3 vulnerability-research/api-bola-multi-tenant/lab/test_api.py
docker compose -p research-bola -f vulnerability-research/api-bola-multi-tenant/lab/compose.yaml run --build --rm lab

The following sanitized requests omit the generated cookie. test_api.py supplies it from the in-process bootstrap; no placeholder token needs replacing.

Preconditions and request Vulnerable observed result Remediated observed result Why/fix and residual surface Alice GET /documents/doc-b 200, title SYNTHETIC_B 404 not_found Repository now requires tenant and owner; timing enumeration not measured Alice GET /documents/doc-aaron (same tenant, different owner) 200 404 Tenant-only checks would miss horizontal access; this contract additionally requires ownership Alice PATCH /documents/doc-b with {"title":"changed"} 200, foreign row changed 404; state unchanged Predicate applies before mutation; no asynchronous update path modeled Alice DELETE /documents/doc-b 200, row removed 404; state unchanged Same predicate; no backup/restore path tested Alice patches her document with {"tenant":"tenant-b","owner":"bob"} 200, ownership fields changed 400 invalid_fields; state unchanged Only a bounded title update is accepted; schema changes need new tests Alice GET /export with X-Tenant-ID: tenant-b 200, only doc-b 200, only doc-a Session scopes data-access export; client header ignored Alice POST /documents/doc-b/refund with {} 200, refund record appended 404; no refund Authorize object before deriving customer and amount Alice POST /agent/refund with {"document":"doc-b"} 200, refund as owner Bob 404; no refund Agent retains original caller context; no service-wide authority substitution Alice reads missing 404 Same status/body as foreign object Content enumeration reduced; response-time side channels remain unmeasured

Positive matrix cases are own read, own title update, own delete, own refund and own agent refund. They return 200 under both configurations. The full matrix has 14 paired cases / 28 HTTP evaluations, plus session/role/context checks. This denominator is a finite test corpus, not a claim about population-wide authorization coverage.

docs.title: Evidence ledger
docs.text:
Claim Tier Artifact Foreign title is returned by vulnerable read T4 cross-read response assertion Vulnerable foreign update/delete have actual effects T4 Seed state assertions after HTTP calls Secure denied matrix calls do not mutate state T3/T4 Whole-state equality and deny audit assertions Export honors server context T4 Exact returned-key set in each mode Agent cannot create a foreign refund after fix T4 HTTP result and refund-list length Foreign and absent IDs have identical error content T3 test_session_and_enumeration Tamper-proof audit persistence Not established Audit is process memory only

Observed sanitized secure response:

{"error":"not_found"}

The runner's output includes case, mode, status and decision. Audit fields contain operation, authenticated principal/tenant, outcome and reason; no cookie, document title or body is retained. The harness scans audit JSON for the session and selected sentinels. It does not claim exhaustive data-loss prevention.

docs.title: Root cause and practical architecture guidance
docs.text:
Identifiers are selectors, not grants. In the vulnerable path the route's successful session check does not constrain the later lookup. Export and the agent introduce separate authority sources, so fixing only GET /documents/{id} leaves other paths open. Mass assignment also lets a caller mutate the fields later used as authority.

Put the predicate in the repository so every route consumes the same scoped context. Reject client updates to tenant, owner, customer and amount. Derive sensitive-action arguments from the authorized row and verify related customer ownership. Keep operation grants separate from row visibility. A production SQL repository should use tenant-scoped queries and independently reviewed RLS where appropriate; the PostgreSQL lab exercises that different boundary.

docs.title: Business impact and severity reasoning
docs.text: Observed: foreign synthetic content is disclosed and modified, records are removed, and synthetic refund entries are created. Likely under additional assumptions: comparable defects over customer documents or payment instructions would affect confidentiality and integrity. No money moves here. There is no established account takeover, administrator access, or complete system compromise. Severity is qualitatively high for the lab's tenant-isolation objective because an ordinary authenticated principal crosses it with one request; this is not a vendor severity rating or CVSS assessment.

docs.title: Remediation, verified fix and regression matrix
docs.text:
The secure path checks valid nonexpired session, tenant and owner, action allowlist, role for update/delete/refund, closed update schema and document/customer consistency. Absent or unauthorized objects return the same 404 body. The agent invokes the same repository as direct requests. Denials emit minimal events.

Mutation assertions distinguish “HTTP denied” from “no side effect.” Fresh per-case seeding prevents an earlier deletion from turning a later test into an accidental 404 success. Legitimate calls prevent deny-all implementations from passing. Add every new bulk, job, search, cache and tool endpoint to the matrix before release.

docs.title: Detection engineering and compensating controls
docs.text:
The executable detection predicates recognize denied object operations as blocked attempts. A production correlation should group principal, operation and time window, distinguish missing/stale sessions from object denials, and compare to baseline support activity. Thresholds are illustrative until representative data exists. Missing-source monitoring needs an independent canary.

Opaque identifiers reduce guessing convenience; they do not authorize access. Apply request budgets, export quotas, purpose-bound agent grants and independently protected audit storage. Require a separate approval for high-impact refunds and reconcile idempotency against downstream state; neither control is implemented in this toy API. Do not respond to repository failures by falling back to global reads.

docs.title: Limitations and what was not tested
docs.text:
No real SaaS, LLM, MCP transport, external issuer, browser, CSRF protection, cookie issuance, SQL engine, database pool, distributed cache, asynchronous job, real refund, refund idempotency, transaction rollback or production concurrency/load was tested. The repository lock serializes toy mutations; it is not a distributed transaction. A session thief inherits that user's permitted operations. Ownership-only semantics also deliberately omit shared documents, support roles and administrator exceptions.

Response-time enumeration, time to detect, time to contain, production false-positive rates and operating cost are not measured in this lab. Review status remains requires-review pending an independent evidence review.

docs.title: Open questions
docs.text: Can a SQL implementation retain the same predicate under pooled transactions and bulk export? How should delegated agent grants narrow action, purpose and lifetime? Can response timing leak foreign-object existence? What transaction/idempotency contract prevents duplicate refunds during retries and partial downstream failure?

docs.title: Reproduce the multi-tenant authorization experiment
docs.text: Status: tested bounded HTTP target; production controls not tested. See the research article for the per-operation matrix and residual risks.

docs.title: Objective and threat model
docs.text:
Compare the same seeded API under vulnerable and remediated data-access behavior. Alice controls IDs, JSON and a tenant header; she cannot edit her server-side session. Assets are synthetic customer/document/refund records. The trusted session map supplies tenant/user/role; the API and agent wrapper must not replace that context with client or object-owner authority. Manager may operate on owned rows; reader may read/export owned rows and cannot update/delete/refund them.

flowchart LR
  T[Generated Alice session and HTTP request] --> A[Loopback API]
  A --> S[Session map]
  A --> R[Repository authorization]
  S --> R
  R --> D[Synthetic tenant and owner records]
  R --> L[In-memory audit]

docs.title: Prerequisites and isolation
docs.text: Python 3.13+ or Docker with Compose; no package installation or credential is required. Docker uses network_mode: none, an unprivileged user and a read-only filesystem. No ports are published. Servers bind only to 127.0.0.1 at randomly assigned ports even when run directly on a host. Reserve about 128 MiB and 15–20 seconds per full run. No cloud costs or persistent volumes exist.

docs.title: Setup and validation — tested
docs.text:
From the repository root, either command runs the entire real-HTTP experiment:

python3 vulnerability-research/api-bola-multi-tenant/lab/test_api.py

docker compose -p research-bola -f vulnerability-research/api-bola-multi-tenant/lab/compose.yaml config --quiet
docker compose -p research-bola -f vulnerability-research/api-bola-multi-tenant/lab/compose.yaml run --build --rm lab

api.py contains seed data, runtime-generated sessions, data access and both configurations. test_api.py is the copy-and-run client: it creates the targets, obtains generated sessions in-process, sends requests, asserts results and closes the servers. The APIs have no unauthenticated session-bootstrap HTTP endpoint.

Expected: two test methods pass, with 14 paired cases / 28 HTTP matrix evaluations, plus expiry, invalid-session, enumeration, role and header checks. The runner returns nonzero if a secure denial changes state or an expected response differs. No raw session material is printed. Cookie: lab_session=<generated-at-runtime> is only a description of the authentication contract, not a credential to paste.

docs.title: Evidence and measurement
docs.text:
mkdir -p .artifacts/research
python3 vulnerability-research/api-bola-multi-tenant/lab/test_api.py > .artifacts/research/bola-http.txt 2>&1
python3 vulnerability-research/detection.py --test

Output lists case, mode, status and decision. State assertions establish returned foreign titles, modified/deleted rows, exact export keys, refund count and absence of secure side effects. Audit assertions check selected content/session sentinels. The response-body equality check reduces content enumeration; timing is not measured. Production false positives, TTD/TTC, browser security, refund idempotency, distributed transactions and a real database are not measured or implemented by this lab.

docs.title: Teardown — tested
docs.text:
Each run closes both servers; --rm removes its container. For any interrupted run:

docker compose -p research-bola -f vulnerability-research/api-bola-multi-tenant/lab/compose.yaml down --volumes --remove-orphans

All data and sessions are in memory. Delete retained evidence after review.

docs.title: CI/CD Workload Identity: Trust Binding, Permission Ceilings and Persistence
docs.text:
Vulnerability Research · Research

Terraform-exported trust and permissions are tested in a local policy model, including environment replay and explicit deny boundaries.

docs.title: Executive summary
docs.text:
Observed, T1: pinned-provider Terraform validates and produces separate staging and production identities in mocked plans. Observed, T3/T4 in a local model: exact subject/audience checks reject foreign contexts, and exported boundaries reject modeled identity-management, cross-environment and runtime-modification requests even with a broader identity grant.

Not established: any AWS STS exchange, AWS authorization decision or GitHub hosted-workflow outcome. The lab does not create cloud resources. An authenticated approved workflow remains able to alter the artifacts its role permits; federation does not remove that trust.

docs.title: Research question and hypothesis
docs.text:
Can an environment-bound workload identity publish only its own release artifacts without acquiring role-management, credential-creation or cross-environment authority?

Hypothesis: exact OIDC trust plus a resource-scoped identity policy and explicit deny boundary reject the declared escalation matrix. A modeled allowed management operation, foreign subject admission or foreign artifact access refutes the local hypothesis. Cloud enforcement is a separate future hypothesis requiring negative STS/API calls in an authorized disposable account.

docs.title: Threat model
docs.text:
Element Scope Assets Role trust, permissions boundary, environment artifact prefixes, workflow/infrastructure integrity, independently retained audit evidence Actor A Workflow in another repository/branch/environment with an authentic issuer assertion Actor B Code execution in the approved workflow with all authority granted to its deployment session Entry points Federation audience/subject/provider, artifact APIs, IAM mutation APIs, runtime/repository update APIs Trust boundaries Issuer → exchange trust; role → permissions; staging → production; deployment → bootstrap administration; workload → log archive Trusted/assumed GitHub issuer, protected environment rules, bootstrap administrator, existing isolated bucket/OIDC provider and log owner Tested impact Local model admits or denies requests; no remote role or artifact is changed 
flowchart LR
  U[Foreign workflow context] --> T[Exact provider, audience, subject]
  A[Approved workflow context] --> T
  T --> R[Environment-specific session]
  R --> I[Identity permission and explicit boundary]
  I --> S[Own artifact prefix]
  I -.->|Deny| X[IAM, credentials, federation, runtime and other environment]
  B[Separate bootstrap administrator] --> T
  B --> I
  L[Independent audit and canary owner] -.-> R

docs.title: Affected lab component and vulnerability class
docs.text:
The affected component is a deliberately weak local trust/permissions model: provider-only admission and a wildcard identity policy. It is not a deployable vulnerable AWS configuration; real AWS validates token signatures/claims and imposes GitHub subject-policy requirements. The study concerns excessive federation trust, privilege escalation and persistence opportunities from deployment authority.

The remediated documents come from main.tf, exported by a verbose mocked terraform test plan and consumed by evaluate.py. This avoids testing an unrelated hand-maintained JSON copy.

docs.title: Prerequisites, isolation and assumptions
docs.text: Use Terraform 1.7+ (recorded run: 1.16.5), Python 3.13+ and the locked AWS 6.20.0 provider. Provider initialization downloads code; tests replace the provider with a mock and use the all-zero synthetic account. No cloud credential is needed. Do not run apply. Existing provider, bucket, resource policy, KMS, organization controls and log archive are assumptions, not resources proven by this lab.

docs.title: Vulnerable implementation and controlled misuse paths
docs.text:
The vulnerable local model accepts matching provider identity without subject or audience authorization and grants Action: *, Resource: *. That is a comparative teaching condition, not a claim that an arbitrary self-edited token works at AWS. The evaluator treats assertions and permissions as separate stages.

Tested command, from repository root:

bash vulnerability-research/cicd-identity-escalation/lab/validate.sh
Precondition / controlled request Vulnerable local result Remediated local result and reason Remaining surface Authentic foreign repository or staging subject presented to production trust Provider-only model allows Exact subject rejects Compromised approved repository remains trusted Branch-form subject presented to environment-bound trust Provider-only model allows Environment subject required Branch approval is an external GitHub protection rule Wrong audience Provider-only model allows Exact sts.amazonaws.com rejects Actual provider verification not executed Different OIDC provider ARN Denied Denied This case verifies the model's common baseline s3:PutObject to own environment prefix Allowed Allowed Malicious approved release content is still possible s3:PutObject to other environment prefix Allowed Explicit boundary deny Resource policies and other accounts not fully interpreted iam:CreateRole, policy attach/put/version creation Allowed Explicit deny of every nonapproved API Bootstrap administrator is a separate trusted identity Boundary remove/replace; trust or federation creation Allowed Explicit deny No claim of real IAM boundary-removal test iam:CreateAccessKey, iam:PassRole, sts:AssumeRole Allowed Explicit deny Other credentials accessible to approved code remain a separate risk lambda:UpdateFunctionCode, codecommit:GitPush, cloudtrail:StopLogging Allowed Explicit deny GitHub repository write authority is controlled outside AWS Reuse identical locally signed assertion in staging trust Not a cloud test Rejected by subject mismatch Same-context replay within lifetime remains accepted

docs.title: Evidence and observed output
docs.text:
The recorded local run ends:

PASS: 28 offline policy decisions; no STS calls

These consist of six trust cases, eighteen permission cases and four local signed assertion/replay cases. The assertion format uses runtime-generated HMAC material; it is not a GitHub JWT/JWS verifier. Expired and tampered assertions are rejected. The same valid assertion is accepted twice in its authorized context. This is an intentional residual finding: subject binding is not a single-use replay cache.

Each output record contains the case, stage, allow verdict and boundary verdict. No token, HMAC key, session credential or production identifier is emitted. Terraform also rejects wildcard subjects in a negative variable test. These are T1/T3/T4 local artifacts; they do not imply observed AWS API denials.

docs.title: Root-cause analysis
docs.text:
Federation trust answers who may obtain the role; permissions answer what the session may do. Either can be broader than intended. A deployment session able to edit roles, trust, boundaries, credentials, workflows or privileged runtime code can potentially outlive its original purpose. Source-level code update authority can itself be persistence authority even without IAM management.

The AWS boundary documentation distinguishes identity-policy intersections from direct role-session resource grants. The lab therefore uses explicit denies for nonapproved APIs and S3 resources outside the environment prefix. This is a narrow design, not a complete IAM interpreter.

docs.title: Remediation and verified-fix matrix
docs.text:
Control Artifact/tier What still needs verification Dedicated environment roles Terraform mock plan, T1 Real role creation and exchange Exact provider/audience/subject Exported policy plus negative model cases, T3 Actual issuer keys, token format and environment rules Own-prefix GetObject/PutObject only Permission model, T3/T4 Bucket/KMS/SCP/resource-policy interactions Boundary denies nonapproved APIs and foreign prefixes Explicit-deny model, T3 AWS authorization for session principals and service-specific conditions Runtime cannot modify its boundary IAM mutations denied in model Independent bootstrap control and drift alert Workflow requests short session Illustrative workflow, T1 Hosted runner and environment configuration Audit independence Declared output assumptions, T0 Trail selectors, delivery, archive access and alerting

AWS documents that GetCallerIdentity returns identity information even when an explicit deny exists; it is not an escalation test. The illustrative workflow uses that introspection operation only (T0, AWS API reference below).

The role is intentionally an artifact deployment identity, not an infrastructure administrator. Do not enlarge its permissions to make this Terraform module apply itself. Bootstrap and runtime identities have different responsibilities.

GitHub's AWS guidance documents exact subject conditions and environment-specific subject forms. Inspect the subject actually issued for the repository, including immutable-ID formats where applicable; the example names are synthetic. Environment approval and branch restrictions must be configured independently. The workflow example is outside .github/workflows and performs only identity inspection.

docs.title: Business impact and severity reasoning
docs.text: Likely, conditional on actual excessive authority: a compromised CI session could alter deployment roles or future code paths. The local wildcard model supports the permission precondition only; it does not establish an exploit against AWS or a successful cloud persistence action. Severity depends on actual role, resource policies, environment separation, reachable secrets and repository controls. The lab's corrected artifact role still permits replacing own-prefix artifacts; provenance and independent release approval are separate required boundaries.

docs.title: Detection engineering
docs.text:
The runnable synthetic detector distinguishes failed attempts from reported-success IAM/runtime/logging changes attributed to a known lab runtime role. Production attribution must derive role identity from trusted CloudTrail session fields, not an input boolean. Audit event names such as UpdateAssumeRolePolicy and DeleteRolePermissionsBoundary are candidate signals; iam:PassRole is authorization evaluated during a destination service operation, not a standalone event to search for.

An illustrative, not executed Sentinel query for a deployment-role inventory is in detection.kql. Validate schema, event coverage, service errors and session issuer before deployment. Capture STS exchange, downstream resource access, IAM/policy mutation and workflow changes separately. S3 object access requires selected data events; management-event coverage alone is insufficient.

docs.title: Containment runbook and compensating controls
docs.text:
1. Stop the affected release path and preserve workflow revision, artifact digests, triggering identity and relevant events before deleting evidence.
  2. Restrict exact role trust to prevent new exchanges. Do not assume this revokes already issued sessions. Follow a separately reviewed provider session-revocation procedure and verify access loss against a disposable canary resource.
  3. Inspect role/policy/boundary/federation/credential changes and runtime/repository modifications, including versions created during the exposure window.
  4. Rotate downstream credentials actually exposed; restore reviewed trust and code from an independent administrator; verify allowed and denied operations again.
  5. Re-enable releases only after environment governance, evidence collection and artifact verification have been independently checked.

Use protected environments, reviewed workflows, isolated runners, immutable action pins, separate artifact promotion and a bootstrap administrator outside CI authority. The runbook is not executed here. Time to contain is not measured.

docs.title: Limitations and what was not tested
docs.text:
No AWS account, GitHub hosted job, JWT discovery/signature path, STS exchange, CloudTrail delivery, IAM simulator, credential revocation, real replay, bucket API, production policy or cloud resource was tested. The local policy subset omits full resource/session/SCP/RCP semantics, IAM case rules and service context. It refuses unsupported statement keys rather than silently interpreting them.

Federation does not eliminate compromise of approved code, dependencies, protected workflow maintainers or the bootstrap administrator. A stolen session retains its allowed operations until provider lifetime/revocation controls actually stop it. Pipeline duration impact, live detection coverage and operational cost are not measured in this lab. Independent review remains required.

docs.title: Open questions
docs.text: How quickly does trust removal affect new exchanges versus existing sessions? Do direct session grants remain denied under the target resource policies? Can a release signer independently reject an artifact written by a compromised approved workflow? Which service update APIs create indirect persistence without IAM access?

docs.text:
Consulted 2026-11-02. AWS/GitHub pages are living product documentation. Provider schema is pinned to 6.20.0; Terraform mock support is versioned separately.

docs.title: Reproduce CI/CD identity policy decisions without cloud access
docs.text: Status: partially tested. Terraform schema and mock plans plus a deliberately limited local authorization model are tested. AWS STS, API enforcement, audit collection and GitHub hosted execution are not tested. See the study for the exact evidence boundary and containment runbook.

docs.title: Objective, architecture and threat model
docs.text:
Compare a provider-only/wildcard local model with Terraform-exported exact trust, resource scope and explicit deny controls. The actor controls a foreign workflow context or compromises approved workflow code. Assets are synthetic environment artifact prefixes and the ability to change future identities/code. Bootstrap administration and audit ownership are separate trusted assumptions.

flowchart LR
  T[Mock Terraform plan] --> J[Exported policy documents]
  J --> E[Local policy evaluator]
  F[Foreign contexts and API misuse cases] --> E
  E --> R[Expected allow and deny records]

docs.title: Prerequisites and setup — tested
docs.text:
Terraform >=1.7,<2 (recorded 1.16.5), Python 3.13+, internet for the pinned AWS 6.20.0 provider download, and roughly 1 GiB free disk for provider binaries. No cloud credential, account access, backend or environment variable is required.

From repository root:

bash vulnerability-research/cicd-identity-escalation/lab/validate.sh

The script initializes without a backend, checks formatting/schema, runs three Terraform tests with mock_provider "aws", exports the plan, and evaluates its actual policy output. Expected final line:

PASS: 28 offline policy decisions; no STS calls

Unsupported policy semantics cause a failure. The model handles only the statement keys used by the exported documents; it is not the IAM simulator. Runtime-generated HMAC assertions test local lifetime/tamper/replay decisions, not JWT verification.

docs.title: Terraform design and deployment assumptions
docs.text:
main.tf defines environment-specific deployment roles, exact audience/subject trust, own-prefix artifact permission, and boundaries that explicitly deny every other API and S3 resource. Input subjects must be the exact observed GitHub format; readable and immutable-ID subjects cannot be substituted blindly.

A separately authorized cloud experiment would need an isolated account, an existing reviewed GitHub provider, a private versioned artifact bucket, reviewed KMS/resource/SCP policies, and an independent CloudTrail archive with management and selected S3 data events. The runtime role cannot bootstrap its own infrastructure. No provider or bucket is created by this module. No apply command is part of this lab.

The adjacent workflow is illustrative and inactive outside .github/workflows. It requests a 900-second session only after protected-environment review and prints caller identity, not credentials. Inspect action source and configure repository variables before any separately authorized hosted experiment.

docs.title: Evidence collection and negative matrix
docs.text:
mkdir -p .artifacts/research
terraform -chdir=vulnerability-research/cicd-identity-escalation/lab test -json -verbose > .artifacts/research/cicd-plan.jsonl
python3 vulnerability-research/cicd-identity-escalation/lab/evaluate.py .artifacts/research/cicd-plan.jsonl > .artifacts/research/cicd-decisions.txt
python3 vulnerability-research/detection.py --test

Tests cover wrong provider/audience/repository/environment, branch-form subject, foreign-prefix writes, identity/policy/boundary/federation/key creation and change, PassRole, role chaining, runtime/repository updates, logging disablement, local signed assertion tamper/expiry and replay. Same-context replay remains accepted. The study maps each misuse to its precondition, result, fix and residual capability.

docs.title: Cleanup and cost
docs.text: No cloud resources or real credentials exist. Mock plan tests do not leave managed cloud state. Provider downloads remain under .terraform/; remove that directory and retained .artifacts/research/cicd-* evidence after inspection. Keep the tracked provider lockfile. A future authorized deployment would need separate bootstrap state and a reviewed destroy plan for only its lab roles/policies. Never delete a shared provider, bucket or trail as teardown. Cloud usage cost is not measured.

docs.text:
Three investigations against owned, isolated teaching targets. These are not CVE disclosures, bug-bounty findings, or claims about vulnerabilities in an MCP implementation, cloud provider or third-party application.

Study Disputed boundary Evidence MCP-style tool SSRF Model-influenced URL → server network authority T4 paired HTTP tests; T3 resolver/policy and container path tests Multi-tenant BOLA Authenticated user → object, tenant and sensitive operation T4 paired HTTP cases with seeded state and denial state checks CI/CD workload identity Federated subject → environment role → APIs and persistence T1 Terraform mock plans; T3/T4 local policy/assertion model, no cloud execution

Read the methodology, evidence contract and verification record before interpreting the results. Commands are executed from a repository checkout. Start with each study's lab README; no live credential or cloud deployment is needed for local verification.

docs.title: MCP-style URL-fetch SSRF: Destination and Egress Boundaries
docs.text:
Vulnerability Research · Research

Paired isolated HTTP tests compare an ambient URL fetcher with destination validation and a separate egress gateway.

docs.title: Executive summary
docs.text:
Observed, T4: the vulnerable local fetcher returns a synthetic metadata marker both directly and after a redirect. The remediated gateway denies those requests and permits the intended public-surrogate origin. Observed, T3: the secure container cannot open a direct TCP connection to the mock metadata fixture. These claims concern this lab, not an MCP product vulnerability.

The tool is MCP-style: JSON input represents a model-influenced tool call. It does not implement MCP transport, discovery, authorization or an LLM. The MCP project's security guidance discusses SSRF and token-passthrough risks; that sourced context is T0 here.

docs.title: Research question and hypothesis
docs.text:
Can a URL-fetch tool keep model-controlled destinations from acquiring the server's internal-network authority while preserving a legitimate fetch?

Hypothesis: exact-origin selection, validation of every resolved address, connection pinning, redirect denial and a separate egress boundary reject the enumerated internal-fetch paths. One returned internal marker through the secure path, or a successful direct secure-container connection to metadata, refutes it.

docs.title: Threat model
docs.text:
Element Scope Assets Synthetic internal record, synthetic metadata marker, gateway policy and decision logs Actor Local test caller controls the URL, path, query and redirect entry point Entry point POST /fetch with a single url field Trust boundaries Caller → tool; tool → gateway; gateway → resolved destination; redirect response → next hop Trusted Docker host, immutable lab code, pinned fixture address and gateway administrator Impact tested Retrieval of a marker across the intended boundary; no credential theft or code execution Assumed in a real deployment Tool host may have network access and credentials that the user lacks 
flowchart LR
  U[Untrusted URL input] --> V[Vulnerable fetcher]
  V --> M[Mock metadata and internal record]
  V --> P[Public-surrogate origin]
  P -->|302| M
  U --> S[Remediated tool]
  subgraph E[Separate fetch network]
    S --> G[Destination-validating gateway]
  end
  G -->|Exact pinned lab origin| P
  G -.->|Denied destination or redirect| M
  S -.->|No direct network path| M

docs.title: Affected lab component and vulnerability class
docs.text: fetcher.py deliberately contrasts vulnerable_fetch with FetchPolicy. The insecure path uses the default redirect-following HTTP opener without destination checks. The class is server-side request forgery: controlled input selects a server-side request destination. Agent context can increase the number of untrusted inputs reaching the tool and the authority of the tool host; this amplification is an inference, T0, not a measured model outcome.

docs.title: Prerequisites and isolation requirements
docs.text: Use Python 3.13+ for unit checks and Docker with Compose for topology checks. All origins are repository-owned containers. No port is published; all three networks are internal. Do not use a real metadata service. See the complete setup.

docs.title: Method and vulnerable implementation
docs.text:
The same six requests run against both modes. The “public” origin is private Docker address 172.28.190.10, explicitly pinned to public.lab:8080 in the lab adapter. This exception exists only to replace the internet with an isolated fixture. It must not become a production private-address allowance.

The generic policy requires HTTPS on 443, a configured exact host, no userinfo or fragment, and only global unicast DNS answers. It rejects mapped/transition address forms, mixed public/private answers, and control-character/backslash ambiguity. The connector uses the vetted numeric address; TLS uses the original hostname for SNI and certificate validation. That external TLS branch is not exercised over an external connection; pinning is tested with an injected transport.

docs.title: Controlled misuse paths and evidence
docs.text:
Run from the repository root; these are tested commands:

python3 vulnerability-research/mcp-tool-ssrf/lab/test_fetcher.py
docker compose -p research-ssrf -f vulnerability-research/mcp-tool-ssrf/lab/compose.yaml up -d --build vulnerable secure gateway public metadata
docker compose -p research-ssrf -f vulnerability-research/mcp-tool-ssrf/lab/compose.yaml run --build --rm tests
docker compose -p research-ssrf -f vulnerability-research/mcp-tool-ssrf/lab/compose.yaml exec -T secure python test_egress.py
Precondition and request URL Vulnerable observation Fix and post-fix observation Remaining surface Caller can select http://metadata.lab:8080/metadata 200, SYNTHETIC_METADATA_NO_CREDENTIALS 403; HTTP is denied outside the exact surrogate origin Real metadata protocols and host-level routes not tested Caller can select http://internal.lab:8080/internal 200, SYNTHETIC_INTERNAL_RECORD 403; host/scheme policy prevents fetch Compromised allowed service can still return sensitive data Allowed origin returns 302 from /redirect 200 with metadata marker 403 redirect_denied; no redirect is followed No multi-hop or status-code-specific redirect support is offered Allowed origin returns >4 KiB at /large 200 with truncated body 403 response_too_large Slow-response total deadline and streaming cancellation not implemented Public surrogate /metadata (fixture-separation regression) 400 upstream-not-found 403 upstream_status; no marker returned An allowed-origin compromise remains outside the fixture model Intended origin / 200 PUBLIC_LAB_OK 200 PUBLIC_LAB_OK Fixture success is not public-web availability evidence

Sanitized observed HTTP body for the redirect denial:

{"error":"redirect_denied"}

Sanitized observed gateway event (request ID omitted):

{"event":"tool_fetch","mode":"gateway","decision":"deny","reason":"redirect_denied"}

The runner asserts the returned marker for the vulnerable metadata and redirect cases and absence of a body on denied secure responses. It exits nonzero if any status differs. The direct-network test prints:

PASS: direct secure-container TCP path to mock metadata denied

docs.title: DNS bypasses, allowlists and egress considerations
docs.text:
Observed, T3: resolver fixtures reject a private-only answer and a mixed public/loopback answer for an otherwise allowed HTTPS host. A changing-answer fixture verifies that the transport receives the first vetted numeric address without a second lookup. This is a deterministic TOCTOU regression test, not an observed DNS-server rebinding attack. See test_dns_pin_prevents_second_lookup.

A hostname denylist alone leaves unlisted private ranges, alternate textual forms and redirects to handle. An exact hostname allowlist alone does not establish the IP reached. The OWASP prevention guidance informs the layered design (T0). This implementation selects a deliberately small input language instead of accepting every URL syntax.

The secure tool lacks a route to the target network; only the gateway joins it. The gateway also has no internet route. This topology tests a controlled proxy boundary, not a production firewall, VPC endpoint, service mesh or CNI. Docker-host compromise and an allowed-origin compromise remain outside the hypothesis.

docs.title: Root-cause analysis and impact
docs.text:
The insecure tool turns a user-controlled string into a network action under the server's authority. Redirect following delegates destination selection to a second untrusted party. Schema-valid JSON and a valid user session would not authorize an internal destination. The secure path resolves authorization before connection and keeps redirects from introducing a new destination.

Severity reasoning: material confidentiality impact in the synthetic service, because a caller retrieves an explicitly internal marker. A real severity depends on reachable assets, metadata protocol requirements and the tool's permissions. Credential exposure is not established: the mock deliberately contains no credential, and no real cloud endpoint is contacted. No system compromise is claimed.

docs.title: Remediation and verified-fix matrix
docs.text: Control Tier and artifact Verification limit Scheme, port, userinfo and exact-host restrictions T3 unit negative corpus Restrictive parser contract, not exhaustive URL fuzzing Private, loopback, link-local, shared and metadata-address denial T3 address classifier plus DNS corpus Some cases are pure function checks; no packets sent Resolve all answers and bind connection T3 injected resolver/transport External TLS branch not network-tested Redirect denial and response cap T4 paired HTTP tests Redirects are unsupported, not selectively permitted Tool cannot directly reach metadata T3 actual Docker TCP attempt Host and gateway are trusted Scoped short-lived credentials Not applicable to this fixture No downstream credential exists; real adapters must acquire resource-specific credentials and avoid forwarding caller tokens Structured audit logging T2 emitted events No durable collector or SIEM integration tested

docs.title: Regression tests and detection engineering
docs.text:
Unit cases cover address classes, parser restrictions, empty allowlists, DNS-empty, mixed-answer and pin-mismatch failure. The Compose runner supplies the six paired HTTP cases. Detection predicates are executable:

python3 vulnerability-research/detection.py --test

A denied fetch is a blocked-attempt signal, not proof of malicious intent. Deduplicate tool/gateway events using a propagated correlation ID in a real integration; this lab generates separate IDs. Monitor gateway health and expected canary delivery independently of denials. Never interpret zero events as zero SSRF. A future SIEM integration should alert on denied destinations/redirects and unusual fetch frequency, while retaining reason codes rather than query/body data.

docs.title: Compensating controls, operations and residual capability
docs.text: Separate the gateway's administration, deny arbitrary tool egress, remove ambient cloud roles, and cap body size and request duration. Use a dedicated read-only content service when arbitrary URLs are unnecessary. Fail closed on DNS/gateway errors; do not restore availability by granting a general proxy path. Log minimal metadata and impose retention/access controls. An attacker may still fetch permitted content, consume bounded resources, or exploit a defect in an allowed destination.

docs.title: Limitations and what was not tested
docs.text: No LLM, real MCP server/client, OAuth exchange, real credentials, external HTTPS, DNS server rebinding, IPv6 Docker routing, host firewall, cloud metadata protocol, service-mesh bypass, compression bomb or production rate/load test was executed. Socket timeouts are per operation, not a proven total request deadline. Availability, time to detect/contain and monthly operational cost are not measured in this lab. Review status remains requires-review pending an independent evidence review.

docs.title: Open questions
docs.text: Can the external TLS branch retain pinning across certificate rotation and IPv6? What total deadline prevents a slow-byte origin from monopolizing workers? Does a production gateway prevent alternate resolver/proxy routes? Can correlation survive a gateway failure without recording destination content?

docs.title: References
docs.text:
Consulted 2026-11-02; the OWASP and MCP pages are living guidance, not new CVE advisories.

  • OWASP SSRF Prevention Cheat Sheet
  • MCP security best practices under 2025-11-25 documentation
  • Python 3.13 ipaddress semantics

docs.title: Reproduce the URL-fetch SSRF experiment
docs.text: Status: partially tested. Real isolated HTTP and TCP paths are tested; DNS and external TLS connection selection use injected fixtures. Read the study for threat model, findings and untested bypass surfaces.

docs.title: Objective, architecture and safety
docs.text:
Compare an ambient fetcher to a tool whose only destination-capable path is a separate gateway. Assets are synthetic markers, not credentials. A caller controls URLs and redirects. The secure tool trusts the gateway/Docker host and has no network attachment to the metadata fixture.

flowchart LR
  T[Test runner] --> V[Vulnerable tool]
  T --> S[Secure tool]
  S --> G[Gateway]
  V --> M[Mock metadata]
  V --> P[Public surrogate]
  G --> P
  P -->|Redirect, denied at gateway| M

Prerequisites: Docker Engine, Compose, Python 3.13+ for optional host unit checks, and about 256 MiB of memory. Image builds download a pinned Python patch image; application code has no third-party dependencies. All networks are internal; no ports, host paths, Docker socket, cloud identities or production data are exposed. Subnet 172.28.190.0/24 must be free. If it conflicts, change both Compose fixed addresses and LAB_PUBLIC_IP/test_egress.py together.

docs.title: Setup and validation — tested
docs.text:
From the repository root:

python3 vulnerability-research/mcp-tool-ssrf/lab/test_fetcher.py
docker compose -p research-ssrf -f vulnerability-research/mcp-tool-ssrf/lab/compose.yaml config --quiet
docker compose -p research-ssrf -f vulnerability-research/mcp-tool-ssrf/lab/compose.yaml up -d --build vulnerable secure gateway public metadata
docker compose -p research-ssrf -f vulnerability-research/mcp-tool-ssrf/lab/compose.yaml run --build --rm tests
docker compose -p research-ssrf -f vulnerability-research/mcp-tool-ssrf/lab/compose.yaml exec -T secure python test_egress.py

Expected: six unit test methods pass; six paired HTTP cases pass; direct TCP bypass is denied. All harnesses fail nonzero on unexpected decisions. Run the HTTP cases before the TCP test so a stopped metadata fixture cannot be mistaken for network isolation. The image entrypoint listens only inside its private networks.

compose.yaml supplies both configurations in one isolated experiment. Their code paths live in fetcher.py; fixtures.py supplies the origins. Do not deploy either teaching server as a public proxy. The default generic policy has an empty allowlist; only the explicit synthetic origin is permitted in Compose.

docs.title: Collect evidence
docs.text:
mkdir -p .artifacts/research
docker compose -p research-ssrf -f vulnerability-research/mcp-tool-ssrf/lab/compose.yaml run --build --rm tests > .artifacts/research/ssrf-http.txt
docker compose -p research-ssrf -f vulnerability-research/mcp-tool-ssrf/lab/compose.yaml logs --no-log-prefix secure gateway > .artifacts/research/ssrf-decisions.jsonl
python3 vulnerability-research/detection.py < .artifacts/research/ssrf-decisions.jsonl

Review raw evidence before sharing. Events intentionally omit URLs, queries, headers and fetched bodies. Request IDs are local, not a durable cross-service trace. TTD/TTC, public TLS, real DNS rebinding and cloud metadata remain untested. No cloud cost is incurred; local image/disk/CPU use is the resource cost.

docs.title: Teardown — tested
docs.text:
docker compose -p research-ssrf -f vulnerability-research/mcp-tool-ssrf/lab/compose.yaml down --volumes --remove-orphans

Remove retained .artifacts/research/ssrf-* files after reviewing your evidence. Images/build cache remain local and can be removed through Docker's image manager.

docs.title: Vulnerability-research methodology
docs.text: Use an owned target with a minimal failure mechanism. State the precondition, request, expected result and state invariant before writing the fix. A controlled misuse case belongs in the suite only if it answers a defender's boundary question.

docs.title: Experimental sequence
docs.text:
1. Map the actor's controllable inputs and the target's ambient authority.
  2. Seed synthetic users, records, origins or policies. Generate session material only at runtime; never print or commit it.
  3. Execute the misuse against the intentionally vulnerable path. Capture the response and independently assert the intended state change or disclosure.
  4. Apply the smallest boundary change and rerun the identical case from fresh state.
  5. Assert both rejection and absence of a side effect. Include legitimate operations so a control that denies everything cannot pass the experiment.
  6. Test missing context, stale context, alternate endpoints and lower-layer bypasses.
  7. Record versions, commands, exit status, sanitized evidence and untested surfaces.
  8. Review references and residual capabilities before making a severity statement.

docs.title: Evidence and scope
docs.text:
Use T0–T4 tiers for every major claim. Observed, likely, assumed, not established and not tested have distinct meanings. A model's verdict is evidence about that model. A mocked Terraform plan is not evidence that a cloud token was exchanged or a cloud API was denied. A local HTTP comparison is not a third-party product assessment.

Severity is qualitative and specific to the synthetic assets, actor and operations. No CVSS score or advisory ID is assigned to a teaching target. Business impact is an inference requiring the stated real-world asset assumptions.

docs.title: Isolation and evidence retention
docs.text:
The SSRF topology has only Docker internal networks and no published ports. The BOLA runner uses container loopback and network_mode: none. Keep both on a workstation reserved for local testing. Do not add host networking, a Docker socket, real datasets or cloud credentials. Terraform commands stop at validation and mock plans. Downloading dependencies requires internet access; the targets do not.

Keep raw generated evidence under ignored .artifacts/research/, review it for sensitive values, and retain only sanitized summaries in source control. Correlate by generated request ID; do not retain cookies, raw assertion bytes, URL queries or response bodies in audit events. Delete containers, volumes and evidence after use.

docs.title: Verification record — 2026-11-02
docs.text: This record covers local source, owned targets and offline models. Cloud deployment, production access, real third-party vulnerability testing and a public-site rollout were not performed. The validation results below were observed on the working branch before PR creation.

docs.title: Observed lab results
docs.text:
• SSRF: six unit methods; six paired isolated HTTP cases; secure-container direct TCP access to the live mock metadata fixture denied.
  • BOLA: two test methods containing 14 paired HTTP cases and additional session/role/context checks. State assertions accompany denial and misuse tests.
  • CI/CD identity: Terraform schema validation, three mocked plans and 28 exported policy/local signed-assertion decisions. No STS call.
  • Azure: AzureRM schema validation and three mocked-plan tests. No Azure API call.
  • PostgreSQL: SQL runtime/boundary/catalog suites and pg 8.22.0 pool tests pass; containers and disposable storage are removed by the runner.
  • OPA: native 1.17.0 runs for secure, insecure, unknown and deleted-control fixtures.
  • Kyverno: native 1.18.2 pod policy: seven tests passed, zero failed. Darwin ARM64 archive SHA-256 matched the release checksum: cc69bc6638da1993146c134943fac91cbc9dd0ce60a3e88c6d7c518ae00f1abc. Checksum comparison does not claim Sigstore signature verification.
  • Lifecycle: six methods include deterministic freshness and zero-execution assertions. Detection predicates: nine labeled synthetic events.

docs.title: Scope and remaining checks
docs.text:
No LLM/MCP transport, real cloud metadata, actual DNS rebinding server, external TLS destination, AWS/Azure token exchange, production secret rotation, real refund, live CNI, hosted release or Sentinel alert was executed. Retained research/source inspection claims require independent source review and remain requires-review.

The lab audit maps commands to proof limits. The deployment review records the main/gh-pages boundary. This branch is intended for a PR into main; publication follows merge and the gated artifact workflow.

GitHub's existing full-history Gitleaks job remains required before publication

The four updated visual baselines were inspected: mobile article evidence status, article navigation/scrolled content, and the compatible Mermaid runtime update. Screenshots and raw local logs are retained under ignored .artifacts/ rather than published as unsanitized evidence. The published lifecycle JSON endpoint is now copied from the same canonical registry and checked against it by the HTML suite. Interpreter cache files are excluded from canonical source hashing.

docs.title: Runtime and review limitations
docs.text:
The recorded host used Node.js 24.22.0, Terraform 1.16.5, Docker Engine 29.8.0 and Compose 5.5.1 on macOS ARM64. Container HTTP targets use Python 3.13.9 and a pinned image digest. AWS provider 6.20.0 and AzureRM 4.50.0 are locked; dependency initialization requires downloads even though cloud validation makes no provider API calls. The existing content-quality workflow was found automatically disabled for inactivity. It was re-enabled and dispatched against this branch for hosted Ubuntu/Node/Python verification. Check the linked PR/run result independently of the recorded host run. Publication still requires a push to main.

Five low-severity transitive documentation-tool advisories remain in npm audit; the compatible lock refresh and explicit parser overrides leave zero moderate, high or critical advisories in that audit result. This is dependency metadata, not an exploitability assessment or a claim that the toolchain is vulnerability-free. No major-version dependency migration is implied.

Six pre-existing freshness warnings remain for domain overviews and certification notes. Five pre-existing References-section warnings remain for archived/tutorial/ certification material outside the maintained research set. They are not reported as independently reviewed. This work adds protocols to all 21 maintained research articles and retains conservative review status. PowerShell scripts were parsed; the PostgreSQL integration was executed through the POSIX runner, not PowerShell.

docs.title: Observed configuration
docs.text:
• GitHub Pages API: build_type: legacy, source.branch: gh-pages, source.path: /, custom domain docs.jasonachkardiab.com.
  • .github/workflows/content-quality.yml runs quality, secret scanning and a canonical MkDocs build. PR runs produce artifacts without publication.
  • deploy-docs runs only on a push to main, depends on all three checks, and downloads verified-docs-${github.sha}. It does not rebuild at publication.
  • scripts/publish-gh-pages.sh replaces the isolated publication checkout with that artifact and commits only generated files to gh-pages.
  • docs-pipeline.json and the MkDocs hook map canonical Markdown into the site; publishing/content-status.json governs route lifecycle and indexability.

These are T1 configuration observations, not evidence of a successful deployment of the changes in this branch. The read-only Pages settings check was:

gh api repos/jasonachkar/cybersecurity-writeups/pages

docs.title: Workflow activation
docs.text: The workflow registry reported content-quality.yml as disabled_inactivity before hosted verification. It was re-enabled for branch validation as part of this work. A workflow_dispatch against research-depth-upgrade exercises the checks; the publication job still requires a push to main. The separate legacy Pages workflow serves the generated gh-pages branch.

Change Destination Research, methodology, labs, tests, navigation, build inputs research-depth-upgrade → PR into main Rendered HTML, search index, sitemap, copied assets, manifest and CNAME CI-generated gh-pages commit after merge Cloud resources No deployment authorized or performed by this work

Preserve existing URLs, lifecycle records, custom domain, search and sitemap. Mount new source roots through both the canonical inventory and MkDocs hook. Check the built routes and local HTML links before proposing a merge.

docs.title: About this site
docs.text: I'm Jason Achkar Diab. This repository contains my cybersecurity research, labs, scripts, and study notes across cloud security, application security, DevSecOps, and threat intelligence.

docs.title: How it is organized
docs.text:
• Research documents a security decision or architecture question and states what was tested versus what remains conceptual.
  • Labs exercise bounded decisions locally with positive and negative fixtures.
  • Scripts are small tools or packages developed alongside the research.
  • Study notes summarize official certification material; they are not implementation evidence.

docs.title: Research methodology
docs.text:
Markdown, metadata, examples, and the documentation build are validated on main. The staged site includes a source-and-artifact manifest, and publication is blocked whenever canonical routes or lifecycle classifications drift.

Article source metadata records the implementation scope, review state, and source quality. The articles and linked labs describe what was tested and what remains illustrative. A current review date is not itself proof that the guidance is correct: material remains marked requires-review until it has been checked against its declared validatedAgainst sources.

The research methodology defines evidence tiers, claim scope, measurements and testable open questions. The vulnerability studies compare owned local targets and fixes without claiming third-party product findings.

Passing repository checks means the documented local tests behaved as expected. It does not claim that every design was deployed to a live environment.

The publishing flow is deliberately one-way: canonical inputs are validated on main, and only the resulting verified static artifact is written to gh-pages.

flowchart TD
    SOURCE["Canonical Markdown, metadata, and source"] --> CATALOG["Catalog and deterministic build"]
    CATALOG --> QA["Content, security, UI, visual, and accessibility checks"]
    QA --> SITE["Verified static artifact"]
    SITE --> PAGES["Generated gh-pages branch"]
